items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
**Source check:** the linked pages were identified by title match; PubMed abstracts could not be opened in this session, so every figure below is from memory and should be checked against the paper before you quote it. Links marked DOI are from memory.

## 8.1 Perioperative risk and cardiac protection (Topic 1)

| Trial | Design | Key result | Exam message | Source check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [POISE](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18479744/) (Lancet 2008) | RCT, 8,351 patients, non-cardiac surgery; metoprolol CR 100 mg pre-op then 200 mg daily vs placebo | Fewer MIs (3.6 vs 5.1%) and lower composite of cardiac death, MI, arrest (5.8 vs 6.9%), but more deaths (3.1 vs 2.3%), stroke (1.0 vs 0.5%) and hypotension | Do not start high-dose beta-blocker on the day of surgery; continue chronic therapy | From memory |
| [POISE-2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24679062/) (NEJM 2014) | 2x2 factorial RCT, about 10,000 patients; aspirin vs placebo, clonidine vs placebo | Aspirin: no reduction in death or MI (about 7% both arms), more major bleeding. Clonidine: no benefit, more hypotension and non-fatal cardiac arrest | Do not start aspirin or clonidine for perioperative protection; continue aspirin in stented patients | From memory |
| [POISE-3](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36053523/) (NEJM 2022) | 2x2 factorial RCT, about 9,500 patients; tranexamic acid vs placebo, plus hypotension-avoidance vs hypertension-avoidance strategy | TXA reduced composite bleeding (about 9 vs 12%) but non-inferiority for the composite vascular safety outcome was not established. The BP-strategy arm was reported separately | TXA reduces bleeding in major surgery; BP management has no simple trial-proven target | From memory; BP-strategy paper not located |
| [CARP](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15625331/) (NEJM 2004) | RCT, 510 patients with stable CAD before vascular surgery; revascularisation vs none | No difference in long-term mortality (about 22 vs 23%) or perioperative MI | No prophylactic revascularisation in stable CAD | From memory |
| [VISION troponin cohort](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28444280/) (JAMA 2017) | Prospective cohort, about 21,800 patients; peak postoperative hs-troponin T | 30-day mortality rises stepwise with peak troponin (about 4% at 20 to under 65 ng/L, about 9% at 65 to under 1,000 ng/L) | Defines MINS; justifies routine troponin surveillance in at-risk patients | From memory |
| [MANAGE report](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31629536/) (Lancet 2018) | RCT, about 1,750 patients with MINS; dabigatran 110 mg twice daily vs placebo | Fewer major vascular complications (about 11 vs 15%) without an increase in major bleeding | Treatment option for MINS; evidence limited by early stopping | From memory; confirm the original paper |
| [STOP-or-NOT](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39212270/) (JAMA 2024) | RCT, about 2,200 patients; continue vs stop ACEi/ARB 48 h before major surgery | No significant difference in the composite of death and major complications; more intraoperative hypotension with continuation | Either approach acceptable; withholding is reasonable in hypertensive patients | From memory |
| [METS](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30070222/) (Lancet 2018) | Prospective cohort, about 1,400 patients before major surgery | Subjective functional capacity did a poor job of predicting events; DASI and NT-proBNP predicted death or MI | Use DASI and BNP rather than clinical impression | From memory |
| [RCRI (Lee)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10477528/) (Circulation 1999) | Derivation and validation cohort | Six predictors; risk of major cardiac complication climbs with each | The standard bedside risk index | From memory |

## 8.2 Acute MI, cardiogenic shock and supportive care (Topic 2)

| Trial | Design | Key result | Exam message | Source check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [SHOCK](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10460813/) (NEJM 1999) | RCT, 302 patients with MI shock; early revascularisation vs initial medical stabilisation | 30-day mortality 46.7 vs 56.0% (not significant); 6-month mortality 50.3 vs 63.1% | Emergency revascularisation is the key treatment | From memory |
| [IABP-SHOCK II](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22920912/) (NEJM 2012) | RCT, 600 patients; IABP vs none | 30-day mortality 39.7 vs 41.3% | No routine IABP in MI shock | From memory |
| [CULPRIT-SHOCK](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29083953/) (NEJM 2017) | RCT, about 700 patients with multivessel disease; culprit-only PCI vs immediate multivessel PCI | Death or renal replacement at 30 days lower with culprit-only (45.9 vs 55.4%) | Treat the culprit vessel only in shock | From memory |
| [DanGer Shock](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38587239/) (NEJM 2024) | RCT, 360 STEMI-shock patients; Impella CP plus standard care vs standard care | 180-day mortality 45.8 vs 58.5%; more bleeding, limb ischaemia and renal replacement | Impella helps in selected STEMI shock (no coma, LV-predominant) | From memory |
| [ECLS-SHOCK](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307227) (NEJM 2023, DOI from memory) | RCT, 420 patients; early VA-ECMO vs standard care | 30-day mortality 47.8 vs 49.0%; more bleeding and vascular complications | VA-ECMO does not routinely improve survival in MI shock | From memory |
| [SOAP II](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20200382/) (NEJM 2010) | RCT, 1,679 patients with shock; dopamine vs noradrenaline | No overall mortality difference; more arrhythmias with dopamine; higher mortality in the cardiogenic shock subgroup with dopamine | Noradrenaline first line | From memory |
| [DETO2X-AMI](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28844200/) (NEJM 2017) | RCT, about 6,600 normoxic patients with suspected MI; oxygen vs room air | One-year mortality about 5% in both arms | No oxygen if SpO2 is 90% or more | From memory |
| [MINT](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37952133/) (NEJM 2023) | RCT, about 3,500 patients with MI and anaemia; restrictive vs liberal transfusion | Death or recurrent MI at 30 days: 16.9% restrictive vs 14.5% liberal (not significant, favours liberal) | Do not be aggressive about restrictive thresholds in acute MI | From memory |

## 8.3 Heart failure and pulmonary oedema (Topics 3 and 5)

| Trial | Design | Key result | Exam message | Source check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [PARADIGM-HF](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25176015/) (NEJM 2014) | RCT, about 8,400 HFrEF patients; sacubitril-valsartan vs enalapril | CV death or HF hospitalisation 21.8 vs 26.5% | ARNI is first-line in HFrEF | From memory |
| [DAPA-HF](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31535829/) (NEJM 2019) | RCT, about 4,700 HFrEF patients; dapagliflozin vs placebo | Worsening HF or CV death 16.3 vs 21.2%, benefit with or without diabetes | SGLT2 inhibitors for HFrEF; hold before surgery | From memory |
| [EMPEROR-Reduced](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32865377/) (NEJM 2020) | RCT, about 3,700 HFrEF patients; empagliflozin vs placebo | CV death or HF hospitalisation 19.4 vs 24.7% | Confirms SGLT2 inhibitor benefit | From memory |
| [DOSE](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21366472/) (NEJM 2011) | RCT, 308 patients with acute decompensated HF; bolus vs infusion and low vs high furosemide dose | No significant difference in symptom score; high dose gave more decongestion and more transient creatinine rise | Dose and mode of loop diuretic matter less than giving enough | From memory |
| [ESCAPE](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.294.13.1625) (JAMA 2005, DOI from memory) | RCT, about 430 patients with advanced HF; PAC-guided vs clinically guided therapy | No difference in days alive and out of hospital; more adverse events with PAC | No routine PAC in acute HF | From memory |
| [3CPO](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18987377/) (NEJM 2008) | RCT, about 1,070 patients with acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; CPAP or NIV vs standard oxygen | 7-day mortality about 9.5 vs 9.8% (not significant); faster relief of dyspnoea and acidosis | NIV or CPAP helps symptoms; mortality benefit unproven | From memory |

## 8.4 Valves, anticoagulation and cardiomyopathy (Topics 4 and 6)

| Trial | Design | Key result | Exam message | Source check |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [PARTNER 3](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1814052) (NEJM 2019, DOI from memory) | RCT, about 1,000 low-risk AS patients; TAVI (SAPIEN 3) vs surgery | Death, stroke or rehospitalisation at 1 year 8.5 vs 15.1% | TAVI is an option in low-risk AS | From memory |
| [COAPT](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30280640/) (NEJM 2018) | RCT, 614 HF patients with secondary MR; MitraClip plus medical therapy vs medical therapy | HF hospitalisation 35.8 vs 67.9 per 100 patient-years; 24-month mortality 29.1 vs 46.1% | Edge-to-edge repair in carefully selected secondary MR | From memory |
| [BRIDGE](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1501035) (NEJM 2015, DOI from memory) | RCT, about 1,900 AF patients on warfarin; LMWH bridging vs placebo | Thromboembolism 0.4 vs 0.3% (non-inferior without bridging); major bleeding 1.3 vs 3.2% | No bridging for most AF patients; mechanical valves were excluded | From memory |
| [INVICTUS](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36449436/) (NEJM 2022) | RCT, about 4,500 AF patients with rheumatic heart disease; rivaroxaban vs VKA | Higher rate of the composite outcome and death with rivaroxaban | VKA remains standard in rheumatic AF and moderate to severe MS | From memory |
| [EXPLORER-HCM](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(20)31792-X) (Lancet 2020, DOI from memory) | RCT, 251 symptomatic obstructive HCM patients; mavacamten vs placebo | Primary functional composite met by 37 vs 17% | Myosin inhibitor lowers LVOT gradient and improves function | From memory |

items.title: 4. Valvular heart disease
items.los: IT_PO 1.4 (valvular heart disease component); SS_CS 1.4 (valve pathology component)
items.body:
## 4.1 General principles

- Stenotic lesions are **fixed-output** states and are poorly tolerated by vasodilation, tachycardia and hypovolaemia. Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (AS) and mitral stenosis (MS) carry the highest perioperative risk.
- Regurgitant lesions are volume-loaded and tolerate vasodilation, with moderate tachycardia, better than stenotic lesions.
- Acute valve failure (acute MR, AR) is far worse than chronic disease because the ventricle has not adapted.
- Preoperative assessment aims to define severity, symptoms, ventricular function, pulmonary pressures, rhythm, and anticoagulation.
- Elective non-cardiac surgery should be deferred for severe symptomatic stenosis until the valve is treated (surgical or transcatheter) unless the surgery is urgent.
- Endocarditis prophylaxis (AHA 2021 / Australian Therapeutic Guidelines): indicated only for dental procedures with gingival manipulation in the highest-risk group: prosthetic valve or material, previous endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic congenital disease, repaired congenital disease with prosthetic material within 6 months, and cardiac transplant valvulopathy. Not routinely required for GI or GU procedures.

## 4.2 Overview of severity and haemodynamics

| Lesion | Severe criteria (echo) | Ventricular response | Core haemodynamic goals |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aortic stenosis | AV area below 1.0 cm2 (indexed below 0.6), mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, peak velocity 4 m/s or more, dimensionless index below 0.25. Low-flow low-gradient forms exist | Concentric LVH, diastolic dysfunction, high LVEDP, subendocardial ischaemia | Preload full, rate 60 to 80 (sinus rhythm vital), afterload and SVR maintained, contractility preserved |
| Aortic regurgitation | Regurgitant volume 60 mL or more, fraction 50% or more, EROA 0.3 cm2 or more, vena contracta above 0.6 cm, pressure half-time below 200 ms, holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta | Eccentric dilatation (chronic); wide pulse pressure | Preload full, rate high-normal (80 to 100: shortens diastole), afterload low, contractility maintained |
| Mitral stenosis | MV area 1.5 cm2 or less (progressive MS 1.5 to 2 / severe below 1.5), mean gradient above 10 mmHg at HR 60 to 80, pressure half-time 150 ms or more | LA dilatation, AF, pulmonary hypertension, RV failure; normal LV | Preload adequate not excessive, rate slow (60 to 80, long diastole), sinus rhythm, keep SVR, avoid rises in PVR |
| Mitral regurgitation | EROA 0.4 cm2 or more, regurgitant volume 60 mL or more, vena contracta 0.7 cm or more, systolic flow reversal in pulmonary veins | LV dilatation, normal or low-normal EF 'flatters' LV (EF below 60% already indicates dysfunction) | Preload full, rate normal-to-high (80 to 100), afterload low, avoid raised SVR, support RV |
| Tricuspid | Rare in isolation | RV and RA overload | Maintain preload, avoid raised PVR |

> **Figure (diagram not reproduced):** valve lesions by heart rate and afterload goal. Rate and afterload goals split valve lesions into two groups; preload is kept full in all of them.

## 4.3 Aortic stenosis (most examinable)

**Aetiology:** age-related calcific degeneration (most common), bicuspid valve (younger patients), rheumatic. **Natural history:** long asymptomatic phase with slow progression (peak velocity rises about 0.3 m/s, mean gradient 7 mmHg per year, valve area falls about 0.1 cm2 per year); after the onset of symptoms, mean survival falls steeply: **angina about 5 years, syncope about 3 years, heart failure about 1 to 2 years**; high risk of sudden death once symptomatic.

**Echocardiographic features of haemodynamically significant AS:**

| Feature | Finding |
|---|---|
| Valve morphology | Thickened, calcified leaflets with restricted opening; bicuspid appearance in PLAX or SAX (TOE short axis at 30 to 60 degrees) |
| Peak velocity (CW Doppler through the valve) | 4.0 m/s or more (severe); 3.0 to 3.9 moderate |
| Mean gradient | 40 mmHg or more (severe) |
| Valve area (continuity equation) | AVA = (LVOT area x LVOT VTI) / AV VTI; below 1.0 cm2 severe |
| Dimensionless index (DVI) | LVOT VTI / AV VTI below 0.25 |
| LV | Concentric LVH, preserved or reduced EF, diastolic dysfunction (E/e' raised) |
| Other | Post-stenotic aortic root dilation, MR, LA enlargement, pulmonary hypertension (late) |
| Low-flow low-gradient AS | AVA below 1.0 cm2 with mean gradient below 40, EF below 50% or stroke volume index below 35 mL/m2 (paradoxical). Use dobutamine stress echo or CT calcium score (above 1,300 AU women, above 2,000 AU men) |

**Pathophysiology:** fixed LV outflow obstruction leads to concentric hypertrophy, raised LVEDP, increased wall tension and O2 demand, and reduced coronary flow reserve from elevated LVEDP and low DBP (subendocardial ischaemia in the absence of coronary disease). Loss of atrial kick (AF, junctional rhythm) causes sudden decompensation. Stroke volume cannot rise, so cardiac output depends on heart rate and rhythm.

**Anaesthetic management of severe AS:**

- Avoid the three killers: **hypotension, tachycardia, and loss of sinus rhythm**. Aim for HR 60 to 80, SR, MAP at or above baseline (65 to 70 minimum), euvolaemia to slightly full.
- Vasopressor first (phenylephrine, metaraminol, noradrenaline) at induction and during neuraxial block; avoid pure vasodilators. Pre-emptive vasopressor infusion.
- Defibrillator pads on; treat AF or SVT with early synchronised cardioversion.
- GA with controlled induction and slow titration; avoid spinal single-shot block (rapid sympathectomy); slow epidural or CSE and low-dose spinal with infusion of vasopressors have been used in selected cases.
- Invasive arterial line before induction; consider TOE for major surgery.
- Postoperative HDU.
- If severe symptomatic AS requires urgent non-cardiac surgery, balloon aortic valvuloplasty or TAVI may be considered as a bridge (see trials).

**Management of the valve:** SAVR (low surgical risk, age below 65 to 70) or TAVI (PARTNER 1, 3; SURTAVI; Evolut Low Risk) for symptomatic severe AS; mechanical vs bioprosthetic valve choice influences anticoagulation.

## 4.4 Aortic regurgitation

**Aetiology:** valve disease (bicuspid, rheumatic, endocarditis) or root dilatation (Marfan, hypertension, ankylosing spondylitis, aortic dissection).

**Pathophysiology:** volume overload, eccentric hypertrophy, large stroke volume with wide pulse pressure (peripheral signs: collapsing pulse, de Musset, Quincke), low DBP and reduced coronary perfusion. Acute AR (endocarditis, dissection): LV cannot dilate, so LVEDP rises, premature MV closure, pulmonary oedema and shock.

**Anaesthetic goals:** keep HR **80 to 100** (shortens diastole, reducing regurgitant time), avoid bradycardia (increases regurgitant volume per beat), maintain preload, **reduce SVR** (vasodilators help), maintain contractility. Avoid IABP (contraindicated).

## 4.5 Mitral stenosis

**Aetiology:** rheumatic heart disease (dominant in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Maori and Pacific communities in Australasia), calcific degeneration, congenital.

**Pathophysiology:** obstruction between LA and LV raises LA pressure, then pulmonary venous and arterial pressure, causing pulmonary congestion, pulmonary hypertension and RV failure. The LV is underfilled with preserved EF. **Heart rate dictates filling time:** tachycardia shortens diastole, raising the gradient (gradient depends on flow and diastolic time squared) and LA pressure, causing APO. AF is common (loss of atrial kick, thromboembolism, stroke).

**Perioperative management (including laparoscopic surgery):**

| Issue | Approach |
|---|---|
| Severity | Echo (mean gradient, MVA, PASP), symptoms (dyspnoea, orthopnoea, haemoptysis, embolism). Severe symptomatic MS should be treated (balloon valvotomy or surgery) before elective surgery |
| Rate and rhythm | Continue beta-blocker or diltiazem/digoxin for rate control; avoid premedication that causes anxiety and tachycardia. AF with rapid ventricular response: cardiovert if unstable; beta-blocker or amiodarone; avoid pure inotropes |
| Anticoagulation | AF with MS, or LA thrombus: warfarin (not DOACs in moderate-to-severe rheumatic MS: INVICTUS trial favoured VKA). Bridging as per CHEST 2022 |
| Preload | Maintain; avoid fluid overload (small increments) |
| PVR | Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, nitrous oxide, lung hyperinflation; the RV must not fail |
| SVR | Maintain; avoid vasodilatation (neuraxial block with caution) |
| Pneumoperitoneum | Raised intrathoracic pressure, reduced venous return, CO2 absorption increasing PVR, steep head-down raises LA pressure; use low insufflation pressure (10 to 12 mmHg) and gentle positioning. This patient may be better off with open or regional/field technique depending on severity |
| Monitoring | Arterial line, large-bore access, CVP or PAC are of limited value (PCWP overestimates LVEDP in MS), TOE |
| Drugs | Avoid ketamine and pancuronium (tachycardia); use remifentanil or fentanyl for the pressor response; sugammadex preferred to neostigmine/atropine (reduces tachycardia) |
| Postoperative | HDU; analgesia; early extubation with careful reversal |

## 4.6 Mitral regurgitation

**Primary (degenerative: prolapse, flail, endocarditis, rheumatic) vs secondary (functional: LV dilatation, ischaemic).** Severity depends on the loading conditions, so measure the regurgitation under anaesthesia. Chronic severe MR leads to LA dilatation (large compliance) and AF, then pulmonary hypertension.

**Assessment:** define the mechanism (Carpentier type I normal motion with annular dilation or perforation, II prolapse or flail, IIIa restricted in diastole, IIIb restricted in systole), severity by an integrated approach (EROA, regurgitant volume, vena contracta, pulmonary vein flow reversal), and the consequences: LV size and function, LA size, rhythm (AF), PASP and RV function. In chronic severe MR the LV ejects into a low-pressure LA, which **flatters the ejection fraction**: an EF of 60% or less, or an end-systolic diameter of 40 mm or more, already signals LV dysfunction. BNP and exercise tolerance help detect decompensation.

**Haemodynamic goals:**

| Variable | Goal | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Preload | Maintain; avoid both hypovolaemia and overload | Regurgitant volume depends on LA and LV filling |
| Heart rate | Normal to slightly fast (80 to 100) | Shorter diastole and smaller LV reduce the regurgitant orifice and volume |
| Afterload | Keep SVR low to normal | Vasoconstriction increases regurgitant fraction; vasodilators promote forward flow |
| Contractility | Maintain or support | A failing LV loses the low-impedance escape into the LA |
| Rhythm | Rate-control AF; keep sinus rhythm where possible | Loss of atrial contribution reduces filling |
| Pulmonary vascular resistance | Keep low | Pulmonary hypertension from chronic LA hypertension threatens RV function |

**Pulmonary hypertension and RV protection in MR:** avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia, pain and light anaesthesia, avoid nitrous oxide and high airway pressures, maintain PaCO2 35 to 40 mmHg and pH above 7.35, and keep PEEP modest. Use inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (nitric oxide or epoprostenol) or milrinone when pressures are high, support the RV with dobutamine or milrinone, and maintain systemic pressure above pulmonary artery pressure with noradrenaline or vasopressin to preserve RV coronary perfusion.

**Technique and monitoring:**

- Either general anaesthesia (opioid-based balanced technique; avoid agents that cause bradycardia or marked myocardial depression) or a carefully titrated neuraxial or regional technique are acceptable; neuraxial block reduces afterload and is usually well tolerated in MR, unlike in stenotic lesions.
- Arterial line, large-bore access and ECG with ST analysis; TOE for major surgery and for any instability, because intraoperative loading conditions change the degree of regurgitation (and ischaemic or functional MR is dynamic).
- Treat intraoperative hypotension with agents that avoid raising SVR excessively (small doses of noradrenaline or vasopressin plus inotrope if the LV is failing); avoid bradycardia.
- Acute severe MR (papillary muscle rupture, endocarditis, chordal rupture) presents with pulmonary oedema and shock and needs afterload reduction (nitroprusside), inotropes, IABP support and urgent surgery.

## 4.7 Prosthetic valves and anticoagulation

| Type | Antithrombotic therapy | Key points |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanical AVR (bileaflet, no risk factors) | Warfarin INR 2.5 (range 2.0 to 3.0) | Lifelong |
| Mechanical AVR with risk factors (AF, previous thromboembolism, LV dysfunction, hypercoagulable) or older-generation valve | INR 3.0 (2.5 to 3.5) | |
| Mechanical MVR | INR 3.0 (2.5 to 3.5) | Higher thrombotic risk than AVR |
| Bioprosthetic | Aspirin or warfarin 3 to 6 months after surgery | |
| TAVI | Aspirin; short DAPT or DOAC only if indicated | |
| DOAC | Contraindicated with mechanical valves (RE-ALIGN, dabigatran) | |

**Perioperative anticoagulation for a warfarinised patient with a mechanical valve:** stop warfarin 5 days before surgery (INR 1.5 or below for most surgery; neuraxial at INR below 1.4); **bridging with therapeutic LMWH or UFH is indicated for mechanical mitral valve, caged-ball or tilting disc valve, mechanical valve with a stroke or TIA in the last 6 months, or AF with multiple risk factors**; bridging is not needed for bileaflet aortic valve without risk factors (BRIDGE trial in AF showed no benefit and more bleeding). Start heparin when INR falls below 2.0 (about day 2 to 3), last therapeutic LMWH dose 24 h before surgery (half dose if the surgery is major or neuraxial planned), restart the day after surgery when haemostasis is secure (48 to 72 h for high-bleeding-risk surgery).

**Reversal in an emergency:** vitamin K 1 to 2 mg IV is acceptable (avoid high dose, which makes re-warfarinisation difficult); prothrombin complex concentrate (25 to 50 units/kg) with vitamin K for life-threatening bleeding; FFP less preferred.

**Mechanical heart valves in pregnancy:**

- Highest-risk anticoagulation decision. Warfarin is the most effective for maternal valve protection but is teratogenic (embryopathy: weeks 6 to 12 and fetal bleeding), LMWH or UFH does not cross the placenta but has higher valve thrombosis risk (dose by anti-Xa peak 0.8 to 1.2 U/mL 4 to 6 h post dose, trough above 0.6).
- Options per ESC/ACC: warfarin throughout if dose 5 mg/day or less; LMWH or UFH in the first trimester (weeks 6 to 12) then warfarin from week 13 to week 36; at 36 weeks switch to LMWH or IV UFH; **stop LMWH 24 h before planned delivery** (or IV UFH 4 to 6 h before) for neuraxial block, or switch to IV UFH; recommence the heparin 6 to 12 h after delivery (neuraxial catheter removal at 12 h post prophylactic dose, 24 h after therapeutic); restart warfarin 24 to 48 h and bridge until INR therapeutic; warfarin and breastfeeding is compatible.
- Delivery planning with a multidisciplinary team (cardiology, obstetrics, anaesthesia, haematology) and avoid delivery on warfarin (fetal intracranial haemorrhage risk, preference for caesarean if on warfarin).

## 4.8 Assessment of valve disease (SS_CS 1.4)

| Modality | Information |
|---|---|
| Clinical | Murmur (AS: ejection systolic radiating to carotids; MR: pansystolic to axilla; MS: mid-diastolic rumble with opening snap; AR: early diastolic decrescendo), pulse character, S3/S4, JVP, signs of RV failure |
| ECG | LVH, AF, left atrial enlargement (P mitrale), conduction disease |
| Echo | Valve morphology and mobility, severity (above), chamber size, EF, PASP, RV function, vegetations; TOE for detail and intraoperative use |
| CMR / CT | Quantification of regurgitation; CT for TAVI planning and calcium scoring |
| Catheterisation | Haemodynamics when echo is discordant; coronary angiography before valve surgery |

**Intraoperative TOE views for valves:** ME 4-chamber, ME 2-chamber, ME LAX (MV), ME AV SAX (AV morphology), ME AV LAX (AR jet width, root), TG LAX and deep TG (CW Doppler gradient), colour Doppler jets. Use the Carpentier classification (Type I normal leaflet motion, II prolapse, III restricted: IIIa diastolic, IIIb systolic) for MR mechanism.

items.title: 5. Acute pulmonary oedema
items.body:
## 5.1 Pathophysiology

**Starling forces across the pulmonary capillary:** Jv = Kf x [(Pc - Pi) - sigma x (pi_c - pi_i)]. Oedema forms when capillary hydrostatic pressure rises, oncotic pressure falls, permeability rises (sigma falls, Kf rises), or lymphatic drainage is overwhelmed. Lymphatic flow can increase about tenfold before oedema forms, and the alveolar epithelium is the final barrier, so oedema appears in the interstitium (Kerley lines, peribronchial cuffing) before flooding alveoli.

| Category | Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Cardiogenic (haemostatic) | Raised pulmonary venous pressure (PAOP above 18 mmHg) | LV failure (ischaemia, hypertensive crisis, cardiomyopathy), MS, acute MR or AR, arrhythmia, fluid overload, renal failure |
| Non-cardiogenic (permeability) | Capillary leak, normal PAOP (18 mmHg or less) | ARDS, sepsis, aspiration, trauma, TRALI, pancreatitis |
| Mixed or other | Reduced oncotic pressure, lymphatic obstruction, negative pressure | Negative pressure pulmonary oedema (laryngospasm, airway obstruction), neurogenic, re-expansion, high-altitude, opioid or salicylate toxicity, upper-airway obstruction, TACO |

**Physiological consequences:** reduced compliance (increased work of breathing), shunt and V/Q mismatch (hypoxaemia), and increased sympathetic drive (hypertension, tachycardia, high afterload creates a vicious circle). Positive pressure acts by reducing venous return (preload), lowering LV transmural pressure (afterload), recruiting alveoli, and reducing work of breathing.

**Perioperative triggers:** fluid overload or TACO, myocardial ischaemia, new arrhythmia (AF), hypertensive crisis (emergence), negative pressure pulmonary oedema (after extubation with laryngospasm or airway obstruction; occurs in young, fit patients, resolves in 24 to 48 h), aspiration, anaphylaxis, TRALI or transfusion-associated circulatory overload, neurogenic oedema (subarachnoid haemorrhage, head injury), sepsis or SIRS, drug reaction (protamine), PE, and pre-eclampsia.

## 5.2 Clinical features and diagnosis

- **Symptoms:** acute breathlessness, orthopnoea, agitation, cough with pink frothy sputum.
- **Signs:** tachypnoea, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension (or shock), S3 gallop, bilateral crackles and wheeze ('cardiac asthma'), raised JVP, hypoxaemia.
- **Investigations:** ABG (hypoxaemia, type 1 then type 2 failure with fatigue), ECG (ischaemia, arrhythmia), troponin, BNP/NT-proBNP (high negative predictive value; raised in cardiac but also in renal failure and PE), CXR (bat-wing perihilar shadowing, cardiomegaly, Kerley B lines, effusions; non-cardiogenic oedema shows peripheral patchy shadows and normal heart size), lung ultrasound (B lines: 3 or more per field bilaterally), bedside echo (LV function, valves, IVC, effusion, E/e').

**Differential diagnosis of perioperative pulmonary oedema and acute dyspnoea with frothy secretions:**

| Diagnosis | Clues | Key action |
|---|---|---|
| Negative pressure pulmonary oedema | After laryngospasm or airway obstruction; young and fit; rapid onset | Relieve obstruction; oxygen with CPAP or PEEP; resolves in 12 to 48 h |
| Cardiogenic (LV failure, ischaemia, arrhythmia, valve lesion) | Cardiac history, hypertension, ECG change, raised troponin or BNP | Vasodilator, diuretic, treat ischaemia or rhythm |
| Fluid overload or TACO | Large positive balance, raised JVP, hypertension, responds to diuresis | Stop fluids, diuretic |
| Aspiration (gastric contents or blood) | Witnessed regurgitation or airway soiling; wheeze; focal infiltrate | Suction, oxygen, supportive ventilation |
| Anaphylaxis | Hypotension, bronchospasm, rash, recent drug exposure | Adrenaline; fluid; stop trigger |
| TRALI | Within 6 h of transfusion, fever, hypotension, bilateral infiltrates, normal or low BNP | Supportive (no diuretics); report to the blood service |
| Pulmonary embolism | Sudden hypoxia, tachycardia, raised ETCO2 gradient, right heart strain | See PE guidance |
| Bronchospasm or asthma | Wheeze, prolonged expiration, high peak pressures | Bronchodilators |
| Pneumothorax | Unilateral signs, hypotension, high airway pressure | Decompress |

Management follows the cause: secure the airway and oxygenation, apply CPAP or PEEP, obtain an ECG, troponin, chest X-ray or lung ultrasound, and treat the specific diagnosis.

## 5.3 Initial management (IT_RT 1.2, SS_IC 1.45)

**Principles:** sit upright, high-flow oxygen, early positive pressure, vasodilator, diuretic (if volume-overloaded), and treat the precipitant. Use the mnemonic of immediate steps: **S** it up, **O** xygen/CPAP, **N** itrate, **D** iuretic, **I** nvestigate, **T** reat cause (and the opioid is no longer favoured).

| Step | Details | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Position and oxygen | Sit up with legs dependent; high-flow oxygen aiming SpO2 94 to 98% | |
| CPAP or NIV | CPAP 5 to 10 cmH2O or BiPAP (IPAP 10 to 15 / EPAP 5 to 8) reduces work of breathing, intubation rate and short-term mortality in some meta-analyses | 3CPO: NIV improved dyspnoea, heart rate, acidosis and hypercapnia faster but did not reduce 7-day mortality; CPAP and NIV are equivalent |
| Vasodilator | GTN spray 400 micrograms SL, then infusion 10 to 200 micrograms/min if SBP above 110 (preload and afterload reduction, coronary dilation); sodium nitroprusside for hypertensive crisis | GTN effective in hypertensive acute HF; high-dose isosorbide dinitrate bolus with low-dose furosemide (Cotter) reduced intubation |
| Loop diuretic | Furosemide 40 to 80 mg IV (venodilatation first, diuresis in 15 to 30 min). Lower doses in diuretic-naive patients (20 to 40 mg); higher doses in chronic users | DOSE |
| Opioid | Morphine is no longer recommended routinely (ADHERE: higher mechanical ventilation, ICU admission and mortality in observational data); small doses may help anxiety | |
| Treat precipitant | Ischaemia (reperfusion), arrhythmia (cardioversion), hypertension (vasodilator), valve emergencies (surgery), fluid overload (diuresis, dialysis), anaemia (transfuse) | |
| Intubation | Hypoxaemia and exhaustion despite NIV, GCS reduction, shock, inability to protect the airway. Induce cautiously: pre-oxygenate with CPAP, ketamine or etomidate, vasopressor ready; PEEP up to 10 to 15 cmH2O reduces venous return and afterload | |
| Inotropes and MCS | For hypotension, cold and wet profile (see Topic 3) | |

**Intraoperative pulmonary oedema:**

- Call for help; 100% oxygen; check airway, tube position, ventilation and circuit (rule out airway problem, tube obstruction, endobronchial migration).
- Stop IV fluids and anything causing fluid load; stop surgical irrigation; announce to the surgeon, consider abbreviating the operation.
- Increase PEEP (5 to 10 cmH2O), prolong expiratory time, ventilate to maintain SpO2; suction frothy secretions through the ETT.
- Diagnose the type: ECG and ST analysis, arterial blood gas, ETCO2 (PE), lung ultrasound, TOE (RWMA, valve, LV function), look for anaphylaxis (bronchospasm, flushing, hypotension), transfusion reaction, or negative pressure.
- Treat: vasodilator (GTN) if hypertensive, diuretic if overloaded, inotrope if low output, antiarrhythmic or cardioversion, treat ischaemia, adrenaline if anaphylaxis.
- Plan postoperative ICU/HDU, ventilation, and investigations (troponin, echo, BNP).

## 5.4 Special types

| Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| Negative pressure pulmonary oedema (Type I: acute obstruction; Type II: chronic obstruction relieved) | Forced inspiration against an obstructed airway generates very negative intrapleural pressure (up to -100 cmH2O), increasing venous return and transmural capillary pressure, with sympathetic surge and hypoxia injuring capillaries. Treatment: relieve obstruction, O2, CPAP or PEEP; usually resolves in 12 to 24 h; diuretics seldom needed |
| TACO vs TRALI | TACO: hypertension, raised JVP, raised BNP, responds to diuretic. TRALI: hypotension, fever, normal or low BNP, bilateral infiltrates within 6 h of transfusion, treat as ARDS (no diuretics), and report to the blood service. See Haemorrhage and Transfusion set |
| Re-expansion pulmonary oedema | After rapid drainage of a large pneumothorax or effusion: limit drainage to 1 to 1.5 L at once |
| Neurogenic pulmonary oedema | Sympathetic surge raising pulmonary venous pressure and capillary permeability; treat the neurological cause, supportive ventilation, alpha-blockade in some cases |
| Pre-eclampsia, peripartum cardiomyopathy | Obstetrics sets |

## 5.5 Cardiogenic versus non-cardiogenic oedema (SS_IC 1.45)

| Feature | Cardiogenic | Non-cardiogenic (ARDS) |
|---|---|---|
| History | Cardiac disease, ischaemia, volume overload | Sepsis, aspiration, trauma, transfusion |
| Heart size / vascular pedicle | Enlarged, wide pedicle | Normal heart, narrow pedicle |
| Distribution on CXR | Central perihilar, basal, effusions | Peripheral, patchy, air bronchograms |
| BNP | Raised (above 400 ng/L) | Mildly raised or normal |
| PAOP | Above 18 mmHg | 18 mmHg or less |
| Echo | Poor LV function, valve lesion | Normal LV |
| Oedema fluid protein : plasma protein | Below 0.5 | Above 0.7 |
| Response to diuretic and vasodilator | Prompt | Little |

items.title: 2. Acute myocardial ischaemia, infarction, cardiogenic shock and revascularisation
items.priority: P1 CORE (3 parent LOs) + acute myocardial ischaemia crisis component at P2 HIGH
items.los: SS_CS 1.26; SS_IC 1.31; SS_CS 1.4 (myocardial ischaemia component); IT_RT 1.2 (acute myocardial ischaemia component)
items.body:
## 2.1 Recognition and diagnosis

**Clinical features:** central chest pain (often absent under GA or in diabetics, the elderly and after surgery), dyspnoea, sweating, nausea, arrhythmia, hypotension, new heart failure or cardiogenic shock. Perioperatively, suspect MI with unexplained hypotension, arrhythmia, pulmonary oedema, new ST change, desaturation or agitation.

**Fourth Universal Definition of MI:** a rise and/or fall of cardiac troponin with at least one value above the 99th percentile upper reference limit, together with at least one of: ischaemic symptoms; new ischaemic ECG changes; development of pathological Q waves; imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium or new regional wall motion abnormality; or coronary thrombus on angiography or autopsy.

**ECG criteria (acute ischaemia):**

| Finding | Criteria |
|---|---|
| STEMI | New ST elevation at the J point in 2 contiguous leads: at least 1 mm in all leads except V2 to V3, where it is at least 2 mm in men aged 40 or over (2.5 mm under 40), at least 1.5 mm in women |
| NSTEMI / unstable angina | ST depression (at least 0.5 mm in 2 contiguous leads), T wave inversion (at least 1 mm in leads with prominent R wave) or no change |
| Posterior MI | ST depression V1 to V3 with tall R waves; confirm with posterior leads V7 to V9 |
| Right ventricular MI | ST elevation in V4R, with inferior MI: avoid nitrates and diuretics, support with fluids |
| Equivalents | New LBBB (apply Sgarbossa criteria), de Winter T waves, Wellens' sign (critical LAD stenosis), hyperacute T waves, left main occlusion (ST elevation aVR with diffuse ST depression) |

| Territory | Leads | Artery |
|---|---|---|
| Anterior | V1 to V4 | LAD |
| Septal | V1 to V2 | LAD (septal perforators) |
| Lateral | I, aVL, V5 to V6 | LCx or diagonal |
| Inferior | II, III, aVF | RCA (80%), LCx |
| Posterior | ST depression V1 to V3 | RCA or LCx |
| RV | V4R | Proximal RCA |

**Troponin interpretation:** high-sensitivity troponin rises 3 to 4 h after injury, peaks at 24 to 48 h, and stays elevated 7 to 14 days. Use serial measurements (0 and 1 to 3 h algorithms). Non-MI causes of elevation include PE, sepsis, renal failure, myocarditis, arrhythmia, takotsubo, aortic dissection and cardiac contusion. CK-MB is largely obsolete.

## 2.2 Detection and investigation after surgery

- 12-lead ECG immediately and serially (compare with the preoperative ECG; absent baseline is a common exam trap).
- Serial hs-troponin; CK-MB only if troponin unavailable.
- Bedside echo (FoCUS/TTE): new RWMA, LV function, pericardial effusion, RV strain, valve lesion, mechanical complication.
- Chest X-ray, ABG, electrolytes (K, Mg), Hb, lactate, renal function, glucose, coagulation.
- Differential: PE, aortic dissection, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, pericarditis, oesophageal pathology, takotsubo, myocarditis, anaemia or hypovolaemia with demand ischaemia.
- Coronary angiography for STEMI, high-risk NSTEMI, or unexplained shock.

## 2.3 Initial medical management

Standard ACS approach (Australian Heart Foundation / CSANZ guideline; ESC 2023 ACS guideline), adapted to the perioperative bleeding risk. Never delay reperfusion for investigations.

| Intervention | Details | Perioperative caveat |
|---|---|---|
| Oxygen | Only if SpO2 below 90%: routine oxygen does not help and may harm (DETO2X-AMI, AVOID) | |
| Aspirin | 150 to 300 mg load, then 100 mg daily | Discuss with surgeon if fresh surgical bleeding |
| P2Y12 inhibitor | Ticagrelor 180 mg or prasugrel 60 mg load, or clopidogrel 300 to 600 mg (clopidogrel if fibrinolysis or oral anticoagulant or high bleeding risk) | Bleeding risk; cardiology decision |
| Anticoagulation | Unfractionated heparin (70 to 100 U/kg bolus) or enoxaparin | Fresh surgical site: individualised |
| Analgesia | Titrated IV opioid (fentanyl or morphine); morphine delays absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors | |
| Nitrates | GTN SL or IV for ongoing ischaemia, hypertension or pulmonary oedema | Avoid with SBP below 90, RV infarct, PDE-5 inhibitor within 24 to 48 h |
| Beta-blocker | IV only if tachycardic and hypertensive without heart failure or shock; early oral beta-blocker in stable patients | Avoid in shock, bradycardia, high-grade block, acute HF (COMMIT-CCS2: more cardiogenic shock with early IV metoprolol) |
| Statin | High-intensity atorvastatin 80 mg | |
| ACEi / ARB | Early in anterior MI, HF or LV dysfunction once stable | Avoid in shock or AKI |
| Antiemetic, anxiolytic | As needed | |

**Anaesthetic and perioperative modifications:** treat the cause (hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia, hypoxia), deepen anaesthesia or analgesia, maintain MAP (phenylephrine, noradrenaline), reduce HR, and escalate monitoring with invasive BP and TOE.

## 2.4 Reperfusion strategies

| Option | Indications and key points |
|---|---|
| Primary PCI | Preferred for STEMI; target first medical contact to wire crossing within 90 min (60 min if self-presenting to a PCI centre); within 120 min of diagnosis if transfer needed. Benefit up to 12 h from symptom onset; later if ongoing ischaemia, shock or arrhythmia |
| Fibrinolysis | If primary PCI cannot be achieved in 120 min: tenecteplase, alteplase or reteplase within 30 min of diagnosis; then transfer for angiography within 2 to 24 h (pharmaco-invasive strategy, STREAM). Rescue PCI if failed. **Absolute contraindications:** prior intracranial haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke within 3 months, known intracranial neoplasm or AVM, suspected aortic dissection, active bleeding, significant head or facial trauma in 3 months. **Perioperatively, major surgery within 3 weeks is a relative contraindication**, so PCI is preferred |
| Urgent angiography | NSTEMI with instability, refractory pain, haemodynamic or electrical instability, or heart failure (within 2 h); high-risk (GRACE above 140) within 24 h |
| CABG | Left main or three-vessel disease with diabetes, failed PCI, mechanical complications |

> **Figure (diagram not reproduced):** ACS reperfusion pathway · 1 decision, shock escalation. The ST-elevation decision drives reperfusion route and timing; cardiogenic shock overrides the pathway at any step.

## 2.5 Cardiogenic shock (SS_IC 1.31, SS_CS 1.26)

**Definition:** sustained hypotension (SBP below 90 mmHg for 30 min or vasopressors needed) with evidence of hypoperfusion (lactate above 2 mmol/L, cold peripheries, oliguria, altered mentation) and elevated filling pressures, caused by primary cardiac dysfunction. Cardiac index below 2.2 L/min/m2 with PCWP above 15 mmHg.

**Causes after MI:** pump failure (large infarct, 40% of LV loss), RV infarction, mechanical complications (acute severe MR from papillary muscle rupture, VSD, free wall rupture and tamponade), arrhythmia.

**SCAI staging:**

| Stage | Features |
|---|---|
| A At risk | Risk factors for shock; normal perfusion |
| B Beginning | Hypotension or tachycardia, no hypoperfusion |
| C Classic | Hypoperfusion requiring intervention (drugs, mechanical support); lactate often above 2 |
| D Deteriorating | Worsening despite initial support; escalation needed |
| E Extremis | Cardiac arrest or CPR, on multiple support devices |

**Management principles:**

- **Emergency revascularisation** of the culprit lesion is the key treatment (SHOCK trial: survival benefit at 6 and 12 months). Culprit-only PCI is preferred (CULPRIT-SHOCK).
- **Haemodynamics:** noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor (SOAP II: fewer arrhythmias than dopamine; better 28-day survival in the cardiogenic shock subgroup). Add adrenaline only if refractory (more arrhythmia and refractory shock). Dobutamine 2.5 to 10 micrograms/kg/min as the first-line inotrope; consider levosimendan or milrinone with caution (hypotension; milrinone renal clearance). Vasopressin as an adjunct to spare catecholamines.
- **Avoid excess fluid** (unless RV infarct or hypovolaemia). Cautious 250 mL boluses.
- **Respiratory support:** oxygen, high-flow, NIV or intubation. Anaesthetic induction in shock is dangerous (see below).
- **Mechanical circulatory support (MCS):** see 2.6.
- **Treat arrhythmia, acidosis, anaemia (MINT: liberal transfusion considered), electrolytes.** Avoid hypothermia unless post-arrest.
- **Monitoring:** arterial line, central venous access, serial lactate, ScvO2, echo, consider PA catheter to guide complex shock (PCWP, CO, PVR; the right ventricle matters).

**Haemodynamic profile (Forrester / Stevenson):**

| Profile | Perfusion | Congestion | Typical therapy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warm and dry | Adequate | No | Continue oral therapy |
| Warm and wet | Adequate | Yes | Diuretics, vasodilators |
| Cold and wet | Poor | Yes | Inotrope, vasopressor, MCS, diuretics |
| Cold and dry | Poor | No | Fluids, inotrope |

## 2.6 Mechanical circulatory support

| Device | Mechanism | Evidence | Key limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) | Counterpulsation in the descending aorta: inflates in diastole (raising diastolic pressure and coronary perfusion), deflates just before systole (reduces afterload, LV wall stress and O2 demand). Small rise in CO (about 0.5 L/min) | IABP-SHOCK II: no mortality benefit in MI shock; now class III in ESC/ACC | Aortic regurgitation, aortic dissection, severe peripheral vascular disease; works only with a rhythm that triggers and adequate native output; limb ischaemia, bleeding, thrombocytopenia |
| Impella (percutaneous LV assist, axial flow) | Pumps blood from LV to ascending aorta, giving up to 2.5 to 5.5 L/min depending on model | DanGer Shock (STEMI shock): lower 180-day mortality, more bleeding and limb ischaemia | Haemolysis, vascular complications, LV thrombus is a contraindication, mechanical aortic valve |
| VA-ECMO | Venous drainage to oxygenator and pump, return to femoral artery; full support (4 to 6 L/min) but raises LV afterload and can cause LV distension and pulmonary oedema unless vented (Impella, IABP, balloon septostomy) | ECLS-SHOCK, ECMO-CS: no mortality benefit in unselected shock | Bleeding, limb ischaemia, stroke, harlequin (differential hypoxia) syndrome, infection |
| TandemHeart / ECMO RV support | Right ventricular failure | Small series | |

**IABP waveform.** In the 1:2 assist mode the arterial trace alternates between an assisted and an unassisted beat. Features of a correct assisted beat: the **dicrotic notch** replaced by a sharp V-shaped inflation point; **diastolic augmentation** (peak above the systolic pressure); **assisted end-diastolic pressure** lower than unassisted end-diastolic; **assisted systolic pressure** lower than the unassisted systolic. Timing errors: early inflation (before the notch: aortic valve closes prematurely, reducing SV), late inflation (reduced augmentation), early deflation (loss of afterload reduction, 'U' shape), late deflation (balloon inflates against systole, increases afterload).

> **Figure (diagram not reproduced):** IABP 1:2 arterial pressure trace · points A to F. Compare the assisted and unassisted values: E should sit below A and F below B if counterpulsation is working.

**Physiological principle:** raising diastolic aortic pressure improves coronary perfusion (not in stenosed vessels where flow is fixed), and systolic unloading reduces LV wall tension, so oxygen supply rises while demand falls.

**Pitfall:** the IABP does not provide significant forward flow, so it does not help in profound shock or ventricular arrhythmia.

## 2.7 Anaesthesia for acute revascularisation (SS_CS 1.26)

**For primary PCI or emergency angiography:**

- Most patients can be managed with local anaesthetic and light sedation; the case for GA is airway protection in unstable patients with shock, cardiac arrest, respiratory failure or agitation.
- Avoid sedation that causes hypotension or hypoventilation.
- Consider the contrast load (renal), radiation and positioning.
- Reperfusion arrhythmias (accelerated idioventricular rhythm, VF), bleeding and vascular access complications are the major concerns.

**For emergency CABG (see Set 13 for CPB):**

- Preoperative: DAPT bleeding risk and platelet availability; stabilise with IABP or inotropes.
- Induction in shock: invasive arterial line before induction; titrate induction agent (etomidate or ketamine; reduced dose), maintain MAP with noradrenaline or vasopressin, avoid tachycardia and hypotension; fentanyl-based balanced anaesthesia. Anticipate low cardiac output at induction because sympatholysis unmasks reduced reserve.
- Hypotension at induction in a failing ventricle is treated with vasopressor and inotrope early, not fluid alone.

**For anaesthesia in patients with recent PCI or MI undergoing urgent non-cardiac surgery:** follow Topic 1 (antiplatelet continuation, high-risk perioperative environment, post-operative HDU, troponin surveillance).

## 2.8 Mechanical complications and RV infarction

| Complication | Timing | Features | Management |
|---|---|---|---|
| Papillary muscle rupture (acute severe MR) | 2 to 7 days (posteromedial papillary muscle, single blood supply: PDA) | Pulmonary oedema, shock, soft murmur because of equalised pressures, large v wave | Afterload reduction (nitroprusside), IABP, urgent surgery |
| Ventricular septal rupture | 3 to 5 days | New loud pansystolic murmur, left-to-right shunt, RV overload | IABP, surgical or percutaneous closure |
| Free wall rupture | 5 to 14 days | Tamponade, PEA | Pericardiocentesis, emergency surgery |
| RV infarction | With inferior MI | Hypotension, raised JVP, clear lungs | Fluids to preload optimum, inotropes, maintain AV synchrony, avoid nitrates and diuretics, pacing for AV block |
| Arrhythmia | Reperfusion; VT/VF within 48 h | | Defibrillation, amiodarone, correct K/Mg, beta-blocker |

## 2.9 After the acute event

DAPT for 12 months after ACS (shorter with high bleeding risk), high-intensity statin, beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor or ARB, mineralocorticoid antagonist for LVEF 40% or less with HF or diabetes, cardiac rehabilitation, and secondary prevention. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator evaluation 40 days or more after MI and 3 months after revascularisation if LVEF stays 35% or less.

items.title: 3. Left ventricular systolic and diastolic dysfunction and heart failure
items.los: IT_PO 1.4 (left heart failure component); SS_CS 1.4 (filling status; LV systolic and diastolic function); SS_IC 1.35 (heart failure in intensive care)
items.body:
## 3.1 Definitions and classification

**Heart failure (HF):** clinical syndrome of symptoms and signs caused by structural or functional cardiac abnormality, with raised natriuretic peptides or objective evidence of congestion.

| Type | LVEF | Features |
|---|---|---|
| HFrEF | 40% or less | Systolic dysfunction; dilated LV, reduced contractility |
| HFmrEF | 41 to 49% | Intermediate; treat like HFrEF if symptomatic (ESC 2023) |
| HFpEF | 50% or more | Diastolic dysfunction, LVH, raised filling pressures, LA enlargement; often elderly, hypertensive, diabetic, obese, women |
| HFimpEF | Baseline 40% or less, improved by 10 points to above 40% | Continue therapy |

**Staging:** ACC/AHA stages A to D (A at risk, B structural disease without symptoms, C symptomatic, D refractory). **NYHA class I to IV** by symptoms: I no limitation; II slight, symptoms on ordinary activity; III marked, symptoms on less than ordinary activity; IV symptoms at rest.

**Acute HF presentations:** acute decompensated chronic HF (most), acute pulmonary oedema, cardiogenic shock, hypertensive HF, isolated right HF.

## 3.2 Pathophysiology

- **Systolic dysfunction:** reduced contractility and ejection. Low stroke volume activates the sympathetic nervous system (tachycardia, vasoconstriction), RAAS (sodium and water retention, afterload), and natriuretic peptide release. Chronic activation causes remodelling: eccentric hypertrophy, dilatation, functional MR, and arrhythmia.
- **Diastolic dysfunction:** impaired relaxation (active, energy-dependent early diastole) and increased stiffness (passive compliance). The LV pressure-volume curve shifts up and left: small volume changes cause large pressure changes. Atrial contraction contributes 30 to 40% of filling (instead of 15 to 20%), so AF and tachycardia are badly tolerated.

| Feature | Systolic dysfunction | Diastolic dysfunction |
|---|---|---|
| End-systolic pressure-volume relationship | Shifted down and right (reduced Ees) | Normal |
| End-diastolic pressure-volume relationship | Shifted right (dilated) | Shifted up and left (stiff) |
| EDV | Increased | Normal or reduced |
| EF | Reduced | Preserved |
| Preload response | Plateaus on a flat Starling curve | Steep: small volume changes cause large pressure swings |
| Poorly tolerated | Afterload rise, negative inotropes | Tachycardia, AF, hypovolaemia and hypervolaemia, ischaemia |

## 3.3 Perioperative assessment of LV function and filling status (SS_CS 1.4)

**Clinical:** orthopnoea, PND, oedema, JVP, S3 gallop, crepitations, hepatomegaly, ascites, cool peripheries, exercise tolerance (NYHA, DASI).

**Investigations:**

| Test | Value |
|---|---|
| BNP / NT-proBNP | Rule-out value (BNP below 100 ng/L, NT-proBNP below 300 ng/L); raised by age, renal failure, AF and falls with obesity. Preoperative level predicts MACE (see Topic 1) |
| ECG | Ischaemia, LBBB (dyssynchrony), AF, LVH, QRS duration for CRT |
| CXR | Cardiomegaly, upper-lobe diversion, Kerley B lines, effusions |
| Echo | LVEF (biplane Simpson), regional wall motion, valves, filling pressures, RV function, pulmonary pressures |
| Cardiac MRI, nuclear | Viability, aetiology, EF |
| Invasive | PA catheter data for complex cases |

**Echo assessment of LV systolic function:**

| Parameter | Normal / cut-off |
|---|---|
| LVEF (ASE) | 52 to 72% men, 54 to 74% women; mildly reduced 41 to 51 / 41 to 53 |
| Fractional shortening | 25 to 43% |
| Global longitudinal strain | Normal about -18 to -20% or more negative; a better marker than EF |
| Fractional area change (mid-papillary SAX) | Above 35% (TOE) |
| Qualitative on FoCUS | Normal, mildly, moderately or severely reduced; interventricular septum motion |
| Dimensions | LV end-diastolic diameter 3.9 to 5.3 cm (women), 4.2 to 5.9 cm (men) |

**Echo assessment of diastolic function (ASE/EACVI 2016 algorithm):** four criteria for diastolic dysfunction: annular e' (septal below 7 cm/s or lateral below 10 cm/s), average E/e' above 14, LA volume index above 34 mL/m2, and TR velocity above 2.8 m/s. If more than half are abnormal, diastolic dysfunction is present; if half, indeterminate.

| Grade | E/A | E/e' | Other | LAP |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Normal | 0.8 to 2 | Below 8 to 10 | | Normal |
| I (impaired relaxation) | Below 0.8 | Below 10 | E below 50 cm/s | Normal or low |
| II (pseudonormal) | 0.8 to 2 | 10 to 14 | Valsalva changes E/A (decrease by 0.5 or more), LAVI above 34 | Raised |
| III (restrictive) | Above 2 | Above 14 | Short DT below 160 ms, IVRT below 70 ms | Markedly raised |

**Assessment of filling status and fluid responsiveness (see Set 10 for the underlying haemodynamics):** CVP and PAOP are poor predictors of volume responsiveness. Better: dynamic tests (passive leg raise, SVV and PPV with caveats of tidal volume above 8 mL/kg and sinus rhythm), IVC diameter and collapsibility (diameter 2.1 cm or less with collapse above 50% suggests RAP about 3 mmHg), LVOT VTI change, and E/e' for filling pressure. In HF, fluid challenges should be small (250 mL) and reassessed.

## 3.4 Chronic management of HF (basis of perioperative continuation)

| Drug class | Role | Perioperative note |
|---|---|---|
| ACEi / ARB / ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan) | Mortality benefit in HFrEF (SOLVD, PARADIGM-HF) | Hold morning of surgery in most; omit ARNI 36 h before if switching to ACEi; hypotension risk with anaesthesia |
| Beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) | Mortality benefit (CIBIS-II, MERIT-HF, COPERNICUS) | Continue; avoid abrupt withdrawal |
| MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone) | RALES, EPHESUS | Check K and renal function |
| SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) | DAPA-HF, EMPEROR-Reduced; EMPEROR-Preserved and DELIVER in HFpEF | **Withhold 3 to 4 days before surgery** (euglycaemic ketoacidosis) |
| Loop diuretics | Symptom control | Omit morning dose if euvolaemic; resume early |
| Ivabradine | SHIFT: HR above 70 despite beta-blocker | Continue |
| Digoxin | Symptoms and rate control | Check level, K |
| Hydralazine plus nitrate | For African ancestry (A-HeFT) and ACEi intolerance | |
| Device therapy | ICD (primary prevention LVEF 35% or less), CRT (LBBB, QRS 150 ms or more) | Reprogramme perioperatively (see device guidance in Set 12) |

## 3.5 Anaesthetic implications and perioperative risk (IT_PO 1.4)

HF is a major independent predictor of perioperative mortality, MACE, readmission and prolonged stay. Elective surgery should be deferred if decompensated; optimise euvolaemia and GDMT beforehand.

**Haemodynamic goals:**

| Systolic dysfunction | Diastolic dysfunction |
|---|---|
| Preload: maintain but avoid overload | Preload: maintain, adequate filling is crucial |
| Afterload: low to normal (avoid vasoconstriction; vasodilators help) | Afterload: avoid large rises |
| Heart rate: normal to high-normal (CO depends on HR in a fixed SV state; avoid bradycardia) | Heart rate: slow (50 to 80) to maximise filling time |
| Rhythm: keep sinus rhythm | **Sinus rhythm is critical**; treat AF early (cardioversion if unstable) |
| Contractility: support with inotrope if needed; avoid negative inotropes | Contractility: preserved; avoid excess inotropy |
| Avoid | Avoid tachycardia, ischaemia, hypervolaemia |

**Anaesthetic technique:**

- Choose agents with minimal myocardial depression: etomidate or ketamine (with caution) or slow-titrated propofol for induction; opioid-based, balanced technique; volatile agents are acceptable at low MAC.
- Invasive arterial monitoring before induction for severe LV dysfunction; consider cardiac output monitoring and TOE.
- Vasopressor (noradrenaline) infusion ready before induction; inotrope (dobutamine, adrenaline) or milrinone if low output; vasopressin for vasodilatory states.
- Neuraxial anaesthesia can be well tolerated in compensated HF (controlled onset, slow titration of epidural or CSE; sympathetic block reduces afterload) but severe aortic stenosis or fixed output states are an exception. Maintain MAP with vasopressors. Monitor ECG, SpO2 and blood pressure (arterial line for severe dysfunction), and watch for signs of fluid overload or pulmonary oedema throughout.
- Fluids: restrictive and goal-directed; avoid large crystalloid loads; treat blood loss with blood.
- Postoperative: HDU, early extubation where possible, repeat BNP or troponin, fluid balance, restart GDMT.

## 3.6 Heart failure in the intensive care unit (SS_IC 1.35)

**Aim:** treat the cause, relieve congestion, restore perfusion, and protect organs.

**Initial assessment:** perfusion and congestion profile (warm/cold, wet/dry; see Topic 2); ECG, troponin, BNP, lactate, echo, CXR. Identify precipitants using the mnemonic **CHAMP**: acute **C** oronary syndrome, **H** ypertensive emergency, **A** rrhythmia, acute **M** echanical cause (valve, VSD, rupture), **P** ulmonary embolism. Others: infection, non-adherence, anaemia, thyroid, drugs (NSAIDs, negative inotropes), fluid overload, renal failure.

**Treatment:**

| Goal | Therapy |
|---|---|
| Oxygenation and breathing | Oxygen if SpO2 below 90%; CPAP or NIV for pulmonary oedema (see Topic 5); intubate for exhaustion, shock or failure of NIV |
| Decongestion | IV loop diuretic: furosemide 20 to 40 mg IV bolus (or 1 to 2.5 times the oral dose), infusion if inadequate. DOSE trial: high-dose (2.5 times) vs low-dose and bolus vs infusion gave similar symptom outcomes, with more transient creatinine rise at high dose. Add thiazide (metolazone) or acetazolamide (ADVOR) for resistance; ultrafiltration if refractory |
| Vasodilators | GTN or nitroprusside for hypertensive, congested patients with SBP above 110 (benefit mainly in APO) |
| Perfusion (low-output state) | Dobutamine 2.5 to 20 micrograms/kg/min; milrinone 0.125 to 0.5 micrograms/kg/min (no loading dose in hypotension); levosimendan (calcium sensitiser, vasodilator; SURVIVE and REVIVE mixed results); noradrenaline to maintain MAP above 65; vasopressin |
| Mechanical support | IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO as a bridge to recovery, device or transplant (see Topic 2.6). ECMO also treats refractory VF/cardiac arrest (ECPR) |
| Rhythm | Cardioversion for unstable tachyarrhythmias; amiodarone; pacing for bradycardia |
| Renal and metabolic | Correct K and Mg; monitor creatinine (cardiorenal syndrome); renal replacement or ultrafiltration if needed |
| Other | Venous thromboprophylaxis, nutrition, early mobilisation, palliative care input in advanced HF |

**Pulmonary artery catheter in HF:** ESCAPE showed no benefit of routine PAC-guided therapy in acute decompensated HF, so reserve it for shock of uncertain mechanism, refractory shock, transplant or LVAD assessment and pulmonary hypertension.

**Cardiogenic shock after non-ischaemic causes:** myocarditis, takotsubo, peripartum cardiomyopathy, decompensated chronic HF, drug toxicity. Same principles; VA-ECMO is a bridge to recovery (for example fulminant myocarditis).

**Advanced HF therapies:** LVAD (HeartMate 3, destination therapy or bridge to transplant), heart transplant. Anaesthetic considerations for the LVAD patient: no pulse (use arterial line and MAP, the Doppler MAP), preload and RV function dependence, anticoagulated, driveline infection, and pump thrombosis. Avoid hypovolaemia, high PVR, and tachyarrhythmia.

items.title: 6. Cardiomyopathy
items.body:
## 6.1 Classification

| Type | Key features | Perioperative priority |
|---|---|---|
| Dilated (DCM) | LV dilatation, systolic dysfunction (EF below 40%); causes: idiopathic or familial, ischaemic, alcohol, viral, anthracycline, peripartum, tachycardia-induced, valvular | Treat as HFrEF (Topic 3) |
| Hypertrophic (HCM) | Unexplained LVH (wall 15 mm or more), diastolic dysfunction, myocyte disarray; autosomal dominant sarcomere mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3); dynamic LVOT obstruction in about 70% (rest or provoked) with systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve; SCD risk | **Examiner favourite**; avoid anything that reduces LV size or increases contractility or heart rate |
| Restrictive (RCM) | Stiff ventricle, normal EF, biatrial enlargement; amyloid, sarcoid, haemochromatosis, fibrosis, radiation | Preload-dependent, fixed low output, poor tolerance of tachycardia and AF |
| Arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy | RV fibrofatty replacement, VT | Arrhythmia risk; ICD |
| Takotsubo (stress) | Transient apical ballooning after catecholamine surge; mimics STEMI, normal coronaries | Can occur intraoperatively; supportive care, avoid catecholamines if LVOT obstruction |
| Peripartum | EF below 45% in last month of pregnancy or 5 months postpartum | See obstetrics sets |
| Ischaemic | Not truly a primary cardiomyopathy (CAD) | Topics 1 to 3 |
| Right heart failure | RV pressure or volume overload (pulmonary hypertension, PE, RV infarct) | See 6.6 |

## 6.2 Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy

**Pathophysiology:** asymmetric septal hypertrophy narrows the LV outflow tract. During systole, the Venturi effect and drag forces pull the anterior mitral leaflet toward the septum (SAM), worsening obstruction and causing posterior-directed MR. Obstruction is **dynamic**: it worsens with reduced LV volume (hypovolaemia, vasodilation), increased contractility (catecholamines, inotropes) and tachycardia, and reduced afterload. Diastolic dysfunction from LVH raises LVEDP, and myocardial oxygen supply-demand mismatch causes ischaemia despite normal coronaries.

| Factor | Increases obstruction | Decreases obstruction |
|---|---|---|
| Preload | Hypovolaemia, venodilation, PEEP, positioning (head up) | Volume loading, leg raise, head-down |
| Afterload | Vasodilation, low SVR | Vasoconstrictors (phenylephrine, vasopressin) |
| Contractility | Beta-agonists, dobutamine, ketamine, digoxin, calcium | Beta-blockers, verapamil, volatile agents, disopyramide |
| Heart rate | Tachycardia (shortens diastolic filling and LV size) | Slow rate |
| Rhythm | AF (loss of atrial kick, poor filling) | Sinus rhythm |

**Preoperative assessment:** symptoms (dyspnoea, angina, syncope, palpitation), family history of sudden death, ECG (LVH, strain, deep Q waves), echo (wall thickness, LVOT gradient at rest and with Valsalva, SAM, MR, diastolic function), cardiac MRI (fibrosis, late gadolinium enhancement), Holter monitoring, and review of medications (beta-blocker, verapamil, disopyramide, amiodarone). ICD in situ requires reprogramming (see Set 12). SCD risk markers: previous cardiac arrest, VT, family history, massive LVH (30 mm or more), unexplained syncope, NSVT, abnormal BP response, LVOT gradient above 30 mmHg.

**Perioperative haemodynamic goals:**

- **Preload:** full. Avoid prolonged fasting (maintain IV fluids), avoid venodilators and bowel prep dehydration; maintain preload with fluid or blood.
- **Afterload:** maintain or increase (phenylephrine, vasopressin, noradrenaline).
- **Contractility:** reduce (volatile anaesthetics, beta-blocker).
- **Rate:** low-normal (60 to 70), sinus rhythm (cardiovert early for AF; consider amiodarone).
- **Avoid:** ephedrine, adrenaline, dobutamine, isoprenaline, ketamine, tachycardia, hypovolaemia, and nitrates.

**Technique:**

| Element | Approach |
|---|---|
| Premedication | Continue beta-blocker or verapamil; anxiolysis (reduce catecholamines) |
| Monitoring | Arterial line before induction, ECG with ST, TOE if major surgery or instability, defibrillator pads, CVP of limited value |
| Induction | Slow, titrated propofol or etomidate with fentanyl, vasopressor infusion running (phenylephrine, metaraminol, vasopressin) |
| Maintenance | Volatile agent, opioid, remifentanil; avoid light anaesthesia and pain |
| Neuraxial | Not contraindicated, but sympathectomy lowers preload and afterload: use slow incremental epidural, CSE with low-dose spinal, or avoid; GA is more predictable in severe obstruction. In pregnancy epidural labour analgesia is acceptable with vasopressor cover |
| Hypotension post induction | **Do not give ephedrine or inotropes.** Treat with a pure alpha-agonist (phenylephrine 50 to 100 micrograms, or vasopressin), fluid bolus, reduce volatile concentration, leg elevation, and treat tachycardia (esmolol). Check for another cause (bleeding, anaphylaxis, tension pneumothorax, ischaemia, arrhythmia). If refractory: TOE to confirm SAM and LVOT obstruction, then vasoconstrictor infusions |
| Pneumoperitoneum (laparoscopic cholecystectomy) | Insufflation raises SVR (good), but decreased venous return in head-up (bad). Slow insufflation, low pressure, head-down tilt, fluid loading |
| Arrhythmia | Cardiovert unstable; amiodarone or beta-blocker for AF; do not use digoxin |
| Emergence | Avoid hypertension and tachycardia; extubate smoothly; ICU or HDU postoperative |

**Pregnancy, labour and delivery in HCM:** pregnancy changes that help: rising blood volume (40 to 50%) increases preload and enlarges the LV cavity, reducing the gradient. Changes that harm: falling SVR (more LVOT gradient), tachycardia and pain in labour, catecholamine surges, blood loss at delivery, and aortocaval compression. Principles: left lateral position, early slow-titrated epidural with a vasopressor ready, assisted second stage (avoid prolonged Valsalva), slow oxytocin infusion rather than a bolus (hypotension, tachycardia), avoid tocolytics and beta-agonists (tachycardia), and prompt volume replacement of haemorrhage.

**Alcohol septal ablation, myectomy, mavacamten (EXPLORER-HCM) and ICD** are the disease treatments: myectomy for refractory obstruction; mavacamten (cardiac myosin inhibitor) reduces gradient and improves functional class.

## 6.3 Dilated cardiomyopathy and low EF

Treat as severe LV systolic dysfunction (Topic 3), with attention to arrhythmia, devices and thromboembolism.

**Cardiac implantable devices (pacemaker, ICD, CRT) in cardiomyopathy:**

- **Preoperative:** identify the device, indication and pacing dependence; confirm a recent interrogation (about 12 months for a pacemaker, 6 months for an ICD or CRT) and the current programming. Review medications and the rhythm; echo and BNP if function has changed.
- **Electromagnetic interference:** monopolar diathermy above the umbilicus is the main risk. Use bipolar diathermy or short bursts, place the return pad so the current path avoids the generator, and monitor the pulse waveform (pulse oximeter or arterial line) because the ECG may be distorted.
- **Pacemaker:** a magnet usually produces asynchronous pacing; reprogram to asynchronous mode if the patient is pacemaker-dependent and interference is expected.
- **ICD:** a magnet usually suspends tachyarrhythmia therapies but does not alter pacing. Suspend therapies (magnet or programmer) when diathermy is expected, apply external defibrillation pads first, and have an external defibrillator ready. Restore therapies and re-interrogate before the patient leaves a monitored area.
- **CRT:** loss of biventricular capture reduces cardiac output; confirm capture and treat AF or ectopy that reduces pacing percentage.

**Choosing the anaesthetic technique in severe LV dysfunction:**

| Technique | Advantages | Risks and precautions |
|---|---|---|
| Regional or neuraxial (slow epidural, CSE with incremental local anaesthetic, peripheral nerve block) | Avoids airway instrumentation and positive pressure ventilation; reduces afterload; allows titrated onset | Hypotension from vasodilation (have a vasopressor infusion running, titrate slowly), fluid overload from preloading, and anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy limiting neuraxial use. Single-shot spinal gives abrupt sympathectomy and is riskier |
| General anaesthesia | Controlled airway and ventilation; suits instability, pulmonary oedema or failed block | Loss of sympathetic tone, myocardial depression with induction agents, pressor response to laryngoscopy, reduced venous return with positive pressure ventilation; use titrated induction with arterial monitoring |
| Sedation or local | Minimal haemodynamic disturbance for superficial surgery | Over-sedation with hypoventilation raises PVR and CO2; maintain monitoring |

**Alcohol and thiamine:** alcohol cardiomyopathy may improve with abstinence; give thiamine.

**Anthracycline cardiotoxicity (doxorubicin):** dose-related (cumulative above 450 to 550 mg/m2) and also trastuzumab; check baseline EF and troponin.

## 6.4 Restrictive cardiomyopathy and amyloidosis

- Stiff, non-compliant ventricles: small changes in volume cause large changes in pressure; fixed stroke volume depends on HR (avoid bradycardia); tolerate neither hypovolaemia nor fluid overload; AF is poorly tolerated.
- Amyloid (AL, ATTR): autonomic neuropathy (hypotension), conduction disease, thickened walls with low voltage ECG, and sensitivity to vasodilators and neuraxial block. Avoid digoxin and non-dihydropyridine CCB (bind amyloid fibrils).
- Goals: maintain preload and sinus rhythm, avoid bradycardia and vasodilation, titrate anaesthetic, and use vasopressors (phenylephrine, vasopressin).

## 6.5 Takotsubo and peripartum cardiomyopathy

**Takotsubo:** typically postmenopausal women, emotional or physical stress (includes surgery); chest pain and ST elevation, troponin mildly raised, apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis, normal angiography; 20% have LVOT obstruction (avoid catecholamines). Management: supportive, treat HF, anticoagulate if LV thrombus, MCS if shock; EF recovers in weeks.

**Peripartum cardiomyopathy:** EF below 45%, late pregnancy to 5 months postpartum; HF management with pregnancy-safe agents (beta-blocker, hydralazine, nitrate, diuretic, bromocriptine in selected cases); anticoagulate if EF below 35%; delivery planning.

## 6.6 Right heart failure and pulmonary hypertension (BT_PO 1.5 right heart failure component)

**Aetiology:** pulmonary hypertension (group 1 PAH; group 2 left heart disease; group 3 lung disease or hypoxia; group 4 CTEPH; group 5 multifactorial), RV infarction, PE, congenital shunt, cor pulmonale.

**Pathophysiology:** the RV is a thin-walled, compliant, volume-tolerant pump poorly adapted to high afterload. A rise in PVR dilates the RV, flattens the septum (ventricular interdependence), reduces LV filling, and lowers RV coronary perfusion, causing a vicious spiral of ischaemia, further failure and shock.

**Management principles (perioperative RV failure):**

| Principle | Actions |
|---|---|
| Preload | Avoid both hypovolaemia and overload; aim CVP 8 to 12 mmHg; diurese if overloaded |
| Afterload (PVR) | Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia, pain, high airway pressures and PEEP; use inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (nitric oxide 20 ppm, inhaled epoprostenol), sildenafil, milrinone |
| Contractility | Dobutamine, milrinone, low-dose adrenaline; levosimendan |
| Perfusion pressure | Keep SBP above PASP; noradrenaline or vasopressin (vasopressin raises SVR with less effect on PVR) |
| Rhythm | Maintain sinus rhythm; cardiovert early |
| Mechanical | RVAD, VA-ECMO, atrial septostomy in selected |
| Anaesthetic | Avoid anything that increases PVR (nitrous oxide, N2O, ketamine in large doses, hypoventilation); neuraxial anaesthesia with care; aim for PVR down and SVR up |
| Monitoring | Arterial line, CVP, PA catheter or TOE (RV size, septal position, TAPSE, FAC) |

**Echo of RV function:** TAPSE below 17 mm, S' below 9.5 cm/s, FAC below 35%, RV:LV ratio above 1, septal flattening (D-sign), and PASP from TR velocity (PASP = 4 x v^2 + RAP).

items.title: 7. Heart and great vessel anatomy for ultrasound imaging
items.body:
## 7.1 Cardiac chambers and valves

| Structure | Key anatomy | Echo relevance |
|---|---|---|
| Right atrium | Receives SVC, IVC and coronary sinus; crista terminalis; Eustachian valve; right atrial appendage | Venous return; IVC size estimates RAP; catheter or pacing wire tip lies here |
| Right ventricle | Most anterior chamber, crescentic in cross-section, trabeculated with moderator band; tricuspid valve (3 leaflets: anterior, septal, posterior) at a slightly more apical position than the mitral | RV size and function (TAPSE, S', FAC) |
| Left atrium | Posterior, receives four pulmonary veins; left atrial appendage (LAA) is a common site for thrombus | TOE rules out LAA thrombus before cardioversion |
| Left ventricle | Thick-walled, bullet-shaped; two papillary muscles (anterolateral: dual supply; posteromedial: single supply from PDA); smooth septum | EF, wall motion, wall thickness |
| Interatrial septum | Fossa ovalis (patent foramen ovale in about 25%) | Bubble study; PFO and paradoxical embolism |
| Aortic valve | Tricuspid; right, left and non-coronary cusps; right and left coronary ostia arise from their sinuses | Short-axis 'Mercedes-Benz' sign; cusp morphology |
| Mitral valve | Anterior (aortic) and posterior leaflets; scallops P1 to P3 and A1 to A3; annulus, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles | Mechanism of regurgitation; SAM in HCM |
| Pulmonary valve | Tricuspid, anterior and superior to the aortic valve | Gradient, PR |
| Pericardium | Fibrous and serous layers; 15 to 50 mL of fluid | Effusion, tamponade (RA and RV diastolic collapse) |

**Valve relationships:** the aortic and mitral valves are in fibrous continuity (the aorto-mitral curtain), which is why the LVOT is important in SAM and in AV endocarditis extension. The tricuspid is more apical than the mitral by about 10 mm. The pulmonary valve is the most anterior and cephalad valve.

## 7.2 Coronary arteries

| Vessel | Origin and course | Supplies |
|---|---|---|
| Left main | Left sinus of Valsalva; bifurcates after 1 to 2 cm | LAD and LCx |
| LAD | Anterior interventricular groove to the apex | Anterior LV wall, anterior two-thirds of septum, apex, anterolateral papillary muscle (partly) |
| LCx | AV groove, posterior | Lateral LV wall, posterior wall in left-dominant circulation, SA node in 40% |
| RCA | Right sinus of Valsalva, right AV groove | RA, RV, inferior LV wall, posterior third of septum (via PDA in right dominance, 85%), SA node in 60% and AV node in 90% |
| PDA | From RCA (right dominant 85%), LCx (left dominant 8%) or both | Inferior septum, posteromedial papillary muscle |

**Venous drainage:** coronary sinus (great cardiac vein, middle cardiac vein) drains to the RA; thebesian veins drain directly into the chambers. Anaesthetic relevance: the coronary sinus is cannulated for retrograde cardioplegia, and the great cardiac vein sits close to the left main.

**17-segment AHA/ASE model:** divides the LV into basal (6), mid (6), apical (4) and apex (1); apical and septal segments are LAD, inferolateral and anterolateral usually LCx, and inferior RCA or PDA. Use it to map RWMA to coronary territories.

## 7.3 Great vessels

| Vessel | Anatomy | Echo and anaesthetic relevance |
|---|---|---|
| Ascending aorta | Sinuses of Valsalva, sinotubular junction, ascending aorta to the brachiocephalic artery; normal root up to about 3.7 cm | Dissection (type A), aneurysm; TOE blind spot at the distal ascending aorta |
| Aortic arch | Brachiocephalic, left common carotid, left subclavian arteries | Cannulation and cerebral perfusion in arch surgery; suprasternal view |
| Descending thoracic aorta | Posterior to the left atrium and oesophagus | TOE views (excellent); atheroma grading; IABP tip sits 1 to 2 cm distal to the left subclavian |
| Pulmonary trunk and arteries | Trunk divides into right and left PAs; ligamentum arteriosum | PAC passes through RA, RV and PA; wedge pressure; saddle PE |
| SVC | Formed by brachiocephalic veins; drains to RA with the azygos entering above | CVC tip location: cavo-atrial junction |
| IVC | Enters the RA from below; hepatic veins join below the diaphragm | Subcostal view: IVC diameter and collapsibility |
| Pulmonary veins | Four veins to the LA | Pulsed Doppler (pulmonary vein flow for MR and diastolic function); AF ablation |
| Coronary sinus | Posterior AV groove into the RA | Cardioplegia and CRT lead placement |

## 7.4 Transthoracic windows and standard views

| Window | Views | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| Parasternal (left, 3rd to 4th intercostal space) | Long axis (PLAX): RV, septum, LV, LVOT, aortic valve, mitral valve, LA, descending aorta behind LA. Short axis (PSAX): aortic valve level (Mercedes-Benz sign), mitral level ('fish mouth'), papillary muscle level ('doughnut' for LV wall motion) | LV size, EF, valve morphology, effusion, RV pressure overload (D-shaped septum) |
| Apical (cardiac apex) | 4-chamber, 5-chamber (adds LVOT and aortic valve), 2-chamber, 3-chamber (apical LAX) | Chamber sizes, MV and TV, TAPSE, Doppler gradients (CW alignment) |
| Subcostal | 4-chamber, IVC and hepatic vein view | Used in ventilated or COPD patients and arrests; IVC collapsibility; pericardial fluid |
| Suprasternal | Aortic arch | Arch and descending aorta, coarctation |

**Focused cardiac ultrasound (FoCUS) questions:** Is there pericardial fluid or tamponade? Is LV function grossly normal, reduced or hyperdynamic? Is the RV dilated (RV:LV above 1)? Is the IVC plethoric? Is there a gross valve lesion? Is there a regional wall motion abnormality?

## 7.5 Transoesophageal views (ASE/SCA basic perioperative TOE)

The oesophagus lies posterior to the left atrium. The probe's position is described as upper oesophageal (UE), mid-oesophageal (ME), transgastric (TG) and deep transgastric. Twenty basic views are listed by the ASE/SCA; the examiner favourites are:

| View | Angle | Key structures |
|---|---|---|
| ME four-chamber | 0 to 20 degrees | All four chambers, MV and TV, LV lateral and septal walls, RV function |
| ME two-chamber | 80 to 100 | LA, LAA, MV, LV anterior and inferior walls |
| ME long axis | 120 to 160 | LVOT, aortic valve, MV, LA, proximal ascending aorta (anteroseptal and posterior walls) |
