| ME aortic valve short axis | 30 to 60 | Aortic valve cusps, coronary ostia |
| ME bicaval | 90 to 110 | SVC, IVC, RA, LA and interatrial septum, RAA (catheter position and PFO) |
| ME RV inflow-outflow | 50 to 70 | TV, RVOT, PV, pulmonary artery |
| TG mid short axis | 0 | LV in cross-section at the papillary muscle level, wall motion in all three coronary territories, preload and EF; the best view for ischaemia monitoring |
| Descending aortic short and long axis | 0 and 90 | Atheroma, dissection flap, IABP position |
| Deep TG long axis | 0 to 20 | LVOT and aortic valve alignment for Doppler gradients |
| UE aortic arch | 0 and 90 | Arch branches |

**Normal reference values (adult, ASE 2015):** LV end-diastolic dimension 3.9 to 5.3 cm (women), 4.2 to 5.9 cm (men); septal and posterior wall thickness 0.6 to 0.9 cm (women), 0.6 to 1.0 cm (men); LA diameter 2.7 to 3.8 cm (women), 3.0 to 4.0 cm (men); aortic root at sinuses up to about 3.7 cm; aortic valve area 3 to 4 cm2; mitral valve area 4 to 6 cm2; LVEF 54 to 74% (women), 52 to 72% (men); RV basal diameter up to 4.1 cm; TAPSE 17 mm or more; PASP up to 35 mmHg; IVC diameter 2.1 cm or less.

items.title: Hypotension after induction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
items.source: Example drafted by Claude from the Set 11 chapter 6 notes. Check against your own sources.
items.stem: A 45-year-old man with known hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is booked for laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Five minutes after induction his BP is 70/40 and his heart rate is 95.

points: Treat with a pure alpha-agonist: phenylephrine 50 to 100 micrograms, or vasopressin
Fluid bolus and leg elevation to restore preload
Reduce the volatile concentration
Treat tachycardia (esmolol)
Do NOT give ephedrine or inotropes
Check for another cause: bleeding, anaphylaxis, tension pneumothorax, ischaemia, arrhythmia

stages.prompt: Explain why those measures work and why ephedrine would make things worse.
points: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy narrows the LV outflow tract
In systole the anterior mitral leaflet is pulled toward the septum (SAM, Venturi effect and drag), worsening obstruction and causing posterior-directed MR
Obstruction is dynamic: worse with reduced LV volume (hypovolaemia, vasodilation), increased contractility, tachycardia, and reduced afterload
Diastolic dysfunction from LVH raises LVEDP, so supply-demand mismatch causes ischaemia despite normal coronaries
Ephedrine and beta-agonists raise contractility and heart rate, which increases the gradient

stages.prompt: His BP stays low despite phenylephrine. What next?
points: Use TOE to confirm SAM and LVOT obstruction
Start vasoconstrictor infusions (phenylephrine, vasopressin, noradrenaline)
Keep excluding other causes of hypotension
Call for help and tell the surgeon
Still avoid inotropes

stages.prompt: The surgeon wants to proceed with pneumoperitoneum. What are your concerns?
points: Insufflation raises SVR (helpful) but reduces venous return, especially head-up (harmful)
Slow insufflation at low pressure
Head-down tilt and fluid loading to maintain preload
Keep rate low-normal and sinus rhythm; treat AF early (cardiovert, amiodarone or beta-blocker; avoid digoxin)

items.title: 1. Ischaemic heart disease and chronic hypertension
items.los: IT_PO 2.7 (hypertension, IHD components); IT_PO 1.4 (coronary artery disease, hypertension components)
items.body:
## 1.1 Myocardial oxygen supply and demand

Perioperative ischaemia is an imbalance between supply and demand. Almost all of the heart's O2 extraction (about 70 to 80% at rest) is already used, so demand can only be met by raising coronary flow.

| Supply (determinants of flow) | Demand (determinants of consumption) |
|---|---|
| Coronary perfusion pressure = aortic DBP minus LVEDP (left ventricle) | Heart rate (the biggest lever; also shortens diastole) |
| Diastolic time (LV flow is mainly in diastole; falls with tachycardia) | Wall tension: preload (LVEDV), afterload (SBP), radius and thickness (Laplace: T = P x r / 2h) |
| Arterial O2 content (Hb, SaO2) | Contractility |
| Coronary vessel patency, tone and autoregulation (about 60 to 140 mmHg normally; lost distal to a stenosis) | Basal metabolic and shivering/thermal load |

> **Examiner favourite:** a tachycardic, hypotensive, anaemic patient with LVH is the worst case: demand up, DBP down, LVEDP up, O2 content down. Every part of anaesthetic management for IHD is built on this table.

**Types of myocardial injury (Fourth Universal Definition):**

| Category | Mechanism | Perioperative example |
|---|---|---|
| Type 1 MI | Plaque rupture or erosion with thrombus | Surgical stress, hypercoagulable state, catecholamine surge |
| Type 2 MI | Supply-demand mismatch without acute plaque event (most perioperative MIs) | Hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia, hypoxia |
| MINS (myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery) | Troponin rise of ischaemic aetiology within 30 days, usually asymptomatic; about 1 in 5 patients over 45 undergoing major surgery (VISION) | Detected only by routine troponin surveillance; carries roughly 10% 30-day mortality |
| Non-ischaemic injury | Sepsis, PE, arrhythmia, renal failure | Troponin rise without ischaemic features |

## 1.2 Assessing severity, stability and risk (IT_PO 2.7)

The task is to decide whether the patient is stable and low-risk (you initiate perioperative management) or unstable/high-risk (delay, optimise, involve a cardiologist).

**Step 1: Is there an active cardiac condition?** Delay elective surgery for:
- Acute coronary syndrome or unstable angina
- MI within 60 days (no revascularisation); the first 30 days carry the highest risk
- Decompensated heart failure
- Significant arrhythmia (rapid AF, high-grade AV block, symptomatic VT)
- Severe symptomatic valve disease

**Step 2: Surgical risk.** Low (<1% MACE: cataract, endoscopy, breast), intermediate (1 to 5%: orthopaedic, intraperitoneal, carotid), high (>5%: open aortic and major vascular, emergency major laparotomy).

**Step 3: Functional capacity.** Metabolic equivalents (MET): 1 MET = 3.5 mL/kg/min.

| Capacity | Examples |
|---|---|
| <4 METs (poor) | Cannot climb two flights of stairs or walk up a hill, cannot walk 4 blocks briskly |
| 4 to 7 METs | Climb a flight of stairs, walk on level ground at 6 km/h |
| >10 METs (excellent) | Swimming laps, singles tennis |

The Duke Activity Status Index (DASI) <34 and an inability to climb two flights predict MACE. In the METS study, subjective assessment performed poorly while DASI and NT-proBNP did better.

**Step 4: Risk indices.**

| Tool | Content |
|---|---|
| Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI, Lee 1999) | Six points: high-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, suprainguinal vascular); ischaemic heart disease; heart failure; cerebrovascular disease; insulin-treated diabetes; creatinine >177 micromol/L. Risk of major cardiac complication rises from about 0.4% (0) to 0.9% (1), 6.6% (2) and 11% (3 or more) in the derivation cohort; contemporary cohorts show higher figures |
| NSQIP MICA / Gupta | Online calculators with more predictors (age, ASA, functional status, creatinine, procedure type) |
| Biomarkers | Preoperative BNP or NT-proBNP (CCS 2017 recommends for age 65 or over, RCRI 1 or more, or age 45 to 64 with cardiovascular disease). High risk if BNP 92 ng/L or more, or NT-proBNP 300 ng/L or more |

**Step 5: Further testing only if it changes management.**

| Test | When | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 12-lead ECG | Known IHD, arrhythmia, structural disease, or intermediate/high-risk surgery | Baseline for postoperative comparison |
| Resting echo | Dyspnoea of unknown cause, known HF with change in status, suspected significant valve disease | Not routine |
| Stress testing (exercise ECG, dobutamine stress echo, perfusion scintigraphy) | Poor or unknown functional capacity AND elevated-risk surgery AND result would change management | See radionuclide imaging below |
| Coronary angiography | Only for standard indications (ACS, high-risk stress result) | Not for 'clearing' a patient |
| CT coronary angiography | Emerging, high negative predictive value | Not routine |

**Radionuclide imaging.** Myocardial perfusion scintigraphy (thallium-201 or technetium-99m sestamibi with exercise or pharmacological stress using dipyridamole, adenosine or dobutamine) detects reversible perfusion defects. Strengths: high negative predictive value, quantifies ischaemic burden. Limitations: low positive predictive value, false positives from LBBB or balanced three-vessel disease, cost, and radiation. A reversible defect over 20% of the LV, or multiple territories, predicts perioperative events. Dobutamine stress echo is an alternative that also provides valve and wall motion data; a new wall motion abnormality at a low heart rate (<60% of maximum) predicts worse outcomes.

> **Pitfall:** there is no evidence that testing then revascularising reduces perioperative events in stable IHD (CARP, DECREASE-V; see trials). Revascularise only for indications independent of the surgery.

## 1.3 Recent MI and coronary stents

**Recent MI:** delay elective surgery at least 60 days after MI (guideline consensus; the risk of reinfarction falls steeply over the first 4 to 6 weeks). If surgery cannot wait, explain the risk to the patient and surgeon, get cardiology input about whether revascularisation or DAPT is required first, then plan high-risk anaesthesia in a monitored environment (invasive BP, ST analysis, postoperative HDU, troponin surveillance).

**Stent types and timing:**

| Stent | Antiplatelet duration | Earliest elective non-cardiac surgery (guideline guide; check current local advice) |
|---|---|---|
| Balloon angioplasty alone | 2 to 4 weeks | About 2 weeks |
| Bare-metal stent (BMS) | DAPT at least 1 month | At least 1 month (many suggest 3 months) |
| Drug-eluting stent (DES), stable disease | DAPT 6 months (shorter in high-bleeding-risk patients) | At least 6 months; 3 months only if the delay is harmful |
| DES after ACS | DAPT up to 12 months | Ideally 12 months; time-sensitive surgery after 6 months |

**Mechanisms:** stent thrombosis is the dreaded complication (mortality 20 to 45%). Early premature DAPT cessation is the strongest predictor. Surgery is prothrombotic (catecholamines, inflammation, platelet activation, rebound after antiplatelet withdrawal). Newer-generation DES have faster endothelialisation, so shorter DAPT courses are now accepted.

**Mechanism and duration of clopidogrel.** Prodrug; absorbed, then about 85% is hydrolysed by esterases to inactive metabolite; the remaining 15% is activated by hepatic CYP2C19 (and CYP3A4/2B6) to an active thiol metabolite that irreversibly binds P2Y12 on the platelet. Platelet inhibition therefore lasts the platelet lifespan (7 to 10 days); platelet function recovers at about 10% per day from new platelet production. Loss-of-function CYP2C19 variants reduce effect; PPIs (omeprazole) may interfere via CYP2C19.

| P2Y12 inhibitor | Reversibility | Stop before surgery | Neuraxial block (ASRA/ESRA guide) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clopidogrel | Irreversible | 5 to 7 days | 5 to 7 days |
| Prasugrel | Irreversible, more potent | 7 days | 7 to 10 days |
| Ticagrelor | Reversible, direct acting | 3 to 5 days (5 per ESC) | 5 to 7 days |
| Cangrelor (IV) | Reversible, half-life about 3 to 6 min | Bridging option; stop 1 to 6 h before | n/a |

**Perioperative antiplatelet strategy:**
- Elective surgery: defer until the minimum DAPT period is complete.
- If surgery cannot be deferred, continue aspirin in all stent patients (lifelong in stented patients; the bleeding risk is acceptable in most operations, but see neurosurgery, posterior chamber eye surgery, intramedullary spinal surgery).
- Stop the P2Y12 inhibitor at the appropriate interval only after a joint decision among surgeon, cardiologist and anaesthetist (a joint decision is the typical exam answer). Restart within 24 to 48 hours; give a loading dose if clinically needed.
- High-risk stent (left main, bifurcation, recent ACS, multiple overlapping stents): consider bridging with cangrelor or a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor (tirofiban) under cardiology advice.
- Perform surgery in a hospital with a 24-hour cath lab (PCI is the treatment for stent thrombosis).
- If surgery proceeds with DAPT on board, have platelets available (an exam point: platelet transfusion does not work until the drug has cleared; ticagrelor and active clopidogrel metabolite inactivate transfused platelets for hours).

## 1.4 Perioperative drug therapy in IHD

| Drug | Recommendation | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Beta-blocker | Continue in patients already on one. Do not start on the day of surgery. If starting, begin at least 1 week beforehand and titrate to a resting HR 60 to 80 | POISE: fewer MIs but more deaths and strokes with high fixed-dose metoprolol, from hypotension and bradycardia. DECREASE trials unreliable (data integrity concerns) |
| Statin | Continue; start in vascular surgery or if indicated | Withdrawal increases events; low risk |
| Aspirin | Continue in stented patients and secondary prevention; do not start for primary prevention before surgery | POISE-2: no reduction in death or MI, more major bleeding |
| Clonidine | Do not start; continue only if chronically taking (rebound) | POISE-2: no benefit; more hypotension, non-fatal cardiac arrest |
| ACE inhibitor / ARB | Consider withholding 24 h before major surgery in hypertensive patients without heart failure; continue in HF | Observational links to intraoperative hypotension. STOP-or-NOT randomised trial |
| Nitrates | Continue; avoid abrupt cessation | Rebound angina |
| Calcium channel blockers | Continue | |
| Anticoagulants | Per indication (see valve section for mechanical valves) | CHEST 2022 |

## 1.5 Intraoperative management of IHD

**Haemodynamic goals:** keep HR low-normal (50 to 80), maintain MAP within 20% of baseline (do not allow MAP below 65 mmHg, or below 80 in chronic hypertension), keep preload adequate without overload, preserve contractility, and give oxygen. Avoid anaemia (target Hb above about 80 to 100 g/L; see MINT), hypothermia, shivering, hypercapnia and pain.

**Anaesthetic technique:** no technique is shown to be superior. Use volatile agents (modest ischaemic preconditioning, still debated), TIVA or balanced anaesthesia. Regional anaesthesia gives sympathetic block with reduced HR but can cause hypotension with neuraxial block; thoracic epidural may improve myocardial supply-demand but is not routinely indicated.

**Detection of ischaemia: ECG monitoring and other methods.**

| Method | Sensitivity and notes |
|---|---|
| 5-lead ECG with ST analysis | Lead V5 alone detects about 75% of episodes; II plus V5 about 80%; V4 plus V5 about 90%; II, V4 and V5 about 96% (London). Use monitor diagnostic or ST-trend mode; the standard 0.05 Hz high-pass filter in diagnostic mode (not 0.5 Hz monitor mode) avoids ST distortion |
| ST criteria | New ST depression of at least 1 mm (0.1 mV) horizontal or downsloping, 80 ms after the J point; ST elevation at least 1 mm (at least 2 mm in V1 to V3 depending on sex and age); T wave inversion; new LBBB |
| Limitations | LBBB, LVH with strain, paced rhythm, digoxin, WPW, electrolytes and hypothermia impair interpretation. ECG misses ischaemia in territories not covered (posterior, inferior in lead II only) and most ischaemia is silent under GA |
| TOE | New regional wall motion abnormality precedes ECG change and is more sensitive, but requires an expert operator and is not practical for most non-cardiac cases |
| PA catheter | Rising PAOP, large v waves (ischaemic MR); poor sensitivity |
| Invasive BP and haemodynamics | Hypotension or rising filling pressures are late signs |
| Troponin | Postoperative surveillance (24, 48 and 72 h) detects MINS |

**Treatment of intraoperative ischaemia:** correct the trigger first (hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia, hypoxaemia, pain, light anaesthesia), then use nitrate (GTN infusion if BP allows), a short-acting beta-blocker (esmolol) for tachycardia with adequate BP, phenylephrine or noradrenaline to restore coronary perfusion pressure, and 12-lead ECG. Call cardiology early for ST elevation (cath lab), see Topic 2.

## 1.6 Postoperative: troponin surveillance, MINS and risk reduction

- Most MINS is asymptomatic and occurs in the first 48 hours. Routine troponin on days 1 to 3 in at-risk patients is recommended in CCS and ESC guidance.
- MINS defined (VISION): high-sensitivity troponin T 20 to under 65 ng/L with an absolute rise of 5 ng/L or more, or 65 ng/L or more. Diagnosis of MINS needs no ischaemic symptoms.
- Management: aspirin and statin if not contraindicated; consider dabigatran 110 mg twice daily (MANAGE trial; bleeding risk, evidence limited); cardiology review; look for the cause (anaemia, tachyarrhythmia, sepsis, hypotension).
- Care environment: HDU or monitored bed for high-risk patients; analgesia (multimodal, avoid NSAID in IHD and renal disease), avoid hypothermia, shivering, anaemia, hypotension.

## 1.7 Chronic hypertension (IT_PO 2.7, IT_PO 1.4)

**Definition and grades (Australian/ISH):** clinic BP 140/90 mmHg or more; grade 1 140 to 159 / 90 to 99; grade 2 160 to 179 / 100 to 109; grade 3 180 or more / 110 or more. More than 90% is essential hypertension; secondary causes to consider: renal parenchymal disease and renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism (hypokalaemia), phaeochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, coarctation, OSA, drugs (NSAIDs, steroids, OCP, stimulants).

**Consequences relevant to anaesthesia:**
- Left ventricular hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction: poorly tolerates tachycardia, AF and hypovolaemia; very sensitive to preload.
- Autoregulation curves (cerebral, renal, coronary) are shifted to the right: hypotension at a BP that is normal for others can cause ischaemia (for example brain, kidney).
- Exaggerated hypotension at induction and exaggerated pressor response to laryngoscopy and surgical stimulation.
- Associated IHD, CKD, cerebrovascular disease, heart failure, AF, aortic dilatation.

**Perioperative risk and when to delay:**

| BP | Action |
|---|---|
| Below 180/110 mmHg | Proceed with elective surgery; no evidence that delaying to reduce BP improves outcome |
| 180/110 or above, or symptomatic / end-organ damage | Consider delaying elective surgery to allow gradual control (weeks), after excluding secondary causes. For urgent surgery, proceed and control with IV agents |

**Antihypertensive drugs:**

| Drug class | Perioperative approach |
|---|---|
| Beta-blockers | Continue (withdrawal causes rebound tachycardia and ischaemia) |
| Calcium channel blockers | Continue |
| Clonidine / methyldopa | Continue (rebound hypertension) |
| ACE inhibitor / ARB | Withhold on the day of surgery (24 h before) if used for hypertension; continue for heart failure. Restart when haemodynamically stable. Evidence is mixed (STOP-or-NOT) |
| Diuretics | Omit on the morning of surgery (hypovolaemia, hypokalaemia) |
| Aldosterone antagonists | Check potassium |

**Intraoperative:** limit BP variation. Target MAP within 20% of baseline (POISE-3 hypotension-avoidance vs hypertension-avoidance strategy; avoid MAP below 65 for more than a few minutes). Blunt the laryngoscopy response with an opioid (fentanyl, remifentanil), lidocaine, esmolol or deeper anaesthesia. Treat induction hypotension with phenylephrine or metaraminol rather than large fluid boluses.

**Perioperative hypertensive urgency** (treat when above 180/110 with symptoms or end-organ risk): exclude pain, light anaesthesia, hypercapnia, bladder distension, hypoxia, fluid overload and drug withdrawal. Drugs: labetalol (5 to 20 mg IV), GTN infusion, esmolol, hydralazine, nicardipine or clevidipine. Aim to lower MAP by no more than 20 to 25% in the first hour in chronic hypertension, to avoid watershed ischaemia.

items.title: What determines myocardial oxygen supply and demand?
items.q: What determines myocardial oxygen supply and demand?
items.a:
- Supply: coronary perfusion pressure (aortic diastolic minus LVEDP), diastolic time, arterial oxygen content (Hb, SaO2), vessel patency.
- Demand: heart rate, wall tension (preload, afterload, radius, thickness), contractility.
- Oxygen extraction is already about 70 to 80% at rest, so demand can only be met by raising flow.
- Worst case: tachycardia, hypotension, anaemia and LVH together.


> **Closing point:** Tachycardia hurts both sides: it shortens diastole and raises demand.

items.title: State the six RCRI predictors.
items.q: State the six RCRI predictors.
items.a:
- High-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, suprainguinal vascular).
- Ischaemic heart disease.
- Heart failure.
- Cerebrovascular disease.
- Insulin-treated diabetes.
- Creatinine above 177 micromol/L.


> **Closing point:** Risk of a major cardiac event climbs with each point; it is an estimate, not a decision tool.

items.title: How do you assess functional capacity?
items.q: How do you assess functional capacity?
items.a:
- METs: below 4 (cannot climb two flights of stairs) is poor.
- DASI questionnaire: score below 34 predicts events.
- CPET gives objective measures.
- Subjective assessment performed poorly in the METS study.


> **Closing point:** Use a structured tool, not impression.

items.title: Give the minimum delay before elective surgery after coronary stenting.
items.q: Give the minimum delay before elective surgery after coronary stenting.
items.a:
- Balloon angioplasty alone: about 2 weeks.
- Bare-metal stent: at least 1 month (preferably 3).
- Drug-eluting stent, stable disease: at least 6 months.
- Drug-eluting stent after ACS: 12 months ideally, 6 months if time-sensitive.
- Keep aspirin; stop the P2Y12 inhibitor only by joint decision.


> **Closing point:** Premature DAPT cessation is the biggest driver of stent thrombosis.

items.title: When should you stop each P2Y12 inhibitor before surgery?
items.q: When should you stop each P2Y12 inhibitor before surgery?
items.a:
- Clopidogrel 5 to 7 days (irreversible).
- Prasugrel 7 days (irreversible).
- Ticagrelor 3 to 5 days (reversible).
- Cangrelor: IV bridge, half-life 3 to 6 minutes.
- Platelet transfusion works only once the active drug has cleared.


> **Closing point:** Irreversible agents need platelet turnover of about 10% per day.

items.title: Which cardiac drugs do you continue and which do you not start before surgery?
items.q: Which cardiac drugs do you continue and which do you not start before surgery?
items.a:
- Continue: beta-blocker, statin, aspirin if stented, calcium channel blocker, nitrates, clonidine.
- Consider withholding on the day: ACEi/ARB, diuretics.
- Stop 3 days before: SGLT2 inhibitor.
- Do not start on the day: high-dose beta-blocker (POISE), clonidine and aspirin (POISE-2).


> **Closing point:** Withdrawal of beta-blockers, clonidine and statins is harmful.

items.title: What is MINS and how is it detected?
items.q: What is MINS and how is it detected?
items.a:
- Troponin rise of ischaemic origin within 30 days of surgery, not needing MI criteria.
- VISION hs-troponin T: 20 to under 65 ng/L with a rise of 5 or more, or 65 ng/L or more.
- Over 90% asymptomatic; 30-day mortality about 10%.
- Detect with troponin on days 1 to 3.


> **Closing point:** Most perioperative myocardial injury is silent, so look for it.

items.title: How sensitive is the ECG for intraoperative ischaemia, by lead?
items.q: How sensitive is the ECG for intraoperative ischaemia, by lead?
items.a:
- Lead II alone about 33%.
- V5 alone about 75%.
- II plus V5 about 80%; V4 plus V5 about 90%.
- II, V4 and V5 about 96%.
- Use the diagnostic filter (0.05 Hz).


> **Closing point:** Use a 5-lead system with V5 for at-risk patients.

items.title: What is the approach to a blood pressure of 185/112 before elective surgery?
items.q: What is the approach to a blood pressure of 185/112 before elective surgery?
items.a:
- Confirm the reading and look for end-organ damage and secondary causes.
- At or above 180/110, defer for gradual control; do not lower rapidly.
- Continue beta-blocker, CCB and clonidine; consider withholding ACEi/ARB and diuretic.


> **Closing point:** In chronic hypertension intraoperative hypotension is the bigger danger.

items.title: Why use a risk tool rather than clinical judgement alone?
items.q: Why use a risk tool rather than clinical judgement alone?
items.a:
- Patients are owed an estimate of risk during consent.
- Tools help target HDU or ICU and limited resources.
- SNAP-2 (22,631 patients): judgement was the only documented tool in 79%.
- Judgement plus a tool estimates risk better than judgement alone.


> **Closing point:** Use a tool to support, not replace, judgement.

*Source: Blue Book 2023*

items.title: Discrimination versus calibration: what is the difference?
items.q: Discrimination versus calibration: what is the difference?
items.a:
- Discrimination: separates patients with and without the outcome (AUROC).
- Calibration: predicted risk matches observed risk.
- Calibration drifts, so tools need periodic recalibration.
- Little evidence yet that risk stratification itself improves outcomes.


> **Closing point:** A good AUROC can still give the wrong absolute risk.

*Source: Blue Book 2023*

items.title: Name the main perioperative risk tools and one feature of each.
items.q: Name the main perioperative risk tools and one feature of each.
items.a:
- ASA-PS: not designed as a score but discriminates mortality well; part of SORT and nzRISK.
- RCRI: six-item cardiac risk.
- ACS NSQIP: 21 variables from about 1.4 million US patients; 30-day mortality and morbidity.
- P-POSSUM and SORT: 30-day mortality.
- nzRISK: New Zealand tool predicting mortality to 2 years.


> **Closing point:** Most tools stop at 30 days; nzRISK looks to 2 years.

*Source: Blue Book 2023*

items.title: Which definitions of perioperative myocardial injury should you know?
items.q: Which definitions of perioperative myocardial injury should you know?
items.a:
- MINS (VISION): hs-troponin T above 20 ng/L within 3 days, judged ischaemic, no non-ischaemic cause.
- AHA 2021: troponin above the 99th percentile, change in 30 days, symptoms not required.
- Fourth Universal Definition: injury can have any cause; infarction needs evidence of ischaemia.


> **Closing point:** Injury is a troponin rise; infarction needs ischaemia.

*Source: BJA Educ 2024*

items.title: How common is perioperative myocardial injury and what can you do about it?
items.q: How common is perioperative myocardial injury and what can you do about it?
items.a:
- About 20% of high-risk non-cardiac surgery patients.
- Mostly silent; associated with morbidity and mortality.
- Mechanisms mixed: supply-demand, plaque rupture, non-ischaemic.
- No definitive preventative or treatment strategy: correct triggers, surveillance, cardiology.


> **Closing point:** Surveillance finds it; trigger control is the treatment.

*Source: BJA Educ 2024*

items.title: Should you cancel surgery for a blood pressure above 180/110?
items.q: Should you cancel surgery for a blood pressure above 180/110?
items.a:
- Hypertension alone is not a reason to cancel.
- Decide on overall cardiac risk and end-organ damage.
- AoA/BHS: postpone above 180/110; POQI questions the evidence for a threshold.
- Intraoperative hypotension is the greater danger.


> **Closing point:** The whole patient, not one reading.

*Source: BJA Educ 2021*

items.title: Define MI and give the ECG criteria for STEMI.
items.q: Define MI and give the ECG criteria for STEMI.
items.a:
- Troponin rise and/or fall above the 99th percentile plus ischaemic symptoms, ECG change, Q waves, imaging evidence, or thrombus.
- Type 1: plaque rupture. Type 2: supply-demand mismatch (commonest after surgery).
- STEMI: J-point elevation of 1 mm in two contiguous leads (V2 to V3: 2 mm in men 40 or over, 1.5 mm in women).
- Equivalents: new LBBB with Sgarbossa features, posterior MI, de Winter, left main (aVR elevation).


> **Closing point:** Type 2 MI is treated by correcting the imbalance.

items.title: Match ECG leads to coronary territories.
items.q: Match ECG leads to coronary territories.
items.a:
- Septal V1 to V2 and anterior V3 to V4: LAD.
- Lateral I, aVL, V5 to V6: diagonal or circumflex.
- Inferior II, III, aVF: RCA (80%) or circumflex.
- Posterior: ST depression with tall R in V1 to V3 (confirm V7 to V9).
- RV: V4R.


> **Closing point:** Territory leads to vessel, vessel to complications.

items.title: List the initial management of ACS.
items.q: List the initial management of ACS.
items.a:
- Monitor, 12-lead ECG, titrated opioid; oxygen only if SpO2 below 90%.
- Aspirin 150 to 300 mg and a P2Y12 inhibitor per cardiology.
- Anticoagulation (UFH or enoxaparin); GTN if hypertensive or ongoing pain.
- Beta-blocker only if no heart failure, shock or block; high-intensity statin.
- Early reperfusion.


> **Closing point:** Reperfusion matters more than drugs.

items.title: What are the reperfusion options and why is fibrinolysis a problem after surgery?
items.q: What are the reperfusion options and why is fibrinolysis a problem after surgery?
items.a:
- Primary PCI: first contact to device within 90 minutes (60 if at a PCI centre).
- Fibrinolysis if PCI cannot be done within 120 minutes.
- Major surgery within 3 weeks is a relative contraindication (bleeding).
- Rescue PCI if less than 50% ST resolution.


> **Closing point:** After surgery prefer PCI.

items.title: Define cardiogenic shock and the SCAI stages.
items.q: Define cardiogenic shock and the SCAI stages.
items.a:
- SBP below 90 for 30 minutes or vasopressors needed, with hypoperfusion (lactate above 2, oliguria, cool peripheries) and a cardiac cause.
- Stages: A at risk, B beginning, C classic, D deteriorating, E extremis.
- Mortality about 40 to 50%.


> **Closing point:** Lactate and response to treatment define the stage.

items.title: Which vasoactive drugs for cardiogenic shock?
items.q: Which vasoactive drugs for cardiogenic shock?
items.a:
- Noradrenaline first line (SOAP II).
- Dobutamine for low output once MAP restored.
- Milrinone or levosimendan as alternatives.
- Vasopressin to spare catecholamines.
- Lowest dose for the shortest time.


> **Closing point:** Perfusion pressure first, then flow.

items.title: Compare IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO.
items.q: Compare IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO.
items.a:
- IABP: about 0.5 L/min, afterload reduction; no mortality benefit (IABP-SHOCK II).
- Impella: 2.5 to 5.5 L/min; DanGer Shock showed lower mortality in selected STEMI shock; bleeding and limb ischaemia.
- VA-ECMO: full support; no 30-day benefit in ECLS-SHOCK; raises afterload so vent the LV.


> **Closing point:** Know the exit strategy before insertion.

items.title: How do you read an IABP 1:2 trace?
items.q: How do you read an IABP 1:2 trace?
items.a:
- Inflation at the dicrotic notch; deflation just before systole.
- Diastolic augmentation higher than unassisted systole.
- Assisted end-diastolic and assisted systolic pressures are lower than unassisted.
- Early inflation shortens systole; late deflation raises afterload.


> **Closing point:** Inflate at the notch, deflate before systole.

items.title: What is the mortality of cardiogenic shock after MI and what is the only treatment proven to improve it?
items.q: What is the mortality of cardiogenic shock after MI and what is the only treatment proven to improve it?
items.a:
- Mortality 40 to 70%; about 9% of STEMI.
- Defined by end-organ hypoperfusion, not blood pressure alone.
- PCI revascularisation is the only treatment definitively shown to improve outcome.


> **Closing point:** Revascularise early.

*Source: BJA Educ 2023*

items.title: Quote the maximum output of each mechanical circulatory support device.
items.q: Quote the maximum output of each mechanical circulatory support device.
items.a:
- IABP about 0.8 L/min.
- Impella 2.5 to 5.0 L/min.
- TandemHeart 4.0 L/min.
- VA-ECMO up to 7 L/min.
- Use the least support needed.


> **Closing point:** More support means more complications.

*Source: BJA Educ 2023*

items.title: Why is noradrenaline contentious in cardiogenic shock after MI?
items.q: Why is noradrenaline contentious in cardiogenic shock after MI?
items.a:
- The syndrome has intense intrinsic vasoconstriction and high SVR.
- A pure vasopressor can raise LV afterload and worsen output.
- Inodilators can reduce afterload but cause hypotension and arrhythmia.
- Titrate carefully with invasive monitoring.


> **Closing point:** Perfusion pressure and afterload pull in opposite directions.

*Source: BJA Educ 2023*

items.title: Classify heart failure.
items.q: Classify heart failure.
items.a:
- By EF: HFrEF 40% or less, HFmrEF 41 to 49%, HFpEF 50% or more.
- By severity: NYHA I to IV and ACC/AHA stages A to D.
- By profile: warm/cold and wet/dry.


> **Closing point:** HFpEF is about half of all heart failure.

items.title: Name the four pillars of HFrEF therapy.
items.q: Name the four pillars of HFrEF therapy.
items.a:
- ARNI, ACEi or ARB.
- Beta-blocker.
- Mineralocorticoid antagonist.
- SGLT2 inhibitor.
- All improve survival; restart early after surgery.


> **Closing point:** Hold SGLT2 inhibitors for 3 days before surgery.

items.title: Compare systolic and diastolic dysfunction.
items.q: Compare systolic and diastolic dysfunction.
items.a:
- Systolic: low contractility, dilated LV, flat Starling curve.
- Diastolic: stiff LV, normal EF, steep pressure-volume curve.
- Diastolic failure: tachycardia and AF are poorly tolerated.
- Both: avoid ischaemia.


> **Closing point:** Diastolic failure is a pressure problem.

items.title: How does echo grade diastolic function?
items.q: How does echo grade diastolic function?
items.a:
- Screening: septal e' below 7, lateral e' below 10, E/e' above 14, LAVI above 34, TR velocity above 2.8.
- Grade I: E/A below 0.8. Grade II: pseudonormal, E/e' 10 to 14. Grade III: restrictive, DT below 160 ms.
- Limits: AF, MR, MS, tachycardia.


> **Closing point:** Pseudonormal is the easiest to miss.

items.title: State the haemodynamic goals for induction in EF 20%.
items.q: State the haemodynamic goals for induction in EF 20%.
items.a:
- Arterial line first; vasopressor infusing.
- Reduced doses of etomidate or ketamine, or slowly titrated propofol with fentanyl.
- Preload maintained, afterload low-normal, rate normal-high, sinus rhythm.
- Low mean airway pressure.


> **Closing point:** Pre-empt hypotension with vasopressors.

items.title: Outline the management of acute decompensated heart failure with low output.
items.q: Outline the management of acute decompensated heart failure with low output.
items.a:
- Respiratory support: CPAP/NIV; intubation with vasopressor running.
- Perfusion first: noradrenaline, dobutamine or milrinone.
- Decongest: IV furosemide; resistance: thiazide or acetazolamide.
- Mechanical support if refractory; treat the cause (CHAMP).


> **Closing point:** In the cold and wet patient, perfusion comes before decongestion.

items.title: When do you stop and restart an SGLT2 inhibitor?
items.q: When do you stop and restart an SGLT2 inhibitor?
items.a:
- Stop 3 days before non-day surgery or bowel preparation (day of surgery and 2 days before).
- UK consensus: 2 days, except for prolonged fasting.
- Restart only when eating and drinking normally and the acute illness has resolved.
- Teach a sick-day plan.


> **Closing point:** The danger is euglycaemic DKA: look for ketones, not glucose.

*Source: Blue Book 2021*

items.title: Why do SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure admissions?
items.q: Why do SGLT2 inhibitors reduce heart failure admissions?
items.a:
- Benefit within months, regardless of HbA1c or diabetes status.
- Not explained by glucose lowering.
- Proposed: reverse remodelling (lower LV volumes and mass).
- Proposed: less cardiac fibrosis and better myocardial metabolism.


> **Closing point:** The speed of benefit points away from glucose control.

*Source: Blue Book 2021*

items.title: What are the four phases of diastole?
items.q: What are the four phases of diastole?
items.a:
- Isovolumic relaxation (active, energy-dependent).
- Early rapid filling: suction from LV recoil, up to 80% of filling.
- Diastasis: filling set by compliance.
- Late filling: atrial contraction (lost in AF).


> **Closing point:** Ischaemia impairs relaxation because relaxation uses ATP.

*Source: Blue Book 2017*

items.title: Grade diastolic dysfunction with the simplified E/e' algorithm.
items.q: Grade diastolic dysfunction with the simplified E/e' algorithm.
items.a:
- Grade 1 impaired relaxation: E/e' 8 or less.
- Grade 2 pseudonormal: E/e' 9 to 12.
- Grade 3 restrictive: E/e' above 13.
- Works in AF where there is no A wave.


> **Closing point:** E/e' is the single most useful number.

*Source: Blue Book 2017*

items.title: What conditions travel with HFpEF?
items.q: What conditions travel with HFpEF?
items.a:
- 40 to 50% of all heart failure.
- Hypertension (70 to 88%), AF (30 to 37%), coronary disease, diabetes, pulmonary hypertension.
- Commoner in the elderly, obese and women.
- Mortality is higher than in the general population.


> **Closing point:** Normal EF does not exclude heart failure.

*Source: Blue Book 2017*

items.title: State the anticoagulation targets and plan for an LVAD patient needing surgery.
items.q: State the anticoagulation targets and plan for an LVAD patient needing surgery.
items.a:
- Warfarin: INR 2.5 to 3.5 (HeartMate II), 2.0 to 3.0 (HeartMate 3, HVAD), plus an antiplatelet.
- Elective: stop warfarin 5 days before; bridge with heparin once INR is below 2.0.
- Emergency: factor concentrate (Prothrombinex), not vitamin K, to INR below 1.5.


> **Closing point:** Reverse with factor concentrate because warfarin must restart.

*Source: Blue Book 2021*

items.title: What are the main perioperative problems in a patient with an LVAD?
items.q: What are the main perioperative problems in a patient with an LVAD?
items.a:
- Hypotension is commonest, then AKI, bleeding and arrhythmia.
- Think: haemodynamics, determinants of VAD preload, monitoring, anticoagulation, asepsis.
- Pulses are non-palpable; NIBP may need Doppler.
- Pacemaker or ICD: asynchronous mode, tachy therapies off.


> **Closing point:** Protect the RV and keep the preload up.

*Source: Blue Book 2021*

items.title: Why does atropine fail in a transplanted heart?
items.q: Why does atropine fail in a transplanted heart?
items.a:
- The heart is denervated: vagal tone is gone.
- Resting rate is 90 to 100 beats/min.
- Atropine and glycopyrrolate: no effect.
- Use isoprenaline or a pacemaker for bradycardia.


> **Closing point:** Only direct-acting drugs work.

*Source: Blue Book 2019*

items.title: Which drugs behave differently in a heart transplant recipient?
items.q: Which drugs behave differently in a heart transplant recipient?
items.a:
- Ephedrine: reduced effect (indirect).
- Noradrenaline, adrenaline, dobutamine: exaggerated.
- Phenylephrine and metaraminol: effective, no reflex bradycardia.
- Adenosine: exaggerated bradycardia.
- Neostigmine: bradycardia possible.


> **Closing point:** Titrate catecholamines carefully.

*Source: Blue Book 2019*

items.title: How is the transplanted heart different physiologically?
items.q: How is the transplanted heart different physiologically?
items.a:
- No reflex tachycardia; preload dependent.
- Silent ischaemia: no angina.
- 25% AF or flutter, 10% need a pacemaker.
- Re-innervation is partial and unpredictable (sympathetic from 6 to 8 months).
- Ventricular arrhythmias suggest rejection or vasculopathy.


> **Closing point:** No reflex means volume matters most.

*Source: Blue Book 2019*

items.title: Which first-line treatments does the 2024 HFpEF review recommend?
items.q: Which first-line treatments does the 2024 HFpEF review recommend?
items.a:
- SGLT2 inhibitor.
- Diuretics for congestion.
- Treat comorbidities: hypertension, diabetes.
- Manage atrial fibrillation aggressively.
- Stop SGLT2 inhibitors 2 to 3 days before elective surgery.


> **Closing point:** HFpEF is about 50% of heart failure.

*Source: BJA Educ 2024*

items.title: Give the echo criteria for severe aortic stenosis.
items.q: Give the echo criteria for severe aortic stenosis.
items.a:
- Peak velocity 4 m/s or more.
- Mean gradient 40 mmHg or more.
- Valve area below 1.0 cm2 (indexed below 0.6).
- Dimensionless index below 0.25.
- Low-flow low-gradient: use dobutamine stress or CT calcium score.


> **Closing point:** Gradients depend on flow.

items.title: State the haemodynamic goals in aortic stenosis.
items.q: State the haemodynamic goals in aortic stenosis.
items.a:
- Rate 60 to 80; sinus rhythm.
- Preload full.
- SVR and MAP maintained; vasopressor first.
- Contractility preserved.
- Avoid single-shot spinal.


> **Closing point:** Hypotension, tachycardia and AF are the killers.

items.title: State the haemodynamic goals in aortic regurgitation and mitral stenosis.
items.q: State the haemodynamic goals in aortic regurgitation and mitral stenosis.
items.a:
- AR: rate 80 to 100, full preload, low-normal afterload.
- MS: rate 60 to 80, sinus rhythm, maintain SVR, avoid raised PVR.
- Avoid IABP in AR.
- MS: tachycardia shortens diastole and raises LA pressure.


> **Closing point:** AR likes it fast and vasodilated; MS likes it slow.

items.title: State the goals in mitral regurgitation.
items.q: State the goals in mitral regurgitation.
items.a:
- Rate normal to high-normal (80 to 90).
- Preload maintained.
- Low-normal afterload.
- Support contractility; keep PVR low.
- EF overestimates LV function.


> **Closing point:** Fast, full and vasodilated.

items.title: Give INR targets for mechanical valves and bridging indications.
items.q: Give INR targets for mechanical valves and bridging indications.
items.a:
- Bileaflet aortic without risk factors: 2.5.
- Mitral, tricuspid, or aortic with risk factors: 3.0.
- Bridge: mechanical mitral, caged-ball or tilting-disc, recent stroke.
- DOACs are contraindicated.


> **Closing point:** Valve position and type decide risk.

items.title: Why is warfarin vs heparin a dilemma in pregnancy with a mechanical valve?
items.q: Why is warfarin vs heparin a dilemma in pregnancy with a mechanical valve?
items.a:
- Warfarin: best valve protection; embryopathy at weeks 6 to 12, fetal haemorrhage.
- LMWH/UFH: do not cross placenta; more valve thrombosis; anti-Xa monitoring.
- Switch to LMWH or UFH at about 36 weeks; stop LMWH 24 hours before neuraxial.


> **Closing point:** Maternal valve thrombosis versus fetal harm.

items.title: Why is mitral stenosis dangerous in labour?
items.q: Why is mitral stenosis dangerous in labour?
items.a:
- Pregnancy raises cardiac output; labour adds pain and tachycardia.
- Tachycardia shortens diastolic filling and raises left atrial pressure.
- Result: pulmonary oedema or AF.
- Obstructive left lesions with PH carry 30 to 56% maternal mortality.


> **Closing point:** Keep the heart rate slow.

*Source: Blue Book 2023*

items.title: How should delivery be planned in rheumatic heart disease?
items.q: How should delivery be planned in rheumatic heart disease?
items.a:
- Vaginal delivery preferred if no obstetric indication.
- mWHO II: spontaneous labour if close to hospital.
- mWHO III or IV: planned induction in ICU.
- Planned caesarean can suit the highest-risk patients.


> **Closing point:** Plan timing, people and place before labour starts.

*Source: Blue Book 2023*

items.title: What is rapid ventricular pacing in TAVI?
items.q: What is rapid ventricular pacing in TAVI?
items.a:
- Pacing at 180 to 220 beats/min.
- Drops systolic pressure to below 50 mmHg for 5 to 10 seconds.
- Used during balloon valvuloplasty and valve deployment.
- Have vasopressors ready for recovery.


> **Closing point:** Pace down, then support up.

*Source: BJA Educ 2021*

items.title: List the complications of TAVI.
items.q: List the complications of TAVI.
items.a:
- Femoral artery injury (common).
- Conduction block needing a permanent pacemaker.
- Coronary artery occlusion.
- Stroke.
- Have an emergency bypass plan.


> **Closing point:** Vascular and conduction problems come first.

*Source: BJA Educ 2021*

items.title: Primary versus secondary mitral regurgitation?
items.q: Primary versus secondary mitral regurgitation?
items.a:
- Primary: structural leaflet or chordal abnormality.
- Secondary: LV size and geometry changes.
- Moderate or severe MR in about 10% at age 75.
- Transcatheter repair suits high surgical risk.


> **Closing point:** Secondary MR is a disease of the ventricle.

*Source: BJA Educ 2023*

items.title: Classify causes of pulmonary oedema by Starling mechanism.
items.q: Classify causes of pulmonary oedema by Starling mechanism.
items.a:
- Raised hydrostatic pressure: LV failure, fluid overload, valve disease.
- Increased permeability: ARDS, sepsis, TRALI, aspiration.
- Mixed: negative pressure, neurogenic, re-expansion.


> **Closing point:** Treat the dominant mechanism.

items.title: Give the immediate management of cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
items.q: Give the immediate management of cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
items.a:
- Sit upright; oxygen to SpO2 94% or more.
- CPAP or NIV (3CPO: faster relief).
- GTN if SBP above 100; IV furosemide.
- Treat the cause; avoid routine opioids.


> **Closing point:** CPAP and nitrate treat the pressure.

items.title: What do B-lines on lung ultrasound mean?
items.q: What do B-lines on lung ultrasound mean?
items.a:
- More than two B-lines per zone, in several zones: interstitial syndrome.
- Causes include pulmonary oedema, pneumonia and ARDS.
- A-lines with lung sliding are normal.
- Combine with echo and the clinical picture.


> **Closing point:** B-lines show fluid, not the cause.

*Source: Blue Book 2025*

items.title: List the anaesthetic do and do not for HCM with outflow obstruction.
items.q: List the anaesthetic do and do not for HCM with outflow obstruction.
items.a:
- Do: full preload, slow rate, sinus rhythm, alpha agonist.
- Do not: ephedrine, inotropes, vasodilators, hypovolaemia.
- Single-shot spinal is risky.
- Check the ICD.


> **Closing point:** Full, slow and tight.

items.title: Compare dilated, restrictive and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
items.q: Compare dilated, restrictive and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
items.a:
- Dilated: low EF; treat as HFrEF.
- Restrictive: stiff ventricle, fixed stroke volume; avoid bradycardia and vasodilation.
- Hypertrophic: dynamic obstruction.


> **Closing point:** Is the heart dilated, obstructed or stiff?

items.title: Principles of managing acute RV failure.
items.q: Principles of managing acute RV failure.
items.a:
- Reduce PVR: oxygen, normocarbia, inhaled nitric oxide.
- Perfusion: noradrenaline or vasopressin.
- Preload: avoid overload.
- Contractility: dobutamine or milrinone.


> **Closing point:** The RV needs pressure and a low PVR.

items.title: Which drugs raise pulmonary vascular resistance?
items.q: Which drugs raise pulmonary vascular resistance?
items.a:
- Nitrous oxide and desflurane.
- Large-dose ketamine in adults.
- Hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis, hypothermia and pain also raise PVR.
- Etomidate has the least effect on PVR (available in NZ, not Australia).


> **Closing point:** Avoid anything that raises RV afterload.

*Source: Blue Book 2021*

items.title: What ventilator settings protect the right ventricle?
items.q: What ventilator settings protect the right ventricle?
items.a:
- Avoid hypoxaemia (PaO2 below 60) and hypercapnia (PA pressure up about 1 mmHg per mmHg PaCO2).
- Tidal volume 6 mL/kg; plateau pressure below 30 cmH2O.
- PEEP no more than 10 cmH2O.
- Ventilate near FRC.


> **Closing point:** Both low and high lung volumes raise PVR.

*Source: Blue Book 2021*

items.title: Which vasopressors and inotropes suit a failing right ventricle?
items.q: Which vasopressors and inotropes suit a failing right ventricle?
items.a:
- Noradrenaline below 0.2 microgram/kg/min (PVR rises above 0.5).
- Vasopressin: no rise in PVR.
- Dobutamine 2 to 5 microgram/kg/min.
- Milrinone 0.25 to 0.5 microgram/kg/min, with a vasopressor.
- Amiodarone, not beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers, for arrhythmia.


> **Closing point:** Support perfusion pressure and contractility together.

*Source: Blue Book 2021*

items.title: What are the WHO groups of pulmonary hypertension and why do they matter?
items.q: What are the WHO groups of pulmonary hypertension and why do they matter?
items.a:
- 1 PAH; 2 left heart disease; 3 lung disease or hypoxia; 4 CTEPH; 5 multifactorial.
- Cause changes treatment: sildenafil for PAH, valvuloplasty for mitral stenosis, CPAP for OSA.
- Perioperative mortality 10 to 15%, morbidity about 40%.


> **Closing point:** Find the cause, then optimise.

*Source: Blue Book 2015*

items.title: How is peripartum cardiomyopathy defined and delivered?
items.q: How is peripartum cardiomyopathy defined and delivered?
items.a:
- Heart failure from LV systolic dysfunction (EF below 45%) in late pregnancy or the months after.
- Diagnosis of exclusion; check BNP if orthopnoea or PND.
- Vaginal delivery with neuraxial analgesia where possible.
- Recurrence risk in later pregnancies.


> **Closing point:** Think of it in any breathless postpartum woman.

*Source: BJA Educ 2023*

items.title: Which TOE view best monitors ischaemia in all coronary territories?
items.q: Which TOE view best monitors ischaemia in all coronary territories?
items.a:
- Transgastric mid short-axis.
- Shows all six mid-ventricular segments.
- New regional wall motion abnormality precedes ECG change.


> **Closing point:** One view, three territories.

items.title: 1. Stepwise cardiac risk assessment before major surgery
items.q: A 68-year-old with known IHD and hypertension is booked for open colectomy. He gets breathless on one flight of stairs. Outline your preoperative cardiac assessment and what would change your management.
items.a:
## 1. Why assess

The purposes are to estimate the risk of major adverse cardiac events (MACE: cardiac death, non-fatal MI, cardiac arrest), to identify patients whose management or timing should change, to optimise treatment, and to inform consent and the choice of anaesthetic technique and postoperative location.

## 2. A stepwise approach (ESC, CCS and ACC/AHA guidelines)

**Step 1: Urgency and active cardiac conditions.**
- Emergency surgery proceeds with risk mitigation; no testing that delays it.
- Active conditions that require treatment first: unstable coronary syndromes, decompensated heart failure, significant arrhythmias, severe symptomatic valve disease.

**Step 2: Surgical risk.**
- Low (below 1% MACE): superficial, cataract, endoscopic.
- Intermediate (1 to 5%): intraperitoneal, orthopaedic, head and neck, carotid.
- High (above 5%): open aortic and major vascular, major thoracic and some emergency surgery.
- Open colectomy is intermediate to high risk.

**Step 3: Patient risk.**
- RCRI: high-risk surgery, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, creatinine above 177 micromol/L. This patient scores at least 2 (IHD and high-risk surgery), a MACE risk of about 10%.
- Other tools: NSQIP-MICA, ACS NSQIP risk calculator, and frailty assessment.

**Step 4: Functional capacity.**
- Breathlessness on one flight of stairs implies below 4 METs, which is poor. Poor capacity raises risk and limits the usefulness of exercise testing.
- The DASI questionnaire (score below 34 predicts events) and CPET are more reliable than subjective estimates (METS study showed DASI predicted events, and that clinicians' own estimates were not reliable).

**Step 5: Biomarkers and investigations.**
- Resting 12-lead ECG for all intermediate and high-risk patients: baseline, rhythm, ischaemia, LVH, conduction.
- BNP or NT-proBNP before surgery in patients aged 65 or over, or with cardiovascular disease (CCS guidelines): elevated values predict MACE and mortality (BNP of 92 ng/L or more and NT-proBNP 300 ng/L or more indicate higher risk).
- Echocardiography when the cause of breathlessness is unclear, for new symptoms, murmurs, or suspected HF or valve disease, or in patients with unknown LV function and high-risk surgery.
- Non-invasive stress testing (dobutamine stress echo or myocardial perfusion imaging) only when poor function and high risk coincide and the result would alter management.

**Step 6: Revascularisation.**
- CARP (revascularisation before vascular surgery in stable CAD) and DECREASE-V showed no benefit. Revascularisation is indicated only on its own merits (left main disease, ACS, severe multivessel disease with symptoms). It adds delay and DAPT problems.

## 3. What changes management

| Finding | Response |
|---|---|
| Active ACS, HF or arrhythmia | Defer elective surgery, treat first |
| High risk and poor capacity | Multidisciplinary discussion; consider whether surgery is required, whether a less invasive alternative exists |
| Raised BNP | Higher risk category; closer monitoring |
| Ischaemia on stress testing at low threshold | Cardiology input |
| Severe valve disease | Treat or modify technique (see R15) |

## 4. Optimisation and plan

- Continue beta-blocker, statin, and antihypertensives (hold ACEi/ARB on the day). Start a statin if not on one. Check anaemia, electrolytes and renal function.
- Anaesthetic plan: invasive arterial pressure, avoidance of tachycardia and hypotension, normothermia, avoidance of anaemia, a restrictive-to-goal-directed fluid plan.
- Postoperative: HDU, troponin on days 1 and 2 (VISION showed that troponin elevation within 3 days predicts 30 day mortality).
- Consent: discuss the risks of MI, stroke and death in numerical terms.

> **Examiner lens:** testing is justified only when it changes management; do not recommend routine revascularisation.

items.title: 2. Perioperative risk prediction tools
items.q: Discuss the role and limitations of risk prediction tools in adult non-cardiac surgery. Which tools would you use in Australia and New Zealand, and how does a tool change your management?
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2023, "Adult perioperative risk stratification" (Engelbrecht, Khoyratty, Reilly).

## Why use a tool

There is an ethical duty to give the patient an estimate of risk during consent. Tools can also identify patients who need enhanced monitoring, HDU or ICU, and help allocate limited resources. In the SNAP-2 study of 22,631 patients, **clinician judgement was the only documented tool in 79%**, and using a tool alongside judgement improved risk estimation.

## What makes a good tool

It should be simple, validated in the local population, and judged on two measures:

- **Discrimination:** ability to separate patients who die from those who survive (area under the ROC curve).
- **Calibration:** whether predicted risk matches observed risk. Calibration drifts over time and needs periodic **recalibration**.

## Common tools

| Tool | Notes |
|---|---|
| ASA-PS | Not designed as a risk score but widely used; reasonable discrimination for mortality; a component of SORT and nzRISK |
| RCRI | Six-item major cardiac event estimate |
| ACS NSQIP calculator | About 1.4 million US patients, 21 variables, 30-day mortality and morbidity; proprietary; limits when applied to ANZ patients |
| P-POSSUM | Physiological and operative severity score, mortality and morbidity |
| SORT | Surgical Outcome Risk Tool: 30-day mortality, includes ASA-PS and urgency |
| nzRISK | New Zealand tool predicting mortality to **2 years**, not just 30 days |

## Limitations

- Most tools predict 30-day mortality, but long-term quality of life matters to patients.
- Models can underpredict in a different population; clinicians may adjust the score.
- There is **little evidence that identifying high-risk patients improves outcomes**; the harder task is to show that risk-stratified care changes patient-centred outcomes.

## Applying the result

Use the estimate for informed consent, shared decision making (including whether to proceed), choice of monitoring, and planned postoperative disposition. Add functional capacity and frailty to the numerical score.

## Self-marking checklist

- Gives the consent and resource-allocation rationale
- Quotes that clinician judgement alone is common and a tool adds value
- Distinguishes discrimination from calibration and mentions recalibration
- Names at least four tools with a feature of each (ASA-PS, RCRI, NSQIP, P-POSSUM, SORT, nzRISK)
- Notes nzRISK includes risk to 2 years
- States the limitation that outcome benefit is unproven
- Describes how the result changes consent and disposition

items.title: 3. Antiplatelet plan for a stented patient needing urgent surgery
items.q: A 72-year-old man has a drug-eluting stent placed 4 months ago for NSTEMI and takes aspirin and clopidogrel. He needs a semi-urgent bowel resection. How do you decide what to do with his antiplatelet therapy, and how do you plan the perioperative period?
items.a:
## 1. Framing the problem

- The competing risks are stent thrombosis (catastrophic, with mortality of 20 to 40% when it occurs perioperatively) and surgical bleeding. The surgery is semi-urgent, so the key questions are how long it can safely wait, and what bleeding risk the operation carries.
- Stent thrombosis is driven by: premature cessation of antiplatelet therapy (the strongest predictor), stent placed for ACS, the perioperative prothrombotic and inflammatory state, stent factors (left main, bifurcation, long or overlapping stents, small calibre, under-expansion), and patient factors (diabetes, low EF, renal impairment).
- A DES placed for NSTEMI 4 months ago is still within the high-risk window. Guidelines advise deferring elective surgery for 12 months after ACS (6 months after stable disease with a DES; some newer-generation DES allow 3 months). Surgery between 1 and 6 months after ACS carries a clearly raised MACE rate, which falls progressively with time.

## 2. Decision-making

| Question | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Can surgery wait until 6 months, ideally 12? | Each additional month lowers stent thrombosis risk |
| What is the surgical bleeding risk, and can the operation be done on aspirin alone? | Most abdominal surgery can be done on aspirin; a closed-space operation (neurosurgery, posterior chamber eye) may not |
| Stent characteristics and ACS history | Defines thrombotic risk, via the cardiologist |
| Are there alternatives (non-operative, laparoscopic, staged)? | May reduce risk or delay |

The decision should be made jointly with the surgeon, cardiologist and patient, and documented, including the consent discussion of the risk of MI, stent thrombosis and death.

## 3. Antiplatelet management if surgery cannot wait

- Continue aspirin throughout, unless bleeding risk is prohibitive (in which case discuss with the cardiologist). Aspirin continuation gives most of the protection against stent thrombosis, and POISE-2 showed no benefit to starting it in unselected patients but it does not apply to stented patients.
- Stop the P2Y12 inhibitor at the recommended interval: clopidogrel 5 to 7 days, prasugrel 7 days, ticagrelor 3 to 5 days. Restoring platelet function is the aim.
- Bridging: for very high thrombotic risk (recent stent within 3 months of ACS, left main or multiple overlapping stents, previous stent thrombosis) consider cangrelor, an IV reversible P2Y12 inhibitor with a half-life of 3 to 6 minutes, started 1 to 3 days after stopping the oral agent and stopped about 1 to 6 hours before surgery (BRIDGE trial). Heparin and GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors are alternatives in some centres but have drawbacks. Tirofiban or eptifibatide have been used in some centres.
- Restart the P2Y12 inhibitor as soon as bleeding allows (often within 24 to 48 hours), with a loading dose if the cardiologist advises, to reduce the vulnerable period.

## 4. Perioperative care

- Where: a centre with 24 hour interventional cardiology access (PCI for stent thrombosis is the treatment of choice, with a time-critical goal).
- Monitoring: invasive arterial pressure, five-lead ECG with ST analysis, consider TOE if instability; avoid tachycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, anaemia and pain.
- Anaesthetic technique: both general and regional are acceptable. Neuraxial blockade is only safe after washout (ASRA/ANZCA/ESAIC: clopidogrel 5 to 7 days, ticagrelor 5 to 7 days, prasugrel 7 to 10 days), and aspirin alone is not a contraindication. For this patient general anaesthesia is likely.
- Postoperative: HDU, troponin on days 1 and 2 (and day 3), ECG, early mobilisation, VTE prophylaxis (mechanical first if bleeding risk is high).

## 5. If bleeding or stent thrombosis occurs

- Bleeding on antiplatelet agents: surgical haemostasis, tranexamic acid, desmopressin in some settings; platelet transfusion is only effective after the drug has cleared (active metabolites of clopidogrel and ticagrelor bind transfused platelets), so timing matters.
- Stent thrombosis presents as STEMI. Call the cardiologist for urgent PCI, give aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor, and discuss anticoagulation with the surgeon.

> **Examiner lens:** show that you weigh stent thrombosis against surgical bleeding, keep aspirin, and make it a team decision.

items.title: 4. Perioperative cardioprotective drugs: what works and what harms
items.q: Summarise the evidence for starting or continuing beta-blockers, aspirin, clonidine, statins and ACE inhibitors around non-cardiac surgery.
items.a:
## 1. Rationale

Perioperative MI is mostly supply-demand mismatch (type 2) triggered by tachycardia, hypotension, anaemia and the stress response, with a minority from plaque rupture (type 1). Drugs have been trialled to blunt these mechanisms. The results show that the details (timing, dose, hypotension) are decisive.

## 2. Evidence by drug

| Drug | Trial and result | Mechanism of the finding | Practical conclusion |
|---|---|---|---|
| Beta-blocker | POISE (8351 patients): metoprolol succinate 100 mg started 2 to 4 hours before surgery and continued for 30 days reduced MI (HR about 0.73) but increased death (HR 1.33) and stroke (HR 2.17), with more hypotension and bradycardia. DECREASE-IV (bisoprolol) was positive but the investigator's work (Poldermans) was discredited, and meta-analyses excluding it show harm | Fixed high dose, no titration, started on the day | Continue in patients already taking them. Do not start high-dose on the day of surgery. If starting, begin at least a week before with titration to heart rate and BP. The 2014 ACC/AHA guideline gave a class III recommendation against day-of-surgery initiation |
| Aspirin | POISE-2 (10010 patients): no reduction in death or MI (HR 0.99), 23% more major bleeding. The prior-stent subgroup was small | Bleeding offsets any ischaemic benefit | Continue for stents and established secondary prevention; do not start for primary prevention |
| Clonidine | POISE-2: no reduction in death or MI, more hypotension and non-fatal cardiac arrest | Hypotension, rebound | Do not start. Continue if already taking (rebound hypertension on withdrawal) |
| Statins | DECREASE-III and observational data suggest benefit; withdrawal is associated with increased MI. LOAD trial: no benefit of high-dose loading | Plaque stabilisation, pleiotropic effects | Continue; reasonable to start before vascular surgery, ideally 2 or more weeks before |
| ACEi / ARB | Observational data link continuation with intraoperative hypotension and AKI. STOP-or-NOT (2024) found no significant difference in composite outcome between continuing and stopping before major non-cardiac surgery; POISE-3 supported a hypotension-avoidance strategy | Vasoplegia under anaesthesia | Reasonable either way. Many hold 24 hours before major surgery if used for hypertension; continue in HFrEF if haemodynamics permit |
| Tranexamic acid (POISE-3) | Reduced bleeding with no increase in composite cardiac events | Antifibrinolysis | Reasonable in patients at risk of bleeding |
| Calcium channel blockers | Small studies show reduced ischaemia with diltiazem or verapamil | Rate control, vasodilation | Continue if on them |

## 3. Common themes

- Hypotension is the common mechanism of harm: a MAP below 60 to 65 mmHg for more than a few minutes raises myocardial injury and AKI (VISION, Sessler, Walsh).
- Withdrawal syndromes (beta-blocker, clonidine, statin) are harmful, so continuation is the rule.
- Starting a new drug on the day of surgery has been shown to be ineffective or harmful.

## 4. Summary rule

Continue established cardiac drugs, avoid starting new cardioprotective agents on the day of surgery, avoid hypotension and tachycardia, and tailor ACEi/ARB handling to the indication and the procedure.

> **Examiner lens:** name the trial, the direction of effect and the mechanism of harm (hypotension).

items.title: 5. MINS, perioperative MI and the troponin rise
items.q: Define perioperative myocardial injury (MINS) and perioperative myocardial infarction. How are they detected, and how do you manage a patient with an asymptomatic troponin rise on postoperative day 1?
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Perioperative myocardial injury" (BJA Educ 2024).

## Definitions

Myocardial injury is always diagnosed by a **rise in cardiac troponin**, but there is no single standard definition.

- **MINS (VISION 2017):** myocardial injury judged ischaemic, within 3 days of surgery, with hs-troponin T above 20 ng/L and **no evidence of a non-ischaemic cause** (rapid AF, pulmonary embolus, sepsis). Ischaemic symptoms or signs are not needed.
- **AHA 2021:** troponin above the 99th percentile with an acute change in the first 30 days (typically within 72 hours), presumed ischaemic, with no overt non-ischaemic cause. Symptoms are not required because sedation and analgesia mask them.
- **Fourth Universal Definition:** perioperative myocardial **injury** can have any cause, including extracardiac. **Infarction** additionally requires evidence of ischaemia (symptoms, ECG change, new wall motion abnormality, or thrombus).

## Why it matters

Incidence is about **20% in high-risk patients** having non-cardiac surgery, most without symptoms, and it carries higher morbidity and mortality. The mechanisms are mixed and interact: supply-demand imbalance (hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia, hypoxia), plaque rupture, and non-ischaemic causes (sepsis, AF, PE, renal failure).

## Detection

Postoperative troponin surveillance in high-risk patients, usually on days 1 to 3, because most injury is silent. Use the same assay each time and compare with the baseline.

## Managing an asymptomatic rise

1. Examine the patient, take an ECG and review for a non-ischaemic cause.
2. Correct triggers: hypotension, tachycardia, anaemia, hypoxia, pain, hypervolaemia.
3. Echo if the ECG changes or haemodynamics are unstable.
4. Repeat troponin to see the trend.
5. Involve cardiology; consider aspirin and a statin if bleeding risk allows.
6. Review the plan for further surgery and follow-up.

There is **no definitive preventative or therapeutic strategy**: management is risk factor and trigger control plus the decision to treat as an ACS if ischaemia is evident.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines MINS and perioperative MI and distinguishes injury from infarction
- Gives the 20 ng/L hs-troponin T criterion and notes symptoms are not required
- Quotes incidence about 20% and association with poor outcomes
- Explains mechanisms (supply-demand, plaque rupture, non-ischaemic)
- Describes troponin surveillance on days 1 to 3
- Gives a stepwise plan for an asymptomatic rise
- States no proven preventative therapy

items.title: 6. New ST depression under general anaesthesia
items.q: Thirty minutes into an emergency laparotomy in a patient with known IHD, you see new 2 mm ST depression in V5. Describe your immediate management and how you confirm and treat the cause.
items.a:
## 1. Recognition and verification (first 30 to 60 seconds)

- Announce the finding, ask the surgeon to pause or simplify if the patient is unstable, and call for help early.
- Confirm the change is real: check lead connections and placement, switch the monitor to diagnostic mode (ST analysis in monitor filter mode can distort ST segments), check all leads (II, V5, V4, aVF, V1), look for artefact (diathermy, shivering, movement), and review the rhythm.
- ST depression of 1 mm or more, 60 to 80 ms after the J point, in two leads is the usual criterion. ST elevation of 1 mm or more suggests transmural ischaemia or vasospasm and needs a different approach.
- Sensitivity of leads: V5 alone detects about 75% of ischaemic episodes, II plus V5 about 80%, V4 plus V5 about 90%, and II plus V4 plus V5 about 96% (London). Limitations: LBBB, paced rhythm, digoxin, LVH, hypokalaemia, hypothermia, and posterior or circumflex ischaemia.

## 2. Immediate bedside assessment of supply and demand

| Supply | Demand |
|---|---|
| Hypotension: MAP below 65 or a drop of 20 to 30% from baseline; low diastolic pressure | Tachycardia, hypertension |
| Hypoxia, anaemia (check Hb), hypercarbia | Light anaesthesia, pain, shivering |
| Tachycardia (short diastolic time) | Sympathetic stimulation (laryngoscopy, incision, peritoneal traction) |
| Coronary spasm, embolus, thrombosis | Hypervolaemia, ventricular distension |
| Hypovolaemia, bleeding, vasodilation | Inotropes, exogenous catecholamines |

Check the circuit and ventilation (ETCO2, SpO2, FiO2), temperature, glucose, electrolytes (potassium, magnesium), surgical events (bleeding, retractor pressure on the diaphragm or IVC, pneumoperitoneum, aortic clamping), and recent drugs (vasopressors, ephedrine, adrenaline).

## 3. Immediate treatment (cause directed)

- **Hypotension:** treat promptly with a vasopressor such as phenylephrine or noradrenaline to restore a MAP of at least 65 mmHg (higher in chronic hypertension); a diastolic pressure above 50 to 60 mmHg is useful for coronary flow. Treat bleeding with fluid and blood. Avoid excessive fluid if LV function is poor.
- **Tachycardia:** deepen anaesthesia and analgesia, give esmolol (0.5 mg/kg bolus then infusion) or metoprolol if BP allows, treat AF or SVT with synchronised cardioversion if unstable, amiodarone for rate control.
- **Hypoxia and anaemia:** 100% oxygen, transfuse if Hb is below 80 g/L, or higher with ongoing ischaemia (the threshold of 80 to 100 g/L is guideline-supported).
- **Hypertension and light anaesthesia:** deepen anaesthesia, give an opioid, treat with a short-acting agent.
- **Anti-ischaemic drugs:** GTN infusion (5 to 100 micrograms/min) if the BP is adequate and there is no RV involvement or severe AS; this should not be used to treat hypotension-driven ischaemia. Consider diltiazem for vasospasm.

## 4. Escalation and diagnosis

- Obtain a 12-lead ECG, arterial gas (haemoglobin, lactate, potassium), and an urgent TOE if available: new RWMA in the transgastric mid short-axis view confirms ischaemia, localises the territory and assesses LV and RV function, valves, and tamponade.
- Send troponin, repeating at 3 to 6 hours.
- If ST elevation, haemodynamic collapse, malignant arrhythmia, or persisting ST depression despite treatment: call cardiology early. The options are PCI (consider the antiplatelet requirement and the surgical field), IABP or other mechanical support, and discussion with the surgeon about terminating the operation.
- If the surgery is not time-critical, consider abbreviating it to damage control.

## 5. Afterwards

ICU or HDU, serial ECG and troponin, aspirin and statin if bleeding allows, cardiology review, correction of triggers, and a plan for the antiplatelet and anticoagulant question. Document and disclose to the patient.

> **Examiner lens:** treat the cause before the ECG; know ECG sensitivity (V5 about 75%, II plus V5 about 80%, V4 plus V5 about 90%).

items.title: 7. Blood pressure 185/112 before elective surgery
items.q: A 58-year-old man for elective hip replacement has a clinic blood pressure of 185/112 mmHg. Discuss whether you proceed and how you manage his antihypertensives.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Preoperative hypertension" (BJA Educ 2021).

## Should surgery go ahead?

- High blood pressure **in isolation is not a reason to cancel** elective surgery. The decision should rest on his **overall cardiac risk**, not one reading.
- The AoA/BHS statement suggests postponing if the pressure is **above 180/110**; the more recent POQI consensus questions whether there is enough evidence to set a threshold.
- Confirm the reading (repeat, ambulatory or home measurement). Look for end-organ damage (LV hypertrophy, renal impairment, retinopathy, ischaemia) and secondary causes.
- Postpone if there is end-organ damage or if there is time to improve control; avoid rapid lowering.

## Why

Chronic hypertension shifts the autoregulation curve to the right. Intraoperative hypotension is probably more harmful than preoperative hypertension, and preoperative hypotension may itself signal higher risk.

## Medication

- Continue beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers and other agents.
- **ACE inhibitors and ARBs:** consider withholding on the morning of surgery because of the risk of vasoplegia; restart when haemodynamically stable. Combination tablets complicate this.
- Diuretics: usually withheld on the day if euvolaemic.
- Do not start a beta-blocker or clonidine immediately before surgery.

## Intraoperative and postoperative

Avoid hypotension relative to the baseline (aim within 20% of baseline or MAP above 65 to 70), avoid hypertensive surges at intubation, and treat postoperative pain and withdrawal. Restart antihypertensives early.

## Self-marking checklist

- States that hypertension alone is not a reason to cancel and uses overall cardiac risk
- Quotes the 180/110 AoA/BHS threshold and the POQI position
- Assesses for end-organ damage and secondary causes
- Explains autoregulation shift and the danger of intraoperative hypotension
- Manages ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker and diuretic correctly
- Does not start beta-blocker or clonidine acutely
- Gives intraoperative and postoperative blood pressure targets

items.title: 8. Intraoperative hypotension in IHD and hypertension
items.q: Discuss the significance of intraoperative hypotension in a patient with ischaemic heart disease and hypertension. How would you define it, prevent it and treat it?
items.a:
## Why it matters

Hypotension reduces coronary perfusion pressure (aortic diastolic pressure minus LVEDP), cerebral and renal perfusion. In a hypertensive patient with fixed coronary disease and LVH, tolerance is poor because autoregulation is shifted to the right and subendocardial supply is marginal. Observational data (VISION, Sessler, Walsh) link a **MAP below 65 mmHg for more than a few minutes** with myocardial injury, acute kidney injury and death, with risk rising with depth and duration.

## Definition

There is no single definition. Common thresholds are MAP below 65 mmHg, systolic below 90 to 100 mmHg, or a fall of more than 20 to 30% from baseline. In chronic hypertension, relative thresholds (baseline) are more meaningful. Evidence from POISE-3 and other trials does not give a simple proven target, but avoiding prolonged hypotension is accepted practice.

## Causes

Anaesthetic vasodilatation and myocardial depression, hypovolaemia and bleeding, neuraxial sympathectomy, drugs (ACEi/ARB on the morning), positive pressure ventilation, pneumoperitoneum and positioning, arrhythmia, ischaemia, tension pneumothorax, anaphylaxis, and surgical manipulation.

## Prevention

- Review and consider withholding ACEi/ARB on the morning of major surgery; avoid prolonged fasting and ensure euvolaemia.
- **Arterial line** before induction in high-risk patients; reduced-dose, titrated induction; vasopressor ready or infusing (phenylephrine or noradrenaline).
- Goal-directed haemodynamic therapy, avoiding both hypovolaemia and overload.
- Keep depth of anaesthesia appropriate; use regional techniques with slow titration.

## Treatment

1. Confirm the reading (zero, level, cuff) and check the rhythm and ECG.
2. Look for a cause: bleeding, anaphylaxis, tension pneumothorax, arrhythmia, ischaemia, drug error.
3. Reduce anaesthetic depth, give a vasopressor (phenylephrine, metaraminol, noradrenaline), use fluid or blood if hypovolaemic, treat bradycardia.
4. Persistent hypotension with ST change: 12-lead ECG, TOE, and call for help.

## Aim

Keep MAP at or above baseline-related threshold (about 65 mmHg or within 20% of baseline) and maintain heart rate low-normal.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains the physiological consequences of hypotension for coronary, cerebral and renal perfusion
- Cites the association with myocardial injury, AKI and death, and the MAP 65 threshold
- Acknowledges there is no single proven definition or target; uses relative thresholds in hypertension
- Lists causes
- Gives preventive strategies (ACEi/ARB, arterial line, vasopressors, goal-directed therapy)
- Gives a stepwise treatment plan

items.title: 9. Chest pain and ST elevation in PACU
items.q: A 70-year-old man 2 hours after radical prostatectomy has crushing chest pain, BP 90/50, HR 110 and widespread anterior ST elevation. Describe your immediate management and treatment priorities.
items.a:
## 1. Immediate response (the first 5 minutes)
- Call for help: the PACU team, anaesthetic senior, and the on-call cardiologist. Move to a monitored resuscitation space with defibrillator pads attached.
- Standard monitoring, large-bore IV access, supplemental oxygen only if SpO2 is below 90% (AVOID, DETO2X), a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes, bedside echocardiography, and bloods (troponin, FBC, electrolytes, renal function, coagulation, group and screen, gas).
- Analgesia: titrated IV opioid (fentanyl), with caution because of hypotension.

## 2. Diagnosis
- Widespread anterior ST elevation with chest pain suggests LAD occlusion. This is a type 1 MI or a type 2 MI with ST elevation (rarer).
- Differential: PE (right heart strain), aortic dissection, tamponade, pericarditis, takotsubo cardiomyopathy, coronary vasospasm, coronary embolus (air, paradoxical), and hyperkalaemia.
- Echo helps: anterior wall akinesia (LAD), RV dilation (PE), effusion (tamponade), aortic root and flap (dissection), and global dysfunction (takotsubo).
- Check for bleeding as a cause of hypotension and tachycardia.

## 3. Haemodynamic stabilisation
- BP 90/50 with a rate of 110 suggests low output or hypovolaemia.
- If hypovolaemia (bleeding, third spacing) is suspected, give small fluid or blood boluses of 250 mL, reassessing after each.
- If cardiogenic, avoid large volumes; use noradrenaline to maintain a MAP of at least 65, with dobutamine if low output persists after pressure is restored (see R8).
- Avoid nitrates while hypotensive.

## 4. Reperfusion strategy: the central decision
| Option | Considerations here |
|---|---|
| Primary PCI | The preferred strategy: door-to-device within 90 minutes (60 if already at a PCI centre). It does not need systemic fibrinolysis, and anticoagulation can be limited to the procedural dose. Femoral or radial access with a haemostasis plan |
| Fibrinolysis | Relatively or absolutely contraindicated by major surgery within 3 weeks (a 2-hour-old surgical wound with risk of haemorrhage, particularly after a prostatectomy). Reserve for situations where PCI is unavailable and the surgeon accepts the bleeding risk |
| CABG | Considered for left main or multivessel disease, or if PCI fails, with the cardiothoracic team |
