Communicate with the surgeon about bleeding risk, haemostasis, and drains, and with the cardiologist about the stent choice (a bare-metal or newer DES with short DAPT may be chosen to reduce the duration of dual therapy, and balloon angioplasty alone may be used).

## 5. Antithrombotic therapy in a patient with a surgical wound
- **Aspirin:** 150 to 300 mg loading dose unless surgeon objection is overwhelming. It is the most important agent.
- **P2Y12 inhibitor and heparin:** usually given in the cath lab at the time of PCI; the choice and timing are agreed between cardiologist and surgeon. Options are clopidogrel (less potent, preferred where bleeding risk is high), cangrelor, or a lower heparin dose. GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors increase bleeding.
- Monitor the wound, haemoglobin, and drains.

## 6. Other management
- Beta-blocker only if there is no heart failure, shock or heart block; a high-intensity statin.
- Treat arrhythmias (VF, VT) according to ALS, and electrolytes (potassium above 4, magnesium above 1).
- Cardiogenic shock: see R8, with early consideration of MCS.
- Transfer to the cath lab, then CCU or ICU.

## 7. Priorities, in order
- Recognise and call for help.
- Stabilise haemodynamics and airway.
- Early primary PCI as the reperfusion therapy of choice.
- Minimise bleeding while giving the antithrombotic therapy that is essential.
- Detect and treat complications (shock, arrhythmia, mechanical).
- Communicate with the surgeon, patient and family.

> **Examiner lens:** reperfusion is the priority; explain why lytics are a poor choice after surgery.

items.title: 10. Cardiogenic shock after anterior STEMI
items.q: A 62-year-old man is in cardiogenic shock after an anterior STEMI. Define cardiogenic shock, outline the pathophysiology and discuss your management including mechanical circulatory support.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Management of cardiogenic shock after acute myocardial infarction" (BJA Educ 2023).

## Definition and epidemiology

Cardiogenic shock (CS) is end-organ hypoperfusion and tissue hypoxia from primary cardiac dysfunction. It is the commonest cause of in-hospital death after ACS (**mortality 40 to 70%**) and complicates about 9% of STEMI.

| Haemodynamic | Clinical |
|---|---|
| Persistent SAP below 80 to 90 (or MAP 30 below baseline) with raised filling pressures | Cardiac index below 1.8 (unsupported); SAP below 90 despite volume plus cool peripheries, oliguria, confusion, narrow pulse pressure, raised lactate or creatinine |

A spuriously normal pressure can hide hypoperfusion because compensatory vasoconstriction is intense. **Diagnosis rests on demonstrating end-organ hypoperfusion.**

## Pathophysiology

LV dysfunction reduces output, triggering sympathetic and neurohormonal activation with high SVR, fluid retention and inflammation. The vicious circle: low output and coronary perfusion, ischaemia, further depression. High afterload worsens LV function.

## Management

1. **Revascularisation by PCI is the only treatment definitively shown to improve outcome.**
2. Monitor invasively (arterial line, lactate, echo, PA catheter if available); early ICU or cardiac ICU.
3. Oxygenation and ventilation: NIV or intubation with vasopressors ready.
4. **Drugs:** noradrenaline is usually first line but contentious because SVR is already high, so titrate carefully. Inodilators (dobutamine, milrinone) can reduce afterload but cause hypotension and arrhythmia. Use the lowest dose for the shortest time.
5. **Mechanical circulatory support** is a temporising strategy for refractory CS (only 40 to 50% need it):

| Device | Maximum output |
|---|---|
| IABP | about 0.8 L/min |
| Impella | 2.5 to 5.0 L/min |
| TandemHeart | 4.0 L/min |
| VA-ECMO | up to 7 L/min |

Use the least support needed; trials are sparse or negative, and complexity and bleeding rise with more support (patients are on DAPT plus anticoagulation).
6. Treat arrhythmia, acidosis, and mechanical complications (septal rupture, papillary muscle rupture).

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines cardiogenic shock with perfusion criteria and quotes mortality 40 to 70%
- Notes that blood pressure alone can mislead
- Explains the vicious circle and high SVR
- States PCI is the only proven treatment
- Discusses vasopressor and inodilator choice and the dilemma of afterload
- Lists MCS devices with output and the principle of least support
- Plans monitoring, ventilation and complications

items.title: 11. Mechanical complications after inferior MI
items.q: Three days after an inferior myocardial infarction a patient develops pulmonary oedema, hypotension and a new systolic murmur. Discuss the differential diagnosis and your immediate management.
items.a:
## Differential

A new murmur with shock after MI is a **mechanical complication until proven otherwise**:

| Complication | Timing | Features | Echo |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Papillary muscle rupture** (acute severe MR) | 2 to 7 days, inferior MI (posteromedial muscle, single supply from the PDA) | Flash pulmonary oedema; murmur may be soft or absent due to rapid pressure equalisation | Flail leaflet, severe eccentric MR, hyperdynamic LV |
| **Ventricular septal rupture** | 3 to 5 days | Loud pansystolic murmur with thrill, biventricular failure | Septal defect with left-to-right shunt |
| **Free wall rupture** | Within 2 weeks | Tamponade, PEA, usually no murmur | Effusion with clot |

Other causes: re-infarction, RV infarction, arrhythmia, LVOT obstruction with SAM, ischaemic MR from ventricular remodelling.

## Immediate management

1. **Resuscitate and call the heart team** (cardiology, cardiothoracic surgery, ICU).
2. **Confirm** with TTE/TOE; PA catheter shows giant v waves (papillary rupture) or an oxygen saturation step-up (VSR).
3. **Reduce afterload and improve forward flow:** IABP is the key bridge (reduces afterload and regurgitant or shunt flow, improves coronary perfusion). Cautious nitroprusside or GTN if BP allows; inotropes (dobutamine) if hypotensive; PEEP and ventilation for oedema.
4. **Definitive treatment:** urgent surgery (valve replacement or repair for papillary rupture; patch closure for VSR, delayed if stable). Percutaneous closure for high surgical risk.
5. **Free wall rupture:** pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage, with emergency surgery.

## Anaesthetic points

Arterial line and vasopressor/inotrope before induction; keep SVR low-normal in MR and VSR, avoid bradycardia (MR) and raised PVR; TOE for diagnosis and assessment after repair. Mortality is very high without surgery.

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies papillary muscle rupture, VSR and free wall rupture with typical timing and murmurs
- Explains the single blood supply of the posteromedial papillary muscle
- Confirms with echo and describes PA catheter findings
- Uses IABP and afterload reduction as a bridge
- States that definitive surgical treatment is urgent
- Gives anaesthetic points for induction in these patients

items.title: 12. Induction with an ejection fraction of 20%
items.q: You must anaesthetise a patient with an ejection fraction of 20% and marginal blood pressure for an emergency laparotomy. Discuss your preparation and induction.
items.a:
## Physiological problem

A flat Starling curve with raised filling pressures, dependent on sympathetic tone and preload. Induction agents reduce sympathetic tone, vasodilate, venodilate and depress contractility; positive pressure ventilation reduces venous return. Circulation time is prolonged, so drugs act slowly and overshoot; requirements are reduced (often a quarter to a third of the usual dose).

## Preparation

- Senior anaesthetist and skilled assistant; pads on.
- Resuscitate: cautious fluid or diuresis as indicated, correct K and Mg, treat arrhythmia and acidosis.
- Investigate rapidly: ECG, echo (EF, RV, valves, tamponade), lactate.
- Discuss whether a less invasive option (regional, sedation) or mechanical support is appropriate.
- **Monitoring:** arterial line before induction under local anaesthetic, large-bore access, central line with a vasopressor ready, ST analysis, capnography, cardiac output monitor or TOE.

## Induction

| Element | Choice |
|---|---|
| Vasopressor | Noradrenaline infusion or phenylephrine/metaraminol boluses running before induction; inotrope available (adrenaline, dobutamine) |
| Agent | Etomidate (haemodynamically stable), or ketamine (maintains sympathetic tone) in reduced dose, or slowly titrated reduced propofol with fentanyl |
| Opioid | Fentanyl or remifentanil in titrated doses |
| Relaxant | Rocuronium (aspiration risk, RSI), allowing for slow onset |
| Preoxygenation | Careful, head-up, high-flow nasal oxygen |

## Maintenance and ventilation

Low-dose volatile or TIVA with depth monitoring, accepting awareness risk; minimal mean airway pressure and modest PEEP; maintain MAP above 65 mmHg, sinus rhythm and a normal-to-high heart rate; judicious fluid; transfuse blood loss.

## Postoperative

ICU, inotrope or vasopressor support, planned ventilation and weaning, early mechanical support if refractory.

**Key principle:** pre-empt the induction hypotension with vasopressors rather than treating it afterwards with fluid alone.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains why induction is dangerous in low EF (sympathetic dependence, venodilation, slow circulation)
- Prepares: team, pads, resuscitation, arterial line before induction
- Has a vasopressor infusion running and an inotrope available
- Chooses haemodynamically stable agents in reduced doses
- Describes ventilation strategy that limits venous return reduction
- Plans postoperative ICU and escalation

items.title: 13. HFrEF on full medical therapy for elective surgery
items.q: A 65-year-old with HFrEF (EF 30%) on sacubitril-valsartan, bisoprolol, spironolactone, dapagliflozin and furosemide is booked for elective major surgery. How do you assess him and manage his medications, fluids and monitoring?
items.a:
## Is he optimised?

Review symptoms (NYHA class), weight, JVP, oedema and recent admissions. **Decompensated heart failure is a reason to defer elective surgery.** Investigations: ECG, echo (EF, RV, valves; repeat if clinical change or older than 12 months), BNP or NT-proBNP, electrolytes (K, Mg), renal function, FBC. Check any device (ICD/CRT interrogation). HFrEF is a strong predictor of perioperative HF, AKI and death.

## Medications

| Drug | Plan | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Bisoprolol | **Continue**, including the morning | Withdrawal causes tachycardia and ischaemia |
| Sacubitril-valsartan (ARNI), ACEi, ARB | Often omit the morning dose (24 hours before major surgery); restart when stable | Vasoplegia and hypotension under anaesthesia |
| Spironolactone | Continue if stable, hold if poor intake, renal impairment or hyperkalaemia | Hyperkalaemia, AKI |
| Dapagliflozin | **Stop 3 days before** | Euglycaemic ketoacidosis |
| Furosemide | Omit if euvolaemic, continue if congested | Avoid hypovolaemia |
| Digoxin, amiodarone, ivabradine | Continue | Rate and rhythm control |
| Anticoagulants | Per indication | |

Restart each drug as soon as the patient is eating and haemodynamically stable.

## Anaesthetic plan

- Technique that preserves haemodynamics (see R10 for induction); regional or titrated neuraxial where suitable.
- Invasive arterial pressure, cardiac output monitoring or TOE for major surgery, ST analysis, temperature, urine output.
- Goals: preload maintained but not overloaded, afterload low-normal with adequate MAP, contractility supported, sinus rhythm, rate normal to high-normal.
- Lung-protective ventilation, modest PEEP, avoid hypoxia and hypercarbia.

## Fluids

Both hypovolaemia and overload are poorly tolerated, so use goal-directed therapy (stroke volume or VTI guided) with balanced crystalloid in small boluses (250 mL), replace blood loss with blood, and use a vasopressor or inotrope early instead of repeated fluid.

## Postoperative

HDU for major surgery, early extubation, multimodal analgesia (avoid NSAIDs), daily weights, repeat BNP/troponin, early restart of GDMT, and early recognition of decompensation.

## Self-marking checklist

- Assesses optimisation and defers elective surgery if decompensated
- Continues beta-blocker, omits ARNI/ACEi on the morning, stops SGLT2 inhibitor 3 days before
- Handles MRA and loop diuretic appropriately
- Checks device and investigations (echo, BNP, electrolytes)
- Sets haemodynamic goals and monitoring
- Fluid strategy and postoperative restart of therapy

items.title: 14. SGLT2 inhibitors in heart failure and the perioperative plan
items.q: A 66-year-old man with HFrEF and type 2 diabetes takes dapagliflozin and is booked for elective bowel resection. Outline your perioperative management of the SGLT2 inhibitor, and explain why these drugs are now relevant to non-diabetic patients as well.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2021, "The expanding role of SGLT-2 inhibitors in the treatment of heart failure" (Pym et al).

## Why you will meet them more often

SGLT2 inhibitors are approved for heart failure as well as type 2 diabetes, and may extend to type 1 diabetes and non-diabetic chronic kidney disease. Large trials (EMPA-REG OUTCOME and the heart failure trials) show fewer heart failure admissions within **months** of starting, in patients with good glycaemic control (HbA1c below 6.5%) and in non-diabetics. The speed and independence from glucose lowering suggest a non-glycaemic mechanism. Proposed mechanisms are reverse remodelling (lower LV volumes and mass) and reduced cardiac fibrosis, so many surgical patients will be on them without diabetes.

## Perioperative risks

- **Euglycaemic DKA:** life threatening, with normal or near-normal glucose. More likely with fasting, bowel preparation, emergency or major surgery, acute illness, poor oral intake or relative insulin deficiency. All forms of diabetes carry a similar risk.
- **Genitourinary infection:** common and usually mild, but may be severe, with a theoretical risk to prosthetic implants. Reinforce genital hygiene; consider urine dipstick screening before high-risk surgery (joint replacement, cardiac surgery) and think carefully before catheterising.
- **Volume depletion and hypotension** from osmotic diuresis on top of loop diuretic.

## Management

- **Elective surgery:** stop **3 days before** (day of surgery and the 2 days before), the local and FDA advice for non-day surgery and bowel preparation. BJA Education 2024 (HFpEF) advises stopping 2 to 3 days before elective surgery. A UK consensus statement accepts 2 days (day of surgery and 1 day before) except with prolonged fasting.
- **Preoperatively:** check ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate) and a gas if the drug was taken in the last 3 days or the patient is unwell; keep fasting short.
- **Emergency surgery:** assume the drug is active and check ketones, gas, anion gap and glucose before induction.
- **Restart** only when eating and drinking normally and the acute illness has resolved.
- **Sick-day plan:** teach every patient on these drugs to withhold them when unwell.

## If euDKA develops

Treat with IV fluid, **dextrose plus a fixed-rate insulin infusion** (to stop ketogenesis rather than to correct glucose) and potassium, and treat the precipitant. The effect lasts for days after the last dose.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains the heart failure indication and that benefit is largely independent of glucose lowering
- Names euglycaemic DKA and its precipitants
- Mentions genitourinary infection and volume depletion
- States the stopping interval (3 days) and acknowledges the shorter UK advice
- Describes ketone and gas testing, including in emergency surgery
- States restart criteria and a sick-day plan
- Treats euDKA with dextrose, insulin infusion, fluid and potassium

items.title: 15. HFpEF: diastole, echo grading and management
items.q: A 74-year-old woman with hypertension, diabetes and atrial fibrillation has heart failure with a normal ejection fraction. Describe the physiology of diastole, how echo grades diastolic dysfunction, and your perioperative management.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2017, "Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction: Diastole is important too!" (Drummond).

## Concept and epidemiology

HFpEF is the clinical syndrome of heart failure with a normal or low-normal EF; **diastolic dysfunction** is the abnormal myocardial mechanics behind it. It accounts for **40 to 50%** of heart failure, and is commoner in the elderly, obese and women. Associations: hypertension (70 to 88%), diabetes, atrial fibrillation (30 to 37%), coronary disease and pulmonary hypertension. It is not benign: mortality is higher than the general population.

## The four phases of diastole

1. **Isovolumic relaxation:** active, energy-dependent (ischaemia impairs it).
2. **Early rapid filling:** suction from LV recoil; up to 80% of filling.
3. **Diastasis:** filling set by compliance (stiffness, mass, pericardium).
4. **Atrial contraction:** the atrial kick, lost in AF.

## Grading (simplified tissue Doppler algorithm)

Uses mitral annular early velocity (e') and E/e', which works in AF where there is no A wave.

| Grade | Pattern | E/e' |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Impaired relaxation | 8 or less |
| 2 | Pseudonormal | 9 to 12 |
| 3 | Restrictive | above 13 |

Supporting signs: dilated left atrium, LV hypertrophy, raised PA pressure.

> **BJA Education:** "Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction" (BJA Educ 2024): HFpEF is about 50% of heart failure; diagnosis needs symptoms and signs plus preserved LV systolic function and raised filling pressures; **first-line treatment is an SGLT2 inhibitor, diuretics and treating comorbidities (hypertension, diabetes), with aggressive management of AF**; stop SGLT2 inhibitors 2 to 3 days before elective surgery.

## Perioperative management

- Optimise before elective surgery: diuretic for congestion, rate control of AF (tachycardia shortens filling time), control hypertension (the most important risk factor).
- Trials of beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and others are inconsistent; spironolactone reduces admissions and candesartan modestly so. Treatment is individualised.
- Intraoperatively: avoid **tachycardia and ischaemia**, keep sinus rhythm (cardiovert AF with instability), avoid both hypovolaemia and fluid overload (steep pressure-volume curve: small volume changes cause large pressure changes), treat hypertension and avoid hypotension.
- Expect a poor response to the usual systolic failure treatments; use echo to guide.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines HFpEF versus diastolic dysfunction and quotes prevalence
- Lists the associated conditions (hypertension, diabetes, AF, CAD)
- Describes the phases of diastole and the ATP-dependent relaxation
- Grades diastolic dysfunction with E/e' and notes the use in AF
- Optimises preoperatively (rate, hypertension, congestion)
- Avoids tachycardia, ischaemia and fluid extremes intraoperatively

items.title: 16. Echocardiographic assessment of LV function and filling
items.q: Describe how you assess LV systolic function, diastolic function and filling status with echo, and how the findings alter a fluid decision in theatre.
items.a:
## 1. Why echo
TTE or TOE provides a rapid, direct assessment of ventricular function, filling, valves, pericardium and volume status in the anaesthetic or ICU setting, and is recommended in unexplained haemodynamic instability (ASE/SCA and ANZCA guidance).

## 2. Systolic function
- **Qualitative:** visual estimate of LV function across views (mid-oesophageal four-chamber, two-chamber, long axis; transgastric mid short-axis), with the wall motion assessed in the 17-segment model (normal, hypokinetic, akinetic, dyskinetic). A new regional wall motion abnormality (RWMA) suggests ischaemia.
- **Quantitative:** biplane Simpson method (normal EF 52 to 72% in men and 54 to 74% in women), fractional area change from the transgastric mid short-axis view (normal 35 to 65%), fractional shortening, mitral annular systolic velocity (S'), and global longitudinal strain (normal about -18 to -22%, a sensitive marker of early dysfunction).
- **Stroke volume and cardiac output:** LVOT diameter and velocity time integral (VTI): SV = LVOT area x VTI; CO = SV x HR. A VTI below 18 to 20 cm suggests low stroke volume.
- **Pitfalls:** EF depends on loading conditions (it is overestimated in MR and vasodilation, underestimated in high afterload), is poor in the presence of RWMA or paced rhythm, and is unreliable in tachycardia.

## 3. Diastolic function
- Measurements: mitral inflow E and A velocities, E/A ratio, deceleration time, septal and lateral e' (tissue Doppler), average E/e', left atrial volume index, and TR velocity.
- The four screening criteria (ASE/EACVI 2016): septal e' below 7 or lateral e' below 10 cm/s; average E/e' above 14; LAVI above 34 mL/m2; TR velocity above 2.8 m/s. If more than half are positive, diastolic dysfunction is present; if fewer than half, it is normal; if half, it is indeterminate.
- Grades: I (impaired relaxation, E/A below 0.8, normal filling pressure), II (pseudonormal, E/A 0.8 to 2, E/e' 10 to 14, raised filling pressure), III (restrictive, E/A above 2, DT below 160 ms, high filling pressure).
- Limitations: AF (no A wave), significant MR, mitral stenosis, annular calcification, prosthetic valve, tachycardia, and a hyperdynamic LV.

## 4. Filling status and fluid responsiveness
| Parameter | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| LV end-diastolic area (TG SAX) | Small with kissing papillary muscles suggests hypovolaemia (but also vasoplegia or hyperdynamic state) |
| IVC (subcostal; TTE) | Diameter 2.1 cm or less with more than 50% inspiratory collapse suggests RAP about 3 mmHg; above 2.1 cm with less than 50% collapse suggests RAP about 15 mmHg. Unreliable in ventilated patients |
| SVC collapsibility (TOE) | Over 36% collapsibility predicts fluid responsiveness in ventilated patients |
| LVOT VTI variation | A rise of 10 to 15% after a passive leg raise or a 250 mL bolus predicts responsiveness |
| Pulse pressure or stroke volume variation | Above 12 to 13% predicts responsiveness if the patient is in sinus rhythm, ventilated with tidal volumes of 8 mL/kg or more and a closed chest |
| E/e' | Raised E/e' (above 14) suggests elevated LA pressure and a risk of pulmonary oedema with fluid |
| CVP and PAOP | Poor predictors of responsiveness, but high values indicate risk of congestion |

## 5. Applying to the decision to give fluid
- Is the patient hypoperfused or unstable? (Fluid is not indicated if the problem is not preload.)
- Is the patient likely to respond? (Dynamic tests above.)
- Is the patient likely to tolerate fluid? (No raised E/e', no significant RV failure or congestion, no severe valve lesion; lung ultrasound B-lines suggest limited tolerance.)
- If yes to all: give a 250 mL balanced crystalloid bolus and re-measure SV or VTI. If not: use a vasopressor, inotrope or both, and treat the cause.

## 6. Take-home points
Combine function, filling and responsiveness; fluid responsiveness does not equal fluid need, and a heart that responds may still be congested.

> **Examiner lens:** fluid responsiveness is not the same as fluid need; combine dynamic and static measures.

items.title: 17. Decompensated cardiomyopathy on the ICU
items.q: A patient with known cardiomyopathy is admitted to ICU with pulmonary oedema, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, cool peripheries and a rising lactate. Outline your assessment and stepwise management.
items.a:
## Haemodynamic profile

Hypotension, cool peripheries and rising lactate with pulmonary congestion indicate the **cold and wet** profile (low output and congestion), the highest-mortality group, approaching cardiogenic shock (SCAI stage B to C). Assess ABC, perfusion, JVP and chest, and use bedside echo and lung ultrasound.

## Look for the precipitant

Use **CHAMP**: acute **C**oronary syndrome, **H**ypertensive emergency, **A**rrhythmia or acute valve failure, **M**echanical complication, **P**ulmonary embolism. Also sepsis, anaemia, non-adherence, drugs (NSAIDs, negative inotropes), thyroid disease, renal failure, alcohol, myocarditis. Investigate with ECG, troponin, BNP, electrolytes, renal function, lactate, gas, chest X-ray and echo.

## Stepwise management

1. **Respiratory support:** oxygen to SpO2 94 to 98%; CPAP or NIV for distress (3CPO: faster symptom relief, no mortality difference); intubate for exhaustion, refractory hypoxia or shock, with a vasopressor running and a titrated induction.
2. **Restore perfusion first:** noradrenaline to MAP of at least 65 mmHg; dobutamine or milrinone (no bolus) for low output; levosimendan as an alternative. **Avoid vasodilators while hypotensive.**
3. **Decongest:** IV furosemide 40 to 80 mg (or 1 to 2.5 times the oral dose); assess response at 2 hours (urine sodium, output); add thiazide or acetazolamide for resistance; ultrafiltration or renal replacement for refractory overload (DOSE: bolus and infusion, or low and high dose, give similar symptom outcomes).
4. **Mechanical support** (IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO) for refractory shock as a bridge to recovery, device or transplant.
5. **Treat arrhythmia:** cardioversion for unstable AF or VT, amiodarone, correct K and Mg.
6. **Monitor:** arterial line, lactate, urine output, creatinine (cardiorenal syndrome); a PA catheter only for unclear or refractory shock (ESCAPE showed no routine benefit).

## Transition

Once stable restart guideline-directed medical therapy before discharge (STRONG-HF: rapid up-titration), with early follow-up. **In the cold and wet patient, perfusion comes before decongestion.**

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies the cold and wet profile and cardiogenic shock risk
- Searches for the precipitant (CHAMP)
- Provides respiratory support (CPAP/NIV, intubation precautions)
- Restores perfusion first (noradrenaline, inotrope) and avoids vasodilators in hypotension
- Decongests with loop diuretic strategy and resistance options
- Mentions mechanical support, arrhythmia, monitoring and restarting GDMT

items.title: 18. LVAD patient needing urgent laparotomy
items.q: A patient with a durable left ventricular assist device (LVAD) needs an urgent laparotomy. Outline the key perioperative issues and your management.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2021, "The perioperative management of patients with ventricular assist devices undergoing non-cardiac surgery" (Falland, Sidebotham, Allen).

## Context

Between 4 and 33% of VAD patients have non-cardiac surgery while supported, most often GI endoscopy (bleeding on anticoagulation). Outcomes are good when a **multidisciplinary team** is involved. Commonest problems: **hypotension**, acute kidney injury, bleeding and arrhythmia.

## Preoperative

- Team: anaesthetist, proceduralist, heart failure cardiologist, VAD nurse or perfusionist.
- Assess function, organ function, medications and device performance; echo with attention to **RV function**.
- Examination is hard: pulses are often impalpable (non-pulsatile flow), NIBP may need Doppler, and device hum masks heart sounds.
- Pacemaker or ICD: asynchronous mode and tachy therapies off for diathermy.
- Plan ICU or HDU. Expect greater blood loss; crossmatch.

## Anticoagulation

Warfarin with a target INR of 2.5 to 3.5 (HeartMate II) or 2.0 to 3.0 (HeartMate 3, HVAD), plus an antiplatelet. Elective surgery: stop warfarin 5 days before and bridge with unfractionated heparin once the INR is below 2.0. Emergency surgery: reverse to an INR below 1.5 if needed using **factor concentrate (Prothrombinex), not vitamin K**, as warfarin must restart soon.

## Intraoperative

Invasive arterial monitoring and strict asepsis (driveline infection risk). VAD output is preload and afterload dependent: reduced VAD preload (hypovolaemia, RV failure, tamponade, high intrathoracic pressure, arrhythmia) causes low flow and hypotension. Protect the RV (see the right ventricular failure item), avoid raised PVR, replace volume promptly and use vasopressors for vasodilation.

## Key themes (the chapter's five)

Haemodynamics, determinants of VAD performance, monitoring challenges, anticoagulation and asepsis.

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies the multidisciplinary team and the usual complications
- Notes assessment difficulties (non-pulsatile flow, Doppler BP)
- Gives anticoagulation targets and the stop and bridge plan
- Reverses warfarin with factor concentrate, not vitamin K, in emergency
- Programs ICD or pacemaker for diathermy
- Explains determinants of VAD preload and the role of the RV
- Stresses asepsis and postoperative ICU or HDU care

items.title: 19. Heart transplant recipient for non-cardiac surgery
items.q: A patient who received a heart transplant 3 years ago presents for non-cardiac surgery. Describe the physiology of the transplanted heart and the implications for anaesthetic drugs and management.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2019, "Perioperative management of heart transplantation" (Edwards, Allen).

## Physiology of the denervated heart

- Vagal and sympathetic supply is cut. The SA node runs at its intrinsic rate of **90 to 100 beats/min**.
- The heart cannot mount a reflex tachycardia to hypovolaemia, vasodilation or afterload change; cardiac output depends on **preload** and slow rise of circulating catecholamines. It is "preload dependent".
- Angina is absent, so **ischaemia is silent**. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) is suspected from new wall motion or diastolic abnormalities or ventricular arrhythmias; intravascular ultrasound is the gold standard.
- Reinnervation is partial and unpredictable (sympathetic from 6 to 8 months, parasympathetic 1 to 3 years).
- Arrhythmias: conduction delay and heart block, 25% AF or flutter, 10% need a pacemaker; ventricular arrhythmias suggest rejection or CAV. Double P waves can occur. Carotid sinus massage and Valsalva have no effect.

## Drug responses

| Drug | Effect |
|---|---|
| Atropine, glycopyrrolate | **No effect**; ineffective for bradycardia |
| Ephedrine | Reduced (indirect) |
| Noradrenaline, adrenaline, dobutamine | Exaggerated (more adrenoreceptors): titrate |
| Phenylephrine, metaraminol | Effective, no reflex bradycardia |
| Isoprenaline | Effective; use for bradycardia |
| Adenosine | Exaggerated bradycardia |
| Neostigmine | Bradycardia possible, especially beyond 6 months |

## Other issues

BJA Education 2021 (heart transplantation) adds that **primary graft dysfunction** is the main cause of early death, and that mechanical support (ideally ECMO) should be started early when graft dysfunction does not respond to moderate-dose inotropes.


Immunosuppression (calcineurin inhibitors: nephrotoxicity; continue on time), infection risk (asepsis, antibiotics), malignancy (more than 10% develop de novo cancer; skin cancers 100 times), tricuspid regurgitation, and drug interactions with tacrolimus or ciclosporin. Monitor ECG, arterial line for major surgery, and warm, preload-aware induction.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains denervation, resting rate of 90 to 100 and absent reflex tachycardia
- Notes preload dependence and silent ischaemia
- Gives atropine and glycopyrrolate as ineffective and names the effective alternatives
- Describes exaggerated responses to catecholamines
- Mentions CAV, arrhythmias and pacemaker risk
- Covers immunosuppression and infection precautions

items.title: 20. Severe aortic stenosis for major abdominal surgery
items.q: A 76-year-old with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis is booked for elective major abdominal surgery. Discuss the preoperative decision-making and your anaesthetic management.
items.a:
## Pathophysiology

A fixed LV outflow obstruction produces concentric LVH, diastolic dysfunction and raised LVEDP. Cardiac output cannot rise, so it depends on rate and rhythm. Subendocardial ischaemia occurs with a low diastolic pressure even if the coronaries are normal. The three poorly tolerated states are **hypotension, tachycardia and loss of sinus rhythm.**

## Decision-making

- **Symptomatic severe AS** (Vmax 4 m/s or more, mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, AVA below 1.0 cm2) carries a high perioperative risk of MI, heart failure and death.
- **Elective surgery should wait:** treat the valve first by surgical or transcatheter replacement (TAVI), then proceed. Non-cardiac surgery can usually follow TAVI within weeks.
- If the surgery cannot wait, proceed with optimal anaesthesia (balloon valvuloplasty can bridge but is short lived).
- Consider whether a less invasive operation is possible.
- Multidisciplinary discussion (cardiologist, surgeon, anaesthetist) and documented consent.

## Preoperative assessment

Symptoms (angina, syncope, dyspnoea), ECG (LVH, strain, AF), recent echo (gradient, area, LV function, other valves), BNP, renal function, medication and frailty.

## Anaesthetic goals and technique

| Goal | How |
|---|---|
| Rate 60 to 80, sinus rhythm | Avoid tachycardia (pain, ketamine, pancuronium); pads on; cardiovert AF early |
| Preload full | Careful fluid titration |
| SVR and MAP maintained | **Vasopressor infusion running before induction** (phenylephrine, noradrenaline) |
| Contractility preserved | Avoid large doses of depressants |

- Arterial line before induction; TOE for major surgery if available.
- Controlled GA with slow titrated induction (etomidate or reduced propofol with opioid); avoid single-shot spinal; slow epidural or CSE only in experienced hands with vasopressor cover.
- Treat hypotension early with alpha agonists and volume, not by waiting.
- Postoperative HDU, troponin surveillance, multimodal analgesia.
- External cardiac massage is ineffective across a fixed obstruction, so prevention is vital.

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes the fixed outflow obstruction and why hypotension, tachycardia and AF are poorly tolerated
- Decides on treating the valve first (TAVI/SAVR) for elective surgery, with MDT input
- Gives severity criteria (Vmax, gradient, AVA) and preoperative assessment
- States goals: rate 60 to 80, sinus rhythm, preload, SVR
- Technique: arterial line, vasopressor infusion, slow induction, avoid single-shot spinal
- Postoperative HDU and troponin surveillance

items.title: 21. Aortic regurgitation: pathophysiology and anaesthesia
items.q: Describe the pathophysiology of chronic and acute aortic regurgitation and outline the anaesthetic management of a patient with severe chronic aortic regurgitation for non-cardiac surgery.
items.a:
## Causes

Valve disease (bicuspid, rheumatic, endocarditis, degenerative) or aortic root dilatation (hypertension, Marfan, ankylosing spondylitis, aortitis, dissection).

## Pathophysiology

- **Chronic AR:** diastolic regurgitation causes volume overload, with eccentric LV hypertrophy and dilatation. Stroke volume is large, with a **wide pulse pressure** (high systolic, low diastolic pressure), so coronary perfusion falls (low diastolic pressure, raised LV wall tension). Compensation lasts years, then the LV fails.
- **Acute AR** (endocarditis, dissection, trauma): the unprepared ventricle cannot dilate, so LVEDP rises sharply, causing premature mitral valve closure, pulmonary oedema, tachycardia and shock. This needs urgent surgery.

## Severity (echo)

Vena contracta above 6 mm, regurgitant volume 60 mL or more, regurgitant fraction 50% or more, EROA 0.3 cm2 or more, pressure half-time below 200 ms, holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta, LV dilatation. Clinical signs: collapsing pulse, early diastolic murmur.

## Haemodynamic goals

| Variable | Goal | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Heart rate | High-normal (80 to 100) | Shortens diastole, so less regurgitant time; bradycardia worsens AR |
| Preload | Full | Large regurgitant volume |
| Afterload | Low-normal; avoid increases | Vasoconstriction increases regurgitant fraction |
| Contractility | Maintained | Failing LV needs support |
| Rhythm | Sinus | |

## Anaesthetic management

- Assess symptoms, LV size and function, aortic root size, and endocarditis risk.
- Arterial line for major surgery; TOE if unstable.
- Neuraxial anaesthesia is usually well tolerated, because the afterload reduction is helpful (slow titration).
- GA with agents that do not depress contractility or cause bradycardia; avoid drugs that raise SVR sharply (use modest doses of vasopressors) and treat hypotension with an inotrope or vasodilator-sparing vasopressor.
- **Avoid IABP** (contraindicated: counterpulsation worsens regurgitation) and avoid bradycardic drugs.
- Postoperatively use HDU for severe AR or LV dysfunction.

## Self-marking checklist

- Gives causes and distinguishes chronic from acute AR physiology
- Explains wide pulse pressure and coronary perfusion problem
- Gives echo severity criteria
- States goals: rate 80 to 100, full preload, low-normal afterload, maintained contractility
- Notes neuraxial techniques are often tolerated; avoids bradycardia and raised SVR
- Notes IABP is contraindicated

items.title: 22. Rheumatic mitral stenosis and pulmonary hypertension in pregnancy
items.q: A 28-year-old woman at 34 weeks has rheumatic mitral stenosis with pulmonary hypertension. Discuss her risk and your plan for delivery and anaesthesia.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2023, "Obstetric anaesthesia in rheumatic heart disease" (Jhummon-Mahadnac et al).

## Why this is dangerous

Pregnancy raises cardiac output (about 40 to 50%) and heart rate, and labour adds pain-driven tachycardia and an autotransfusion after delivery. In mitral stenosis, tachycardia shortens diastolic filling, raising left atrial pressure and causing **pulmonary oedema** or AF. The hypercoagulable state also risks pulmonary embolism, which can precipitate acute RV failure.

## Risk stratification

Use the modified WHO (mWHO) classification with cardiology. Left-sided stenotic lesions and **pulmonary hypertension carry the highest risk**; obstructive left lesions with PH have a maternal mortality of 30 to 56%, and worse with RV dysfunction or poor functional class. Regurgitant lesions are generally tolerated unless there is heart failure or PH. Haemodynamic targets follow the most severe lesion, but moderate lesions in series add up.

## Delivery planning

- Without an obstetric indication, **vaginal delivery** is preferred (less haemorrhage, infection and thromboembolism).
- mWHO II: spontaneous labour is reasonable if the patient lives close to the hospital.
- mWHO III and IV: **planned induction in ICU**, allowing continuous monitoring and optimisation of volume, rate control and anticoagulation before neuraxial block. Planned caesarean can suit the highest-risk patients.
- Consider cultural and social factors: relocating remote women near term removes support at a stressful time.

## Anaesthetic aims in mitral stenosis

- Keep the heart rate slow and sinus rhythm; treat AF promptly.
- Early, **slowly titrated epidural analgesia** to blunt the pain response; avoid abrupt falls in SVR.
- Maintain preload without volume overload; avoid anything that raises PVR (hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis).
- Vasopressors: phenylephrine or metaraminol rather than ephedrine.
- Anticoagulation: check timing before neuraxial block.
- Prosthetic valves: bioprosthetic valves avoid therapeutic anticoagulation but degrade; mechanical valves need it, with the warfarin versus heparin dilemma.
- Postpartum: ICU or HDU monitoring for the autotransfusion.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains the physiology of pregnancy and labour in mitral stenosis
- Uses mWHO classification and identifies PH and stenosis as highest risk
- Prefers vaginal delivery and states criteria for ICU induction
- Aims for slow heart rate, sinus rhythm and slowly titrated epidural
- Avoids precipitants of raised PVR and sudden SVR drop
- Addresses anticoagulation and valve type
- Plans postpartum monitoring

items.title: 23. Mitral regurgitation and transcatheter edge-to-edge repair
items.q: Discuss the pathophysiology of severe mitral regurgitation and the anaesthetic management of a patient having transcatheter edge-to-edge mitral valve repair.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Anaesthesia for transcatheter mitral valve repair" (BJA Educ 2023).

## Pathophysiology

Mitral regurgitation (MR) is common (moderate or severe in about 10% at 75 years). **Primary MR** is a leaflet or chordal abnormality; **secondary MR** results from LV size and geometry changes (functional). Severe MR causes volume overload, LV and LA dilatation, atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension and heart failure (about 50% more heart failure admissions per year, excess mortality about 6% a year). The LVEF can look falsely normal because part of the stroke volume goes backwards.

## Indication

Transcatheter repair suits favourable anatomy, high surgical risk and symptomatic severe MR despite medical therapy. Anaesthetists are key members of the structural heart team.

## Anaesthetic principles

- General anaesthesia with TOE guidance is usual; the technique should **allow rapid recovery**.
- Physiology: moderate **preload**, **faster heart rate (70 to 90)**, **low to normal afterload** and avoid raised PVR.
- Manipulating physiology to **decrease mitral annular size and increase leaflet coaptation** (adequate preload and afterload, sinus rhythm) helps the procedure.
- Heparin and ACT monitoring during transseptal access.

## Complications to anticipate

Cardiac tamponade (transseptal puncture), iatrogenic ASD, single leaflet device attachment, mitral stenosis after clip, embolism, vascular injury.

## Self-marking checklist

- Distinguishes primary and secondary MR and explains the physiological consequences
- Notes the limits of EF in MR
- States indications for transcatheter repair
- Chooses general anaesthesia with TOE and a recovery-focused technique
- Sets haemodynamic goals for MR (preload, faster rate, low afterload)
- Names procedural complications such as tamponade and iatrogenic ASD

items.title: 24. Mechanical valves, anticoagulation and pregnancy
items.q: Describe how you manage anticoagulation for a patient with a mechanical mitral valve having elective surgery, and how the problem changes in pregnancy.
items.a:
## 1. Thromboembolic risk of mechanical valves
- **Without anticoagulation** the risk of valve thrombosis and systemic embolism is about 4% per year for aortic valves and 8% for mitral valves (higher with caged-ball or tilting disc designs).
- **Risk stratification (ACC/AHA, ESC, CHEST/ACCP):**
- **Low risk:** bileaflet mechanical aortic valve without risk factors.
- **Intermediate:** bileaflet aortic valve with one risk factor (AF, previous thromboembolism, LV dysfunction with EF below 35%, hypercoagulable state, older-generation valve).
- **High:** any mechanical mitral valve, caged-ball or tilting disc aortic valve, recent stroke or TIA (within 6 months), or an aortic valve with multiple risk factors.
- **INR targets:** bileaflet aortic with no risk factors 2.5 (2.0 to 3.0); mechanical aortic with risk factors, and mechanical mitral or tricuspid 3.0 (2.5 to 3.5).
- DOACs are contraindicated (RE-ALIGN: dabigatran caused more thromboembolism and bleeding; PROACT Xa: apixaban was stopped for excess thromboembolism). Warfarin is the only recommended oral agent.

## 2. Perioperative plan
| Step | Management |
|---|---|
| Preoperative assessment | Valve type and position, INR target, other risk factors, bleeding risk of the procedure, and renal function. For minor procedures (dental, cataract, minor skin) warfarin can be continued with INR in range |
| Stopping warfarin | Stop 5 days before surgery (INR 1.5 or below for most major surgery; INR below 1.4 or normal for neuraxial block), with INR check the day before. Low-dose oral vitamin K (1 to 2 mg) may be used if INR is still above 1.5 the day before |
| Bridging | Indicated for high-risk valves (mechanical mitral, caged-ball, tilting disc, recent stroke, AF with multiple risk factors). Start therapeutic LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily) or IV UFH when INR is below 2.0 (about day 3 before surgery); the last LMWH dose is given 24 hours before surgery (half the daily dose in some protocols), UFH stopped 4 to 6 hours before. Not required for low-risk bileaflet aortic valves |
| Evidence | BRIDGE (1884 patients with AF) found that no bridging was non-inferior for thromboembolism and caused less major bleeding, but mechanical valves were excluded; the data for mechanical valves are therefore observational and expert-based |
| Postoperative | Restart warfarin within 12 to 24 hours of surgery (evening of the operation if haemostasis is secure), with LMWH 48 to 72 hours after major surgery with high bleeding risk (24 hours after low bleeding risk), until INR is therapeutic |
| Neuraxial block | Wait for INR below 1.4; wait 12 hours (prophylactic dose) or 24 hours (therapeutic dose) after LMWH before needle placement; catheter removal timing per ANZCA PG/ASRA guidelines |

## 3. Emergency surgery or bleeding
- Reverse with prothrombin complex concentrate (25 to 50 units/kg, based on INR) plus vitamin K 5 to 10 mg IV for life-threatening bleeding; fresh frozen plasma is a second-line option.
- Vitamin K in high doses can delay re-anticoagulation for days, so lower doses (1 to 2 mg) are used for non-life-threatening cases.
- Resume anticoagulation as soon as the bleeding has been controlled.

## 4. Pregnancy
- **Problem:** pregnancy is hypercoagulable, and the options all carry risk.
- **Warfarin:** the most effective at preventing valve thrombosis, but crosses the placenta, causing embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses; risk of about 6% at 6 to 12 weeks, dose-dependent, higher above 5 mg/day), fetal bleeding and miscarriage.
- **LMWH or UFH:** do not cross the placenta, but are less effective at preventing valve thrombosis (up to 5 to 10% in mitral valves) and have monitoring challenges (anti-Xa levels, aPTT) with changing weight and renal clearance.
- **Strategy (ESC 2018 and 2021; ACC/AHA):**
- Informed shared decision-making before conception, in a pregnancy heart team.
- If the warfarin dose is 5 mg/day or less: continue warfarin through the first trimester (lowest risk of valve thrombosis) or switch to LMWH twice daily with anti-Xa monitoring between 6 and 12 weeks if the patient prefers; if above 5 mg/day, use LMWH or UFH in the first trimester.
- Warfarin from week 13 to about week 36.
- Switch to LMWH or IV UFH from week 36 (or earlier if labour is anticipated) because of fetal bleeding risk and to permit regional anaesthesia.
- Stop LMWH 24 hours before planned induction or caesarean section; use IV UFH, stopped 4 to 6 hours before delivery. Restart 6 to 12 hours after vaginal delivery (UFH or LMWH) and warfarin once bleeding is controlled.
- If delivery occurs on warfarin, an urgent caesarean section is advised (neonatal intracranial haemorrhage), with vitamin K and PCC.
- **Anaesthetic implications:** delivery planning in a tertiary centre; neuraxial analgesia in labour is possible if the INR and heparin timings are met; careful haemodynamic monitoring (increased volume, MS and AF risk).

## 5. Key messages
Know the INR targets, who needs bridging, the avoidance of DOACs, and the trade-off between maternal valve thrombosis and fetal harm in pregnancy.

> **Examiner lens:** know the INR targets, who needs bridging, and the trade-off in pregnancy.

items.title: 25. Transfemoral TAVI
items.q: Discuss the anaesthetic considerations for a high-risk elderly patient with severe aortic stenosis having transfemoral TAVI.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Advances in transcatheter aortic valve implantation" (part 2, BJA Educ 2021).

## The anaesthetist's roles

Preparation, leadership of the team, risk mitigation and management of complications. TAVI avoids sternotomy and bypass, so recovery is faster.

## Preparation

Heart-team decision and CT assessment of access. Review of AS severity, LV function, coronary disease, renal function, frailty and conduction. Group and screen; blood available. Check pacing wires and defibrillator pads.

## Technique

The commonest approach is **transfemoral** (14 to 20 Fr femoral artery access). Local anaesthesia with sedation (a **minimalist** approach) or general anaesthesia with TOE are both used. General anaesthesia suits difficult anatomy, TOE, poor tolerance of lying flat, or anticipated complications; sedation allows quick recovery and early neurological assessment.

## Haemodynamic goals in AS

Preserve preload, sinus rhythm and afterload; avoid hypotension and tachycardia (coronary perfusion falls). Use vasopressors early (phenylephrine or noradrenaline), arterial line, and defibrillator pads.

## Key steps

- **Rapid ventricular pacing at 180 to 220 beats/min** drops the systolic pressure to below 50 mmHg for 5 to 10 seconds during balloon valvuloplasty and valve deployment. Vasopressors should be ready for recovery.
- Valve deployment: watch for coronary occlusion, aortic regurgitation, annular rupture, tamponade.

## Complications

Femoral artery injury (common; open repair under general anaesthesia may be needed), **conduction abnormalities** (heart block needing a permanent pacemaker), coronary artery occlusion, stroke and acute kidney injury. Have a plan for emergency sternotomy and bypass.

## Self-marking checklist

- States roles of the anaesthetist and the benefit of TAVI over surgery
- Describes preoperative preparation and risk assessment
- Compares minimalist sedation with general anaesthesia
- Sets haemodynamic goals for aortic stenosis
- Explains rapid pacing at 180 to 220 and its haemodynamic effect
- Lists the main complications (vascular, heart block, coronary occlusion, stroke)
- Plans for emergency conversion

items.title: 26. Acute pulmonary oedema: cardiogenic versus non-cardiogenic
items.q: Describe the pathophysiology of acute pulmonary oedema and outline how you would distinguish cardiogenic from non-cardiogenic causes and manage each.
items.a:
## Pathophysiology

Starling forces determine fluid filtration across the pulmonary capillary: net flow = Kf x [(Pc - Pi) - sigma x (pi_c - pi_i)]. Oedema develops when **capillary hydrostatic pressure rises**, **oncotic pressure falls**, **permeability increases**, or **lymphatic drainage** is overwhelmed (lymphatic flow can increase about tenfold first). Interstitial oedema (Kerley lines) precedes alveolar flooding. Consequences: reduced compliance, shunt and V/Q mismatch, hypoxaemia, increased work of breathing and sympathetic activation (a vicious circle with raised afterload).

| Mechanism | Examples |
|---|---|
| Raised hydrostatic pressure | LV failure, ischaemia, arrhythmia, valve disease, fluid overload (TACO), renal failure |
| Increased permeability | ARDS, sepsis, aspiration, TRALI, pancreatitis, burns |
| Mixed or other | Negative pressure (laryngospasm), neurogenic, re-expansion, high altitude, opioid or salicylate toxicity |

## Distinguishing features

| Feature | Cardiogenic | Non-cardiogenic |
|---|---|---|
| History | Cardiac disease, hypertension, volume overload | Sepsis, aspiration, transfusion, trauma |
| CXR | Cardiomegaly, vascular redistribution, septal lines, bat-wing, effusions | Normal heart size, peripheral patchy infiltrates |
| BNP | Raised (above 400 pg/mL) | Low to mildly raised |
| Echo | Poor LV function, valve disease, high E/e' | Often normal LV |
| PAOP | Above 18 mmHg | 18 mmHg or less |
| Response to diuretic | Prompt | Poor |

Mixed pictures are common.

## Lung ultrasound

> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2025, "B-lines and beyond: Lung ultrasound for the perioperative clinician" (Kim, Lau).

Lung ultrasound is quick, bedside and has a gentler learning curve than echo. In the BLUE protocol the anterior (upper BLUE point, 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular), lateral (4th intercostal space, anterior axillary line) and PLAPS points are scanned. A-lines with lung sliding are normal; **more than two B-lines per zone, in multiple zones**, indicate interstitial syndrome such as pulmonary oedema. The pattern does not prove a cause (pneumonia and ARDS also cause B-lines), so combine with cardiac echo, history and the clinical context. Use it to guide diuresis and fluid management in unstable patients and to follow response.

## Management

**All causes:** sit upright, high-flow oxygen, monitoring, early CPAP (5 to 10 cmH2O) or NIV, ECG, gas, chest X-ray, lung ultrasound, BNP, troponin, treat the trigger.

**Cardiogenic:** GTN (if SBP above 100), IV loop diuretic, treat ischaemia, arrhythmia or hypertension; inotrope if low output; avoid routine opioids.

**TACO:** stop fluids and diurese. **TRALI:** supportive care, no diuretic, report to the blood service. **Negative pressure oedema:** relieve obstruction, CPAP, usually resolves in 12 to 48 hours. **ARDS:** lung-protective ventilation, conservative fluids, prone position if severe.

**Intubation** for exhaustion or refractory hypoxia, with preoxygenation by CPAP and a vasopressor ready.

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes Starling forces and the mechanisms of oedema formation
- Categorises causes (hydrostatic, permeability, mixed)
- Distinguishes cardiogenic from non-cardiogenic using history, CXR, BNP, echo, response to diuretic
- Gives immediate management common to all (positioning, oxygen, CPAP)
- Gives cause-specific treatment (GTN/diuretic, TACO/TRALI, negative pressure, ARDS)
- Plans intubation precautions
- Uses lung ultrasound (B-lines) with its limits

items.title: 27. Pulmonary oedema during anaesthesia
items.q: Frothy pink fluid appears in the endotracheal tube 40 minutes into a general anaesthetic with falling SpO2. Describe your immediate management and the differential.
items.a:
## 1. Immediate response
- State the problem aloud and call for help. Ask the surgeon to stop or limit surgical stimulation if the patient is unstable.
- Increase FiO2 to 100%, hand-ventilate to assess compliance, listen to the chest, check the capnogram, SpO2 and airway pressures.
- Confirm tube position (depth, kinking, cuff, endobronchial migration, blockage), the circuit and the ventilator. Suction the tube. Disconnect from the ventilator if a circuit problem is suspected.
- Frothy pink sputum in the tube is a hallmark of severe pulmonary oedema, usually with falling compliance, rising airway pressure and desaturation.

## 2. Initial treatment of hypoxia
- Increase PEEP (start at 8 to 10 cmH2O and titrate to oxygenation and haemodynamics), and consider recruitment manoeuvres cautiously because of haemodynamic effects.
- Maintain adequate ventilation (tidal volume 6 to 8 mL/kg PBW, plateau pressure below 30).
- Stop fluids and any irrigation fluid absorption (hysteroscopy, TURP, arthroscopy, laparoscopic surgery with pressure).
- Treat bronchospasm if present.

## 3. Differential diagnosis and how to separate causes
| Cause | Clues | Quick tests |
|---|---|---|
| Cardiogenic (ischaemia, arrhythmia, valve failure, LV failure) | ST change, hypotension, arrhythmia, high filling pressure, known heart disease | ECG with ST analysis, TOE for new RWMA or valve problem, BNP, PAOP |
| Fluid overload or irrigation absorption (TURP syndrome, hysteroscopy) | Volume balance, hyponatraemia, glycine toxicity, visual changes | Sodium, osmolality, fluid balance |
| Negative pressure oedema | Preceding laryngospasm or obstruction, young fit patient | History, airway events |
| Aspiration | Witnessed regurgitation, bronchospasm | Suction, bronchoscopy |
| Anaphylaxis | Hypotension, bronchospasm, flushing, rash | Tryptase, drug exposure |
| Transfusion reaction (TRALI, TACO) | Recent blood products, fever, hypotension | BNP, response to diuresis |
| Pulmonary embolism (air, thrombus, fat, amniotic) | Falling ETCO2, hypotension, RV strain | TOE |
| Pneumothorax | Unilateral signs, high pressures | Ultrasound, decompression |
| Sepsis or ARDS | Fever, source, vasodilation | Cultures, lactate |

## 4. Treatment according to cause
- **Ischaemia or LV failure:** treat as per R5 and R14; GTN if BP allows, diuretic (furosemide 20 to 40 mg IV), inotrope if low output, vasopressors to protect the coronary perfusion pressure, and consider IABP.
- **Arrhythmia:** synchronised cardioversion if unstable, amiodarone for rate control.
- **Hypertension:** GTN, labetalol.
- **Anaphylaxis:** adrenaline 50 to 100 micrograms IV titrated, fluids, stop the trigger.
- **TRALI / TACO:** stop the transfusion, supportive care, diuretic for TACO only.
- **Fluid overload:** stop infusions, diurese; renal replacement if oliguric.
- **NPPE:** PEEP, supportive; resolution within 24 to 48 hours.

## 5. Anaesthetic and surgical management
- Discuss with the surgeon to finish quickly or abandon.
- Maintain anaesthesia with a technique that minimises myocardial depression.
- Place an arterial line, send ABG, and consider TOE.

## 6. Postoperative care
ICU or HDU, ongoing ventilation or CPAP, serial ECG, troponin and echo, review of fluid balance, and communication with the patient and family (open disclosure, if there was an incident). Document the event and report if a transfusion or drug reaction is suspected.

> **Examiner lens:** airway and oxygenation first, then cause-directed therapy.

items.title: 28. Cardiomyopathy classification and anaesthetic implications
items.q: Compare dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive and takotsubo cardiomyopathy in terms of physiology, haemodynamic goals and anaesthetic pitfalls.
items.a:
## 1. Definition and classification
Cardiomyopathy is a disorder of the myocardium with structural and functional abnormality in the absence of coronary disease, hypertension, valve disease or congenital heart disease sufficient to cause the abnormality (ESC 2008; AHA 2006 classify by genetic or acquired causes). Phenotypes: dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive, arrhythmogenic right ventricular, and unclassified (including takotsubo and non-compaction).

## 2. Comparison
| Feature | Dilated (DCM) | Hypertrophic (HCM) | Restrictive (RCM) | Takotsubo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Causes | Idiopathic and genetic (titin), alcohol, viral, peripartum, chemotherapy (anthracycline), tachycardia-induced, iron overload, thyroid disease | Autosomal dominant sarcomere mutation; sometimes Fabry or Friedreich | Amyloid, sarcoid, haemochromatosis, radiation, endomyocardial fibrosis, scleroderma | Emotional or physical stress; catecholamine surge; postmenopausal women; subarachnoid haemorrhage; phaeochromocytoma |
| Haemodynamics | Dilated LV, low EF, high filling pressures, secondary MR, RV failure | Small LV cavity, hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, dynamic LVOT obstruction, MR | Stiff ventricles with small cavity, normal or mildly reduced EF, high filling pressures, fixed stroke volume, atrial enlargement | Apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis, reduced EF (recovers in 4 to 8 weeks), possible LVOT obstruction |
| Echo | Dilated, globally hypokinetic, thin walls | LVH, SAM, asymmetric septal hypertrophy | Thick walls (amyloid sparkling), biatrial dilation, restrictive filling (E/A above 2, short DT) | Apical akinesia and ballooning; no coronary territory pattern |
| ECG | LBBB, AF, ventricular ectopy | LVH, deep Q waves, T wave inversion | Low voltage (amyloid), AF, conduction disease | ST elevation or T wave inversion mimicking MI |
| Risk | Heart failure, arrhythmia, thromboembolism, sudden death | Sudden death (VT/VF), AF, HF, outflow obstruction | Heart failure, AF, thromboembolism | Heart failure, shock, arrhythmia, LVOT obstruction |
| Anaesthetic goals | Treat as HFrEF: maintain preload, afterload low-normal, support contractility, normal heart rate, sinus rhythm; low-dose induction; arterial line, cardiac output monitoring | Full preload, slow heart rate, sinus rhythm, maintain afterload, avoid inotropes and vasodilators (R19) | Maintain preload and heart rate (stroke volume is fixed), avoid bradycardia, vasodilation and tachycardia, treat AF early, avoid negative inotropes | Supportive; inotropes for shock if there is no obstruction, otherwise fluids and beta-blocker; mechanical support if refractory |
| Pitfalls | Sensitivity to induction agents, arrhythmia, LV thrombus, ICD/CRT | Ephedrine, hypovolaemia, tachycardia, high-dose volatile | Amyloid autonomic neuropathy (hypotension), digoxin and calcium channel blockers toxicity, difficult positive pressure ventilation | Catecholamine administration may worsen; recurrence |

## 3. Perioperative principles for all
- Preoperative echo and ECG, review of medications and any ICD or pacemaker (see R21), assessment of functional capacity, and consideration of a high-risk pathway.
- Arterial line before induction; invasive monitoring and TOE when appropriate.
- Anticipate arrhythmia and have pads on; correct potassium and magnesium.
- Anticoagulation in AF or LV thrombus is managed per guidelines.
- Postoperative HDU monitoring.

## 4. Key message
Decide whether the physiology is dilated, obstructed or stiff, then apply the matching goals; the pitfalls arise when a dilated-heart strategy (inotropes, vasodilators) is applied to an obstructed or stiff heart.

> **Examiner lens:** know the one-line physiology and the one key avoidance for each.

items.title: 29. Restrictive cardiomyopathy and amyloidosis
items.q: Compare restrictive and dilated cardiomyopathy and outline the anaesthetic management of a patient with cardiac amyloidosis.
items.a:
## Restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM)

A stiff, non-compliant ventricle with normal or mildly reduced EF, biatrial enlargement and restrictive filling (E/A above 2, short deceleration time, raised filling pressures). Causes: amyloid (AL, transthyretin), sarcoid, haemochromatosis, radiation, endomyocardial fibrosis.

| Feature | Dilated | Restrictive |
|---|---|---|
| Ventricle | Dilated, thin, low EF | Small cavity, normal EF, thick walls (amyloid) |
| Problem | Systolic failure | Diastolic failure; fixed stroke volume |
| Heart rate | Normal to high-normal | Rate-dependent output, avoid bradycardia |
| AF | Poorly tolerated | Very poorly tolerated |
| Preload | Maintain, avoid overload | Narrow window: both hypovolaemia and overload poorly tolerated |

## Cardiac amyloidosis

Amyloid infiltration thickens the walls (low-voltage ECG with thick walls on echo), causes conduction disease and arrhythmia, **autonomic neuropathy** (hypotension), and heart failure. It may be associated with macroglossia, nephrotic syndrome and carpal tunnel. Digoxin and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers bind amyloid fibrils and are avoided. Transthyretin amyloid is increasingly diagnosed in older patients and is treatable (tafamidis).

## Anaesthetic management

- **Assess:** symptoms, echo (wall thickness, strain with apical sparing, diastolic grade), ECG, troponin/BNP, rhythm, autonomic function, renal function, device; consider airway (macroglossia).
- **Goals:** maintain preload and **heart rate** (avoid bradycardia), preserve sinus rhythm (cardiovert AF early), avoid vasodilation and sympathetic block, maintain contractility without tachycardia.
- **Monitoring:** arterial line before induction, cardiac output monitoring or TOE for major surgery, pacing pads.
- **Technique:** titrated induction with etomidate or reduced propofol and opioid, vasopressors (phenylephrine, vasopressin) ready; avoid large neuraxial blocks because of unmasked autonomic dysfunction; low-dose, slowly titrated regional if used.
- **Hypotension:** treat with vasopressor and judicious fluid; avoid ephedrine-induced tachycardia and large boluses.
- **Postoperative:** HDU, analgesia, early mobilisation, anticoagulation decisions.

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes RCM physiology (stiff ventricle, fixed stroke volume, restrictive filling) and compares with dilated cardiomyopathy
- Describes amyloid features: conduction disease, autonomic neuropathy, thick walls
- Avoids digoxin and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
- Haemodynamic goals: preload, heart rate (avoid bradycardia), sinus rhythm, avoid vasodilation
- Technique and monitoring: arterial line, titrated induction, vasopressors, care with neuraxial block
- Postoperative HDU

items.title: 30. HCM: hypotension after induction
items.q: A 40-year-old with HCM becomes profoundly hypotensive after induction of general anaesthesia. Explain the mechanism, your treatment, and why ephedrine is a poor choice.
items.a:
## 1. Background: the physiology of HCM
- HCM is an autosomal dominant sarcomere disorder (MYH7, MYBPC3) with unexplained LV hypertrophy (wall thickness 15 mm or more), a small LV cavity, myocardial disarray, diastolic dysfunction, and microvascular ischaemia. About one-third have resting LVOT obstruction (gradient 30 mmHg or more) and another third have latent obstruction provoked by exercise or Valsalva.
- Dynamic LVOT obstruction arises from systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the anterior mitral valve leaflet, pulled into the outflow tract by the Venturi effect and drag as flow accelerates through a narrowed, abnormally positioned outflow tract. SAM also causes mitral regurgitation (posteriorly directed jet).

## 2. Why the patient is hypotensive after induction
The obstruction worsens with:

- **Reduced preload** (venodilation, fasting, bleeding): the cavity shrinks, bringing the septum and mitral valve closer.
- **Reduced afterload** (vasodilation from propofol or volatile): less pressure to keep the leaflet away from the septum, and a higher flow velocity.
- **Increased contractility** (sympathetic stimulation, inotropes) and **tachycardia** (shorter filling time).

Thus the hypotension from induction (loss of SVR and preload) increases obstruction, lowers stroke volume, and causes a downward spiral of hypotension, ischaemia and tachycardia.

## 3. Management of acute hypotension
- Call for help and confirm the diagnosis (look for other causes of hypotension: bleeding, anaphylaxis, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, arrhythmia, ischaemia, high spinal).
- Give a **pure alpha agonist** (phenylephrine 50 to 100 micrograms boluses, or an infusion; vasopressin 1 to 2 units) to restore SVR and afterload.
- Give a **fluid bolus** (250 to 500 mL crystalloid or colloid) to restore preload; elevate the legs.
- Reduce volatile concentration and treat pain/anaesthesia depth to reduce vasodilation.
- Slow tachycardia with esmolol (0.5 mg/kg then infusion) if BP has been restored; this prolongs diastolic filling and reduces contractility.
- TOE: look for SAM, LVOT gradient, MR, LV cavity size, and RWMA.
- Cardioversion for AF or haemodynamically significant arrhythmia (loss of atrial kick can precipitate collapse).

## 4. Why ephedrine and other inotropes are a poor choice
- Ephedrine has beta-1 effects (positive inotropy and chronotropy), which narrow the LVOT, increase SAM, and shorten diastolic filling.
- Adrenaline, dobutamine, dopamine, isoprenaline, and milrinone have the same effect and may precipitate haemodynamic collapse.
- Nitrates and other vasodilators lower afterload and preload and worsen the gradient.
- Large doses of volatile agents and propofol vasodilate and depress preload.
- Digoxin and other inotropes are also avoided.

## 5. Refractory hypotension
- Escalate vasopressor infusions (phenylephrine, vasopressin, noradrenaline), continue fluid, and use esmolol if tachycardic.
- Consider an arterial line, and check ABG, potassium and calcium.
- If there is still no response, consider VA-ECMO as a bridge (avoid IABP, which can increase obstruction), and call cardiology and ICU.
- CPR in HCM may be ineffective in the presence of obstruction; ensure the patient has pads on and an ICD interrogation plan.

## 6. Prevention
- Assess the risk preoperatively: symptoms, gradient (rest and Valsalva), MR, ICD, family history of sudden cardiac death, drugs (beta-blocker, verapamil, disopyramide, mavacamten).
- Continue beta-blockers, verapamil or disopyramide on the day.
- Avoid prolonged fasting; give IV fluid before induction.
- Insert an arterial line before induction, with a phenylephrine infusion prepared.
- Slow titrated induction with etomidate or reduced propofol and an opioid, avoid ketamine and pancuronium, maintain with volatile or TIVA titrated to avoid vasodilation.
- Neuraxial: slowly titrated epidural may be acceptable; avoid a single-shot spinal.
- ICD management (see R21).

> **Examiner lens:** explain by the dynamic obstruction (Venturi and SAM), not by memory.

items.title: 31. Takotsubo cardiomyopathy after emergence
items.q: Following emergence from anaesthesia a patient has chest pain, ST elevation and hypotension. Coronary angiography is normal and echo shows apical ballooning. Discuss takotsubo cardiomyopathy and your management.
items.a:
## Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy

A transient, reversible LV dysfunction after emotional or physical stress, thought to result from a **catecholamine surge** (myocardial stunning, microvascular dysfunction). It occurs mostly in postmenopausal women and is triggered by surgery, pain, critical illness, subarachnoid haemorrhage, phaeochromocytoma and exogenous catecholamines.

## Presentation and diagnosis

Chest pain, dyspnoea, ST elevation or T-wave inversion, a modest troponin rise, and arrhythmia or shock. **Echo** shows apical akinesia with basal hyperkinesis (the classic pattern; basal, mid-ventricular and focal variants exist) in a territory that does not match a coronary artery. Angiography shows no culprit lesion. Differential: acute MI, myocarditis, PE, perioperative LVOT obstruction. Complications: cardiogenic shock, LVOT obstruction (about 20%) with SAM, MR, arrhythmia, LV thrombus and tamponade.

## Management

- Treat as ACS until angiography excludes coronary disease (cardiology, cath lab).
- **Supportive:** oxygen if hypoxic, monitoring, treat arrhythmia, correct electrolytes.
- **Heart failure:** diuretic, ACE inhibitor/ARB, beta-blocker once stable.
- **Shock:** the choice depends on echo. If **LVOT obstruction** is present, avoid catecholamines and inotropes; give fluids, phenylephrine and a short-acting beta-blocker (esmolol). If there is pump failure without obstruction, use levosimendan or mechanical support (IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO) rather than catecholamines.
- Anticoagulate if LV thrombus.
- Stop or minimise exogenous catecholamines and treat pain and anxiety.

## Prognosis

EF recovers in about 4 to 8 weeks in most; in-hospital mortality is similar to ACS in some series, with a recurrence risk.

## Anaesthetic relevance

Avoid unnecessary catecholamines, treat pain and anxiety, and be alert to the pattern of new LV dysfunction after surgery.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines takotsubo and its catecholamine-driven mechanism and triggers
- Describes diagnosis: apical ballooning with basal hyperkinesis, normal angiography
- Lists complications (shock, LVOT obstruction, arrhythmia, thrombus)
- Initial management as ACS until coronary disease is excluded
- Distinguishes management of LVOT obstruction (avoid inotropes) from pump failure
- Mentions recovery and avoiding catecholamines

items.title: 32. Peripartum cardiomyopathy
items.q: A woman presents 2 weeks postpartum with breathlessness and orthopnoea and is found to have LV systolic dysfunction. Discuss peripartum cardiomyopathy and the anaesthetic considerations for a future delivery.
items.a:
> **BJA Education:** "Anaesthesia and peripartum cardiomyopathy" (BJA Educ 2023).

## Definition

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an **idiopathic cardiomyopathy causing heart failure from LV systolic dysfunction** (EF nearly always below 45%) **towards the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery**, with no other cause. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and occurs in previously healthy women. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of pregnancy-related death in high-income countries.

## Recognition

Symptoms (fatigue, dyspnoea) overlap with normal pregnancy, so diagnosis is delayed. **Measure BNP** in women with orthopnoea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, then ECG and echo.

## Management

- Specialist-centre, **multidisciplinary pregnancy heart team** including the anaesthetist.
- Heart failure treatment adjusted for pregnancy or lactation: diuretics, beta-blocker, vasodilators (hydralazine and nitrate while pregnant; ACE inhibitors after delivery).
- Anticoagulation if EF is very low because of thrombus risk.
- Advanced support (ECLS, VAD) in refractory cases.

## Delivery

- **Vaginal delivery with neuraxial analgesia** where possible. Early, slowly titrated epidural reduces pain, tachycardia and preload and afterload swings.
- Caesarean for obstetric indication or haemodynamic instability; titrated epidural or CSE, or general anaesthesia with invasive monitoring.
- Invasive arterial monitoring in unstable patients; avoid fluid overload; oxytocin by slow infusion.
- Postpartum HDU or ICU.

## Prognosis

Recovery of EF is common, but women are at **increased risk of recurrent heart failure in later pregnancies**, and counselling is needed.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines PPCM with timing, EF below 45% and exclusion of other causes
- Recommends BNP, ECG and echo for suggestive symptoms
- Uses a multidisciplinary heart team
- Prefers vaginal delivery with neuraxial analgesia
- Plans titrated neuraxial or general anaesthesia for caesarean with monitoring
- Notes recurrence risk and need for counselling

items.title: 33. Cardiac implantable devices in the perioperative period
items.q: A patient with cardiomyopathy and an ICD with CRT needs bowel surgery using monopolar diathermy. How do you plan?
items.a:
## 1. Why devices matter
Cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) include pacemakers, ICDs and CRT systems (CRT-P and CRT-D). Electromagnetic interference (EMI) from monopolar diathermy can cause oversensing, which inhibits pacing (and a pacing-dependent patient may become asystolic), triggers inappropriate ICD shocks, or causes electrical reset. Other sources include radiofrequency ablation, MRI, lithotripsy, nerve stimulators and cardioversion. Risk is greatest when diathermy is monopolar, used above the umbilicus, in long bursts, and when the patient is pacing-dependent.

## 2. Preoperative assessment
- **Identify the device:** type (pacemaker, ICD, CRT), manufacturer and model, indication, date of implantation, and whether the patient is pacemaker-dependent (underlying rhythm absent or inadequate; ask about syncope history, and check the ECG for a paced rhythm).
- **Last interrogation:** a pacemaker should have been checked within 12 months, and an ICD or CRT within 6 months. If out of date or the device has been affected by an event, obtain interrogation by the cardiac physiologist before elective surgery. Check battery, lead function, programmed rate, and ICD therapies.
- **Plan with the cardiologist or device clinic:** reprogramming, magnet use, who attends, and where the device will be rechecked.
- **Surgical considerations:** site (above or below the umbilicus), diathermy type, other equipment, positioning, and the need for cardioversion.
- **Cardiomyopathy assessment:** EF, symptoms, arrhythmia history, medication, and renal function.

## 3. Management of interference
| Strategy | Detail |
|---|---|
| Reduce EMI | Use bipolar diathermy or ultrasonic (Harmonic) scalpel; short bursts (under 5 seconds); lowest effective energy; position the return pad so the current path is away from the generator and leads (for abdominal surgery, on the thigh or buttock); keep the cables away from the device |
| Monitoring | Pulse oximetry plethysmography or arterial line to confirm mechanical rhythm (ECG is distorted by diathermy); set ECG pacing spike detection on; keep external pacing and defibrillation pads in position; ensure that a defibrillator is immediately available |
| Pacemaker | If not pacing-dependent and surgery is below the umbilicus, no change is needed. For above-umbilical monopolar diathermy in a pacing-dependent patient, use a magnet (asynchronous pacing in most pacemakers, though not all; confirm in advance) or reprogram to an asynchronous mode (VOO/DOO) |
| ICD | A magnet suspends tachyarrhythmia therapies (does not affect bradycardia pacing). Alternatively, the device clinic programs tachy therapies off. Pads on and an external defibrillator are mandatory while therapies are suspended. Some devices have no magnet response |
| CRT | A magnet does not turn off biventricular pacing; check that there is high-percentage biventricular pacing preoperatively; AF or ventricular ectopy can reduce capture, and rate-adaptive pacing may increase heart rate in response to minute ventilation sensors (disable if needed) |
| Rate-responsive sensors | Minute ventilation sensors can be misled by ventilation or monitor signals; consider disabling |

## 4. If an arrhythmia occurs while the ICD is disabled
Treat as normal: defibrillate or cardiovert using pads, with anterior-posterior position, and keeping them at least 8 to 10 cm from the generator.

## 5. Postoperative management
- Re-enable ICD therapies before the patient leaves a monitored environment (never leave therapies disabled in the ward or at home).
- Re-interrogate if there was monopolar diathermy near the device, cardioversion, defibrillation, CPR, or if the device was reprogrammed; pacemakers should be checked within 1 month in other situations according to local policy.
- Monitor the ECG continuously until the device is checked.

## 6. Management of the underlying cardiomyopathy
Treat as HFrEF (see R10 and R11), continue guideline-directed medications, and use invasive monitoring.

## 7. Documentation and communication
Record the pre- and postoperative device status, the programming changes, the equipment used and the person responsible for restoring therapies; inform the patient.

> **Examiner lens:** never leave an ICD with therapies disabled outside a monitored environment.

items.title: 34. Anaesthesia for right ventricular dysfunction
items.q: Outline the principles of anaesthetic management for a patient with right ventricular dysfunction presenting for non-cardiac surgery, including ventilation and drug strategy.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2021, "Right ventricular failure – when the right heart goes wrong" (Falland, Drummond, Wylie).

## Principle

Perioperative RV failure is usually an "at-risk" RV (raised PVR, mitral or tricuspid disease, congenital or ischaemic heart disease) meeting a precipitant that alters preload, afterload or contractility. The RV tolerates **acute afterload rises poorly**, so lower or avoid rises in afterload; it handles preload well when healthy but a failing RV may need contractile support. Ischaemic RV failure needs oxygen supply and demand optimised.

## Preparation and monitoring

Optimise preoperatively and continue usual medications. High-risk procedures: venous air, CO2, fat or cement embolism, liver transplant, large rapid infusions and laparoscopy. Use an arterial line, consider a central line (CVP trend, inotrope route; limited reliability for volume), **TOE** for RV function and the septum, and a PA catheter only in experienced centres. Keep the patient warm.

## Anaesthetic technique

Any technique suits if haemodynamics are protected. Neuraxial blocks must be introduced slowly. Avoid nitrous oxide and desflurane (raise PVR); volatiles reduce preload and contractility; propofol and thiopentone reduce contractility and SVR but not PVR; ketamine raises PVR in adults (avoid large doses); opioids judiciously. At induction: preoxygenate, gentle bag-mask ventilation, blunt the sympathetic response, full relaxation before laryngoscopy and vasopressors ready.

## Ventilation
